The study of anisotropy in cosmic ray activity within the NOvA scintillator detectors at the surface, located 3.6 meters above ground, has yielded significant insights into ultra-high energy cosmic rays. By examining photosensors at ground level, researchers collected data on cosmic ray anisotropy, specifically its dipole and quadrupole components, within the energy range of 4 to 40 EeV. Notably, the amplitude of the dipole component increased substantially with energy, while the quadrupole amplitude remained relatively constant. In contrast to previous findings, where the dipole component was found to peak around 10 EeV and then stabilize, this study reveals a more gradual growth in amplitude with energy, extending the trend to higher energy levels. Additionally, the detected quadrupole component exhibits an inline orientation across all energy ranges. By taking into account cosmic ray deflection over varying energies and distances, researchers were able to estimate the rigidity cutoff for ultra-high energy cosmic rays at around 20 EeV. Further analysis also confirms that the detected dipole component does not rely on energy loss in dense astrophysical structures such as magnetic fields or shocks and that it cannot be attributed to miniature jets or self-deflection. The findings of this research provide crucial evidence for the ongoing debate on the source of ultra-high energy cosmic rays. The discovered anisotropy patterns serve as essential references for future investigations, specifically relating to point sources, jets, or other astrophysical phenomena. The anisotropy data collected from NOvA scintillator detectors contribute significantly to the understanding of ultra-high energy cosmic rays and their potential sources. Based on the findings, researchers created a model describing the cosmic ray spectrum, which takes into account a magnetic field and a source with a specific energy and spatial distribution. The anisotropy data, specifically the amplitude of the dipole component, served as a key indicator for confirming the parameters of this model. The study demonstrates that simultaneous analysis of cosmic ray energy and spatial distribution can provide comprehensive insights into the properties of ultra-high energy cosmic rays. The discovered relationship between the amplitude of the dipole component and energy reveals a significant increase in anisotropy at energy levels above 4 EeV. The shift towards digital pathology is rapidly gaining momentum, with the main drivers being improved accuracy and efficiency in disease analysis.  The process of digitizing tissue sections enables comprehensive quantification, including quantification of tumor infiltrating lymphocytes, which is a crucial aspect in understanding disease progression and identifying potential new treatment targets in cancer research.  This document aims to provide a thorough overview of the most recent developments and options for performing specific tasks within digital pathology research, with a particular focus on the MIAS database, which is widely recognized as a benchmark for segmentation evaluation in this field.  These tasks include the identification and delimiting of cells, tissues, and individual proteins, as well as the reconstruction of linear structures such as blood vessels and the derivation of three-dimensional information from whole slide images.  This survey is an update to an earlier publication, with significant additions and updates that encompass new methods in the field, including the enhanced training of deep learning models on multiple-class segmentation tasks and the use of three-dimensional learning approaches.  Specifically, this update features novel methods for epithelial and white blood cell segmentation, whole slide classification using multi-scale learning, the application of atrous dilated networks in digital pathology, and efficient inference protocols for a range of popular classifiers.  Furthermore, this document discusses current challenges in digital pathology research and potential future directions, including the development of digital instruments, three-dimensional information recovery, and the enhanced training of deep learning models on digital pathology.  Finally, this document aims to stimulate further research in digital pathology, encourage assessment of novel digital instruments on benchmark datasets, and promote discussion of the potential applications of digital pathology in other imaging modalities.  The document concludes with a summary of the treated topics and a future outlook in the field of digital pathology. We present a method for creating a versatile gaits library on a quadratic robot using reinforcement learning. This approach empowers the robot to generate a range of gaits without relying on predefined models, thereby accommodating diverse ground conditions and speeds. The training process involves learning a universal control policy, which can be utilized to produce gait trajectories in variable situations. To achieve this, we employ an environment model based on a simple mechanical system, which simplifies the training process. The resulting control policy allows the robot to adapt its motion in response to changing grounds with little to no fine-tuning, as demonstrated through experiments involving a real Mini-Cheetah robot. This model presents a potential solution to the gait planning problem in dynamic systems, offering practical implications for robotics applications. Details of the project can be found at https://gait-rl.github.io/. This work was previously presented in our paper at the International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA 2022). Following the conference, we received feedback from multiple authors, which we incorporated into the final version of the paper by addressing their concerns and incorporating their suggestions into the revised content. The main document showcases our method and experimental outcomes, while the supplementary material provides additional information and explicit formulations of the used environment model. Using archival data from the Chandra X-ray Observatory, we examined the medium-term variability of four close-to-center low-luminosity active galaxies (LLLAGNs) at 2-10 keV, and identified variability in three out of four sources. Our study covered a timescale ranging from hundreds of days to several years, and we discovered that hot winds from LLAGNs play a crucial role in the evolution of galaxies. Although LLAGNs emit significantly less energy in the X-ray spectrum compared to their more luminous counterparts, their unique sub-Eddington state allows their X-ray spectrum to efficiently interact with the surrounding medium, propelling gas and influencing the local environment. Our findings of variable LLAGNs, despite their low X-ray luminosity, suggest that their hot winds contribute to feedback, an essential process in galaxy evolution. We look forward to exploring and confirming this phenomenon more deeply through future observations, such as those made possible by the Stern-Gabadenenko X-ray optical telescope. Our research lays the groundwork for a fresh understanding of LLAGNs as potent agents of galaxy evolution, and their potential to alter the local environment through their hot winds. Furthermore, we discover that one of the LLAGNs, NGC 1097, displays rapid variability, indicating an exceptional high-energy output. We conducted an in-depth analysis of Tononzintla 2, a metal-rich galactic globular cluster in the near vicinity of the M82 galaxy. By leveraging the high-resolution spectra obtained from the Magellan-IMACS and the TNG-ADO spectrometers, we generated catalogs of absorption lines for four member stars. These catalogs enabled us to identify iron, calcium, silicon, magnesium, and aluminum abundances, which we further used to estimate the elemental abundance spread and the overall metallicity of the cluster. Through the application of multiple tests, including microlensing, position analysis, and spread measurements using different lines, we determined that Tononzintla 2 exhibits a high metallicity and considerable abundance variation among its elements. A comparison of these results with observations of other high-metallicity clusters in the galaxy revealed similar characteristics, indicating a probable connection between these phenomena. Furthermore, we used photometric data from the Hubble Space Telescope to examine the color-magnitude diagram of Tononzintla 2, which showed a clear hint of multiple populations distinguished by their distinct colors. These findings provided substantial evidence that these clusters originated from multiple galactic mergers involving metal-rich galaxies that merged into the M82 galaxy. Ultimately, we concluded that the rich chemical composition and diverse elemental abundance in Tononzintla 2 and other high-metallicity clusters in the galaxy reflect multiple episodes of galactic formation that predates the M82 galaxy's formation. These clusters may have originated from galaxies that were themselves the product of earlier galactic mergers and were characterized by rapid star formation and extensive elemental abundance in their younger populations. Additionally, we noted a lack of comparable metal-rich galactic globular clusters in the Andromeda galaxy and suggested the possibility of its underobservation or misidentification as a galactic globular cluster. Two-dimensional active nematics are dynamic solutions to the active fluid model, exhibiting fascinating behavior that draws from both active matter and condensate physics. We model these nematics as a two-component active fluid, comprising polar active particles, and study their response to a varying strength of active force applied randomly. The system's dynamics cause the fluid components to fluctuate and fluctuating components to gravitate towards order. Notably, this ordering process diverges from traditional equilibrium behavior, as it's accompanied by a distinct fluctuation-dissipation relationship. Moreover, the relationship between the fluid's orientational order and its fluctuating component follows a non-intuitive, opposite trend. We experimentally verify these observations using a novel 3D printing technique that produces realistic, two-dimensional active nematic surfaces. The results from both our modeling and experimental analyses align seamlessly, underscoring the significance of our findings. Furthermore, we demonstrate the possibility of adjusting the active force to eradicate the fluid's orientational order without disrupting its fluctuating component. In the analysis of hyperspectral images, an unbalanced ratio between normal and abnormal regions often hinders the model's generalizability and detection performance. Traditional methods divide the image into uniform regions, regardless of the distribution of abnormal areas, making it difficult for the model to distinguish between normal and abnormal samples. This paper proposes a dynamic region partition method that adapts to the image's normal and abnormal regions, effectively balancing their ratios. By partitioning the image into simple regions, this method facilitates efficient extraction of accurate feature data. In addition, the paper presents a supervised by unsupervised (SU) model based on a combined approach of supervised and unsupervised learning, proposing an unsupervised feature selection method to alleviate the issues of feature redundancy and multi-collar noise in HSI data. The proposed method successfully partitions regions and selects features, outperforming existing grid-based and feature selection methods in abnormal area detection. The dynamic region partition method exhibits an average detection accuracy of $97.14\%$ and a average F1-score of $0.9570$ for multiple HSI datasets. Additionally, the method successfully eliminates $55.64\%$ of features of reduced importance, on average. The dynamic region partition method can be directly applied to various intensive labor tasks, such as identifying abnormal tissues in mammography, detecting defects in textiles, and identifying unusual shapes in land formation. This approach is applied to multiple programs and a common base model is used to predict program outputs. Instead, our models suggest a possible divide between disk-shaped and spherical galaxy formations, prompting a reevaluation of the established consensus. While the consensus remains unchanged for galaxies with uniform initial conditions, our models reveal a significant difference in the resulting galaxy shapes. Furthermore, the time it takes for a galaxy to form raises concerns about the feasibility of achieving the desired outcomes through collisionless galaxy evolution, especially when multiple dark matter particles are involved. This research presents an innovative method for precisely measuring vertical aerosol optical depth (AOD) using broad-field photometry and a calibrated relationship between Planck's constant and the solar constant. The approach doesn't require absolute photometric calibration since it uses relative measurements, making it suitable for use with uncalibrated photometers. We demonstrate the method's effectiveness with daytime sky images obtained from two observatories located in different latitudes, making use of a modified version of the Lupton method to estimate AOD. The approach allows for daily monitoring of AOD with a standard error of approximately 0.03. This method is simple, economical, and well-suited for use in wide-field astronomy surveys, potentially providing essential data for future AOD monitoring. We estimate that, in ideal conditions, it could yield an AOD measurement error of about 0.03, which is comparable to or even smaller than the error associated with individual spectrophotometric measurements. Given its suitability for wide-field astronomy surveys, this method offers a valuable avenue for contributing to AOD data, potentially helping to mitigate the impact of aerosols on future cosmological signals and the detection of dark energy and neutrinos. We anticipate that multiple wide-field astronomy surveys, such as LSST, Pan-STARRS, SkyMapper, and VLA Survey, among others, will utilize this approach to obtain critical AOD measurements, making this a valuable tool for wide-field astronomical observations, even if the observatories are not specifically designed for aerosol monitoring. As an alternative to spectrophotometry, this method represents a practical and efficient means of monitoring AOD with wide-field photometry, with potential applications in multiple wide-field astronomy surveys, such as the VLA Survey, the DECam Legacy Survey, the Legacy Survey, and the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESIs) photometric redshift measurements. This method can be used on photometers with various band responses, but for photometers with a single band response, such as those employed in the VLA Survey, we employ a universal AOD model to facilitate easy usage. This method can be applied to monitor aerosols over land and sea, offering monitoring possibilities during both day and night, provided that the solar zenith angle remains below a certain threshold, making it suitable for use in areas where human activity is present. The Graphical Lasso (GL) is widely used to obtain inverse covariance estimates represented as sparse graphical models. The inclusion of latent variables in this framework, known as GL-LV, has demonstrated superior performance in certain scenarios. This paper provides a novel convex relaxation for GL-LV, yielding an equivalent convex optimization problem. Building on this relaxation, we introduce a practical algorithm utilizing proximal point iterations, in addition to deriving conditions for convergence within this framework. Through various numerical experiments, the benefits of our method in terms of both estimation accuracy and the sparsity of latent structure are demonstrated. Further, the significance of our approach is highlighted through the estimation of the genetic network of humans, a complex and important dataset characterized by high dimensionality and complex structural patterns. This analysis not only enhances our understanding of the challenges involved in network inference but also highlights the potential of our proposed method in the accurate reconstruction of latent structures and predictive models from large and complex datasets. In particular, the results of our analysis indicate the presence of at least 26 significant genes associated with Spinal Muscular Atrophy (SMA), a debilitating genetic disorder, and an in-depth examination of its critical features, as well as the systematic construction of a composite network that integrates known pathways and links underlying genetic mechanisms to clinical manifestations. This integration enables the derivation of key insights into the etiology and progression of SMA, paving the way for the use of our method in the systematic inference of latent structures and predictive modeling of complex diseases. This research has been accepted for publication in Journal of Machine Learning Research, 2021. Certain results were previously presented at ICLR 2021. Additional information is available at the website: https://proxlv.github.io.

This model is compared with observations of ALMA and Chandra datasets, considering varying amounts of this star's X-ray emission as a fraction of its ultraviolet emission. This comparison yields constraints on the mass accretion rate and the disk's inner radius, obtaining similar results from both radio and X-ray analysis. For a fixed inner radius of 0.1 solar radii, increasing the X-ray to UV ratio from 10^-4 to 10^-3 causes total disk emission to increase by a factor of 2. This leads to increased scattering of X-rays from the star towards the disk, as seen in the observed Chandra spectrum. This is because higher X-ray ratios result in a greater proportion of X-rays being reflected from the star rather than those originating from the inner disk. This is particularly evident at energies below 1.5 keV, where a high X-ray to UV ratio results in a nearly complete absence of direct stellar X-rays in favour of star-reflected X-rays and disk-free-free emission. This is observed in the varying amounts of direct versus reflected X-ray radiation in the observed Chandra spectrum of MWC 297. We developed a method to accurately determine the pitch frequency of a speaker from a single-channel audio recording, even in noisy environments. Comparing our approach to existing methods revealed that it outperforms them in cases with background interference. Additionally, we created a standard deviation metric for calculated pitch frequencies, which enables assessment of speech recording equipment. Using this metric, we analyzed the quality of recorded samples in the TTS-Synthesis dataset and identified poor quality speech recordings, even those with high signal-to-noise ratios, which contain inaccurately calculated pitch frequencies. Furthermore, we discovered that the speaker's language influences the minimum and maximum possible pitch frequency range. Based on these findings, we proposed two quality indicators for speech recordings, which can serve as parameters in speech synthesis models to account for the effects of recording conditions on a speaker's vocal characteristics. We utilized the PITT database to verify that speakers exhibit distinct pitch frequency ranges and that these individual ranges should be determined prior to conducting frequency analysis. Lastly, we examined the impact of age on speech pitch frequency and verified that it is not a variable in determining a speaker's vocal characteristics. This research paves the way for further investigating how age influences speech and vocalization. Additionally, we successfully applied our method to calculate the pitch frequency in a video collection of animal sounds. This was done to determine whether the species in the collection has a distinct pitch frequency range. The results show that some species share similar pitch frequency ranges, which can be used as criteria for categorizing species. Furthermore, we analyzed the length of audio samples in the decker dataset and identified a lack of representation of longer audio samples with a duration of over 30 seconds, which affects accurate calculations of pitch frequencies in that dataset. This research also contributes to reducing the impact of background noise on pitch frequency calculations through our proposed method. The regularized Anderson acceleration method has proven effective in enhancing the robustness of fixed-point block Newton methods, particularly for solving nonlinear algebraic equations. Building upon this success, an alternative approach, denoted as the DWIFOB method, seeks to further improve robustness by incorporating a non-regularized quasi-Newton step. In this research, we introduce an accelerated variant of the DWIFOB method and investigate its robustness using an absolute local excess criterion. By employing a stochastic model and analytical techniques, along with numerical experiments, we evaluate the robustness of the accelerated DWIFOB method and its proximity to the regularized Anderson acceleration method. Notably, our results indicate that the robustness of the accelerated DWIFOB method approaches that of the regularized Anderson acceleration method, with the former even outperforming the latter in certain situations, albeit at a slower rate of convergence. Moreover, the numerical evidence suggests that the robustness of the accelerated DWIFOB method is insensitive to the specific choice of local parameter and is comparable to or better than that of the regularized Anderson acceleration method across a wide range of values. In addition, we find that the robustness of the accelerated DWIFOB method is primarily sensitive to the absolute excess and can be affected by an appropriate initial estimate of the solution. In contrast, the robustness of the regularized Anderson acceleration method is more susceptible to variations in the local parameter and can be vulnerable to minor disturbances. To summarize, the research indicates that the accelerated DWIFOB method offers an appealing solution, combining robustness and a relatively flexible behavior with minimal dependence on the choice of local parameter. Furthermore, the robust properties of DWIFOB provide a promising foundation for the potential extension of this algorithm to solve nonlinear systems and time-dependent partial differential equations. In this context, an interesting area of investigation could involve the application of an accelerated variant of the DWIFOB method to solve mass transport equations. Introducing more neutrino dimensions beyond the standard model's three leads to the inclusion of new neutrino mass parameters that can be set to specific values within the minimal supersymmetric model's range to generate the observed lightest neutrino mass. This setup allows for the determination of viable points for the (Higgs boson mass)-(lightest neutrino mass) plane, with many of these points falling within the preferred range for the Higgs boson mass. Furthermore, we find that including more than three generations of neutrinos expands the model's parameter space while maintaining natural electroweak symmetry breaking. This investigation demonstrates that incorporating additional neutrino dimensions can facilitate developing a theoretically natural model of electroweak symmetry breaking with an easily explainable Higgs boson mass. This study bridges this gap by exploring how program properties influence neural architecture performance, representing a significant contribution within the NAS field. We demonstrate that tailored architectures generated using program properties excel in diverse task sets, whereas randomly designed networks struggle. Additionally, our research shows that certain program properties yield greater improvements over baseline models than others, thereby allowing for the identification of promising search space configurations. These findings can guide search space construction and adaptation, thereby facilitating the design of more focused search spaces, ultimately promoting domain-specific search that goes beyond the general applicability of evolutionary approaches, but rather tailors the search space to the distinctive characteristics of the target program domain. In our research, Compressed Federated Distillation was found to yield better model accuracy compared to Federated Averaging and equal accuracy to Federated Distillation, while also achieving significant compression ratios with minimal energy consumption costs. By facilitating the integration of data compression and Federated Distillation, Compressed Federated Distillation provides a streamlined solution for industry practitioners seeking to optimize communication efficiency. Our findings are available in the repository https://github.com/qsong/CFD. Specifically, our research demonstrates that CFD can attain x16 compression with merely a 1% accuracy drop, surpassing the capabilities of both Federated Distillation and Federated Averaging. Moreover, CFD was found to deliver compact models comparable in accuracy to state-of-the-art Federated Distillation methods and even surpassing some compression techniques. Our empirical research was conducted across three datasets and four models, showcasing CFD's general applicability and versatility. Furthermore, an in-depth analysis of CFD's resilience to data poisoning and fair partitioning was performed, in addition to an examination of its compatibility with Federated Averaging and other advanced techniques such as Federated Semi-Supervised Learning and Super Vector Machine. These studies highlight the extensive potential uses for Compressed Federated Distillation. In conclusion, our research indicates that Compressed Federated Distillation offers an efficient, precise, and reliable solution for communication efficiency, presenting various avenues for future research on its optimization and the efficient collaborative training of deep neural networks. Our research also prompts several promising research directions for the further development of Compressed Federated Distillation. Lastly, our research indicates the Compressed Federated Distillation has vast implications and will likely influence the development of future research in the field. Recurrent neural networks are prevalent in models of sequence-based data and task-oriented reinforcement learning, but their variability makes them difficult to interpret. By applying a framework that summarizes the behavior of a model using its future predictions, we aim to reduce uncertainty and facilitate understanding. Utilizing only the trained model, we generate a compact representation of its future behavior for a given input sequence. Through counterfactual reasoning, we demonstrate that this representation, known as a behavioral idiom, identifies key variables influencing the model's outcome. Our method identifies the underlying rules governing a simple reinforcement learning task and predicts the results of subsequent actions in a more complex navigation challenge. Importantly, our approach does not require labeled data, yielding an accurate summary of the model's behavior after training. The value of this representation lies in efficiently guiding the development of more effective reinforcement learning algorithms by specifying action conditions and outcome targets. In essence, it serves as a compact, actionable model of the model itself. Based on this understanding, we propose a novel reinforcement learning algorithm using the behavioral idiom to constrain a maximum-entropy model. The empirical results show that our method performs comparably to existing techniques. The code for the model can be found at https://github.com/alexrame/behavioral-idioms. We examine a two-dimensional herringbone lattice, which exhibits properties of both topological insulators and Weyl semimetals. These characteristics can be altered through the application of specific perturbations to the Hamiltonian. Our research utilizes a real-space lattice formulation, allowing for precise calculations of physical properties such as the bulk band structure, interface electronic behavior, and quantized transport phenomena. Particular emphasis is placed on the topological nature of the system, which depends on the type and strength of the perturbation applied. Specifically, we investigate how the lattice geometry influences the electronic band structure near the Fermi level and demonstrate that certain perturbations lead to the disappearance of the Weyl point and the emergence of a Dirac node. Our work also explores the associated electronic and transport properties, including the quantized orbital magnetization and the relationship between a magnetic field and the Hamiltonian. Our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of systems exhibiting both topological and electronic matter behaviors. Furthermore, we outline the potential for adapting our real-space model into a continuum framework, which could facilitate the simulation of related systems through effective field theory. Such an approach could enable the simulation of systems where the wavelength of the electron is comparable to the lattice spacing. Additionally, we identify and discuss potential challenges and limitations of this continuum approximation. Lastly, we outline the prospects for using the real-space model to investigate and understand various phenomena associated with the interaction of topological insulators and electronic wave-like behaviors. Such phenomena may provide valuable insights into the underlying mechanisms of quantum systems. Conversely, the study of these phenomena may also lead to a deeper understanding of the properties of topological insulators and electronic matter. Furthermore, the knowledge gained from these studies may be applied to the development of novel technologies based on the properties of topological insulators and electronic matter. Replay-based algorithms excel in risk-sensitive reinforcement learning, but their performance often relies on high-quality data storage.
In situations where data quality is questionable, their effectiveness wanes.
The rapid growth in demand for online reinforcement learning in areas such as computer vision and the world at large necessitates online reward learning algorithms that can adapt continuously in dynamic environments.
However, current algorithms with reward resetting capabilities are limited, failing to generalize across scenarios and often requiring expert knowledge to function smoothly.
The proposed algorithm, \textit{CRLB}, incorporates elements from both the most advanced replay-based algorithms and risk-sensitive Markov decision processes, enabling it to adapt online in scenarios with changing environments and reward structures.
Our experiments demonstrate the superior performance of \textit{CRLB} in scenarios with occasional or continuous reward resetting and its capacity to surpass the performance of its offline and risk-averse counterparts in bandit problems and a virtual robotic swing-up task. 
The code to implement \textit{CRLB} can be found on GitHub at https://github.com/alevaa/CRLB.

In the context of distributed machine learning, a novel approach to aggregation is provided through the weighted power-p mean (WPM) function. This method incorporates non-linear weights based on the local mini-batch size, contrasting with traditional linear aggregation techniques. A fundamental aspect of deep learning frameworks, the WPM aggregation acts as a parameterized non-linear operator taking the argument vector and scaling factor as inputs. Its dimensionality is equal to the number of data points in the aggregate, obtained via numerical resolution of a specific matrix game that applies to all p values, with p=2 yielding the standard arithmetic mean. When p is not equal to two, the WPM's construction relies on the exponential transformation of the WPM with p=2. It is shown that the latter serves as a nonlinear, contractive map, meeting the requirements of an \alpha-monooperaor. The WPM's optimal properties when p is greater than or equal to one are demonstrated, along with its analytical differentiability, essential for its integration into various algorithms, including stochastic gradient descent. Experimental results showcase the efficacy of the WPM in boosting the training efficiency of neural networks, particularly when p equals 1.5. The accompanying code can be found at https://github.com/magali-lp/wpm_aggregation. A video presentation is available at https://www.youtube.com/watch?al=3.2.10.100000. A basic conceptual design is presented for an advanced ion trap that utilizes a unique combination of the Mono-Mode Ion Trap (MMIT) and a Paul Trap (PT), enabling the simultaneous capture of a single atom and electromagnetic waves captured from the surrounding environment. This innovative device has the potential to play a crucial role in quantum technology applications that rely on single atoms, particularly in contexts where electrical stability is paramount, such as quantum networks and single-photon generation. Key benefits of this design include its capacity for unparalleled electromagnetic field manipulation and the ability to enhance susceptibility of the ion to this field by several orders of magnitude, thereby minimizing unwanted ion motion while efficiently extracting and generating electromagnetic waves at the trap's axis. Preliminary experiments have demonstrated the efficacy of this approach in the context of $\ {}^{40}$Ca$^+$, and simulations for $\ {}^{9}$Be$^+$ and $^{}$Yb$^+$ show great promise for its future application and extension to other optical ion species. The worldwide shortage of medical ventilators forces healthcare workers to use alternative methods of providing patients with life-sustaining oxygen by manually operating a ventilator or utilizing a shared device with adjustable airflow. To address the latter issue, we have developed an open-source, web-based solution allowing healthcare professionals to assign individual tidal volumes to each patient using a single ventilator. Leveraging a load cell to measure torque, our system accurately determines the patient's resistance to airflow and adjusts the ventilator's plunger position to provide the desired tidal volume. Moreover, our method includes an optional feature to monitor and report any abnormal patient responses to ventilation, such as obstructive or protective airway responses. To facilitate the integration of our solution with existing ventilation equipment, we employed a general-purpose Arduino board to control the interaction between the user input, ventilation function, and a database storage. Our system's effectiveness in accurately supplying patients with their required tidal volumes was confirmed through a series of tests conducted in collaboration with healthcare professionals. These experiments yielded a mean absolute error of 25.6 ml, corresponding to 0.96% of the total tidal volume, and demonstrated the feasibility of our system in detecting patient responses to ventilation within 15 seconds. Our open-source code and hardware designs can be freely accessed on GitHub at the specified URLs for the sake of reproducing and validating our results. Nonetheless, before using our guidance in any clinical setting, we urge potential users to consult their local healthcare authorities and obtain necessary ethical approvals. Additionally, while our work primarily targets settings struggling with ventilator shortages, the design presented herein holds potential for enhancing respiratory care through enhanced user input options. Our aim is to contribute to improved patient outcomes by facilitating the provision of precise and customized respiratory support. Lastly, the concept of collaborative ventilation could serve as an innovative solution for delivering non-invasive respiratory therapy in various clinical settings. \par Overall, our objective is to aid in effectively delivering respiratory therapy using alternative methods while minimizing risks to patients, and to harness technology to enhance clinical judgment and improve patient outcomes. To achieve this goal, we seek to collaborate with healthcare professionals in conducting further research focused on the following key issues: Firstly, we aim to refine our system's ability to detect patient responses to ventilation, including identifying common patterns and their associated time frames. Secondly, we seek to explore the potential for utilizing our load cell in weighing patient weights, which could aid in detecting conditions such as obesity that may require adjusted ventilator settings. Thirdly, we intend to investigate the feasibility of integrating our system with existing mobile health platforms

The work of the CLNS Collaboration at CESR is noted for its thorough $\eta$-$\eta'$ mixing analysis, which also takes into account Amyo and Savvidis' ideas from a 2007 paper. This mixing analysis is a component of the broader program aimed at comprehending hadronic properties, particularly in light of the findings from Amyo and Savvidis' work on the hadronic contributions of the vacuum gluon loop in the $\eta$ and $\eta'$ masses. This program includes numerous analyses conducted by the CLNS Collaboration over two decades, focusing on the hadronic matrix elements of the QCD operator $Q_{PQ}$, as well as $\eta$-$\eta'$ mixing in terms of the quark masses and flux tube parameters of the $\eta$ and $\eta'$ particles. This program's findings have significant implications for the understanding of the hadronic system, particularly in light of the Amyo and Savvidis discovery that the anomalous $\eta$ and $\eta'$ decays may be attributed to an energy scale $Lambda \approx 0.86$ GeV, which aligns with the energy scale obtained from the $\eta$-$\eta'$ mixing analysis. This program's findings have also addressed the question of whether the $\eta$ and $\eta'$ masses are a consequence of the quark masses or, alternatively, the energy scale $Lambda$. This program's findings suggest that the mass generated by the energy scale $Lambda$ dominates the $\eta$ and $\eta'$ masses, whereas the quark masses play a subordinate role. This discovery has far-reaching consequences for our comprehension of the hadronic system, particularly in light of the fact that the Amyo and Savvidis discovery challenges the conventional understanding of the hadronic contributions to the $\eta$ and $\eta'$ masses based on the quark masses. This program's findings also shed light on the concept of "accidental symmetry" in the hadronic system, as well as the "accidental degeneracy" of the $\eta$ and $\eta'$ masses, which may in turn be an "accidental consequence" of a more profound symmetry at an energy scale higher than $Lambda$. This program's findings are thus an important contribution to the comprehension of the hadronic system, particularly in light of the fact that the $\eta$ and $\eta'$ decay modes present a challenge to the conventional understanding of the hadronic contributions to the $\eta$ and $\eta'$ masses based on the quark masses. In various disciplines including forensics, biometrics, and cryptography, distinctive signatures are employed for verification, identification, or security purposes. A crucial aspect of these applications is the use of non-tamperable digital containers, known as signature templates, which are generated through a secure protocol using a claimant's unique characteristics. The effectiveness of a forgery detection system relies heavily on the distinctiveness, complexity, and repeatability of these templates. This research proposes a novel, randomized template construction method termed "Multi-Axis Randomized Template Construction" (MARTC), which generates individualized templates for each claimant across various domains. MARTC integrates randomization at both the feature and template levels to produce non-rerepeatable patterns, thus enhancing forgery detection capabilities. The proposed method is domain-agnostic, meaning it can be applied to different applications without modification, and its adaptability is showcased across three distinct domains: image, text, and audio. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of MARTC over existing state-of-the-art randomized template construction methods in terms of distinctiveness, complexity, and repeatability. Additionally, MARTC exhibits enhanced resistance to manipulation and spoofing attacks in forensics and biometrics, respectively. This research paves the way for a standardized, reliable, and efficient forgery detection system across various domains that can be seamlessly integrated into existing systems. The implemented MARTC protocol is now available online at a dedicated repository. All technical details discussed in this research can be accessed at: https://ncspace.ncsu.edu/MARTC. We propose exploring the possibility of a multi-temperature universe, where the initially single source of heat leads to distinct temperatures for dark matter and baryonic matter. This hypothesis subverts the standard understanding of the dark matter relic abundance calculation, requiring a reevaluation of the allowed dark matter-proton cross sections over various scales, from neutron-star mergers to galactic collisions. By examining the initial epoch of baryon-antibaryon annihilation and the subsequent equation-of-state of the relativistic particles, we demonstrate that a multi-temperature universe can yield higher dark matter-proton cross sections relative to the standard model. This possibility presents an exciting area of research, offering a framework that may eventually lead to a more accurate and consistent understanding of particle physics and cosmology. In particular, it offers a potential explanation for the observed discrepancy between dark matter-nucleon scattering experiments and cosmic microwave background measurements. In addition, it may provide a missing link in the baryogenesis process. Lastly, it is plausible that multi-temperature universes could give rise to novel astrophysical signatures associated with dark matter, such as the emission of big fires following dark matter captures in compact objects, or the generation of gravitational waves resulting from dark matter interactions, thereby offering unique avenues for astrophysical experimentation. A deeper, more comprehensive understanding of this hypothesis will necessitate cross-disciplinary analysis, integrating particle physics, cosmology, astrophysics, and experimentation. As such, it is anticipated that multi-temperature universes will serve as an innovative template, facilitating future breakthroughs in our understanding of the universe. The task of colorizing grayscale images by predicting their full-color counterparts is referred to as image super-resolution. In this research, we tackle a more versatile challenge by developing an end-to-end approach for super-resolution that can utilize any paired dataset. Our innovative multi-layered reinforcement learning framework enhances the recall of a base model, showing superior adaptability on a range of datasets and scenarios, particularly in situations involving limited training data, diverse domain transformations, and the reconstruction of images from watercolor, sketches, and abstract art. Additionally, we release the first public dataset comprising watercolor images, which serves as a benchmark for evaluating recent deep learning methods. With the emergence of three top-1 validated benchmark results on the task of transforming sketches to photos, our method showcases significant advancements: it surpasses the performance of the top pre-trained model by a substantial margin of 8.6% and sets a new benchmark, achieving 66.6% compared to the current best-known benchmark of 58.0%. Furthermore, our method successfully applies the learned state and action policies to the generation of watercolor and oil paintings, yielding results that receive high ratings in aesthetic quality. Our project, along with the associated code, dataset, and learned policy configurations, is publicly available for download at https://github.com/visual-learnrl/Visual-LearnRL. Additionally, 1080p high-quality results for the provided dataset and benchmark challenges are available for viewing at https://sceweb.usc.edu/~jzhang21. A significant number of collaborative coding projects rely on shared files, 
managed jointly through various versions of files across different repositories.
Despite this crucial function, maintenance practices for shared files across 
different repositories are largely understudied, particularly in environments 
supporting collaborative work. To bridge this knowledge gap, our study aimed 
to investigate developers' workflows related to maintaining shared files 
across different repositories in collaborative projects, with a focus on GitHub.
Through a combination of research methods, including an empirical study and a 
qualitative analysis of interviews with GitHub users, our results show that 
developers employ two primary approaches to maintaining shared files: synchronous 
repository management, where updates are synchronized across multiple repositories,
and asynchronous management, where changes are manually synced between files and 
repositories. Furthermore, we examined practitioners' recommendations for 
improving the detection and maintenance of shared files across different repositories.
From a practitioner's perspective, we hope this research will contribute to 
developing more effective tools to support collaborative projects by shedding 
light on the diverse approaches to maintaining shared files across different repositories. 
Also, we provide an overview of current tools to handle shared files and their 
limits, as identified through our research. Based on our findings, we propose a new 
tool concept called SFTP, designed to support collaborative projects by 
identifying and synchronizing shared files across different repositories. Finally, 
we highlight promising areas of research for further investigation in this 
domain. Overall, we hope this research will contribute to creating innovative 
tools to enhance collaborative software development, as well as conducting 
extensive qualitative studies on developers' practices. By studying programmers' 
behavior, we hope to understand how different approaches to maintaining shared files 
can impact developers' productivity and project outcomes over time. With this 
knowledge, we can design and implement effective tools to support collaborative 
projects, as well as uncover valuable insights to guide tool development in 
software development domains utilizing file versions. From a theoretical perspective, 
this research can contribute to our understanding of how shared files influence 
software development, as well as explore the practical implications of 
research findings on software tool development. By investigating researchers' and 
practitioners' approaches to maintaining shared files, we hope to uncover 
opportunities for developing innovative tools to streamline collaborative tasks 
and to explore the practical significance of these findings for tool development. 
Additionally, we hope this research will contribute to software tool development 
focused on collaborative projects involving shared files and to understanding

BD And, a binary star system in the constellation Andromeda, has been studied for over a century, with researchers initially identifying it as a binary system that orbits around a central point.  However, in 2018, astronomers discovered that the orbital patterns of its primary components do not match the data collected by the TESS space telescope, leading them to speculate the presence of a third star in the system.  In this research, we examined the data from the activity patterns of BD And and discovered that the evidence supports the theory of a triennial system, with our analysis suggesting that the outer orbit takes approximately 21 days.  This discovery aligns with the data collected by the TESS space telescope.  Further analysis revealed that the stars in the inner orbit are extremely close together, with their average distance apart estimated at approximately 0.15 million kilometers, or about 3.6 times the diameter of the Earth.  This extremely close proximity makes it likely that the stars in the inner orbit have already merged into a single star, with our observations suggesting that the evidence points to this being the case.  This discovery makes BD And an important system to study in the field of astrophysics, particularly in the areas of close binary stars and stellar activity, as well as the means by which binary stars can interact with each other.  Finally, our research suggests that the evidence points to BD And being an equal-binary system rather than a skirt binary star system. Additionally, it was demonstrated that the Yamabe flow is asymptotic to either constant positive or negative solutions under certain initial conditions. A specific rotationally symmetric metric was identified, which is an isometric invariant for the flow and provides a rescaling invariant condition for estimating the solutions' behavior. A method was developed to estimate the solutions' behavior without relying on the maximum principle or certain other tools. To enhance user preference learning in a manner beneficial to all users, we focus on increasing diversity within individual user preferences. Our method addresses this challenge by designing a new module, called Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE), for modern pre-trained models. GAPE acts as an intermediate layer between the pre-trained model and the preference predictor, where it selectively boosts the aspects of a given item that the user demonstrates preference for. GAPE's operation can be viewed as a nonlinear transformation, where the weights and shift values are adaptively calculated through hidden vector projections. The GAPE module seamlessly integrates with pre-trained models to enhance diversity in recommendations. Experimental results on a real-world dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed model. The accompanying code is available on GitHub at: https://github.com/Argkri/GAPE/tree/main. To determine the number of partitions of an integer $N$ that contain no fives as prime factors and have a specific number of threes, we first derive a generating function for a less restrictive set of partitions. Then, by dividing this generating function for the unrestricted set with fives excluded from the prime factors by its counterpart for the unrestricted set with no threes, we obtain the generating function for the desired restricted partition set. Employing standard techniques for generating functions allows us to identify a recursive relationship for the count of these special partitions, as well as an explicit formula using a combinatorial interpretation. We have investigated the effective interactions within charge-doped sites of disordered semiconductors, specifically Si:P and Te-doped CdTe, using cell-models accounting for neighboring ions. The calculation of real-space interactions between nearest neighbor sites, utilizing density functional theory, reveals significant orbital overlap. In silicon with a phosphorus impurity, the effective interactions at the P site exhibit a local moment characteristic, comparable to transition metals, resulting from sp3 orbital overlap on neighboring ions. The computational results show that P's effective interaction with its four nearest neighbor Si atoms is highly variable, with the two Si atoms positioned diagonally across the tetrahedron exhibiting the most significant coupling. A similar local moment behavior is present in Te-doped CdTe, specifically appearing at the Te ion when coupled with its four nearest neighbor Cd ions. The strength of the Te-Cd interactions varies significantly to boot. These findings are relevant to understanding the unconventional magnetic behavior observed in charge-doped semiconductors, specifically Si and Te-doped CdTe, where the presence of magnetic phenomena is widely observed. The research shows that Te-doped CdTe exhibits a wider range of variability in the sum of Te-Cd interactions compared to Si:P, consistent with experimental observations of higher magnetic ordering temperatures in Te-doped CdTe. The research concludes that the magnetic properties observed in charge-doped semiconductors can be attributed to the significant orbital overlap between the doped charge and neighboring ions, resulting in local moments. Furthermore, the research indicates that a detailed understanding of the interactions at a cellular level is necessary to grasp the underlying mechanics of the observed magnetic properties. The research also raises questions about the underlying mechanics of the observed magnetic properties in pure silicon, stating that the absence of magnetic phenomena indicates a lack of the necessary cellular orbital overlap configuration necessary to support local moments. Similarly, the research notes that the absence of magnetic phenomena in Te-doped CdTe's paramagnetic state indicates that the cellular orbital overlap configuration necessary to support local moments is dynamically accessible only when the temperature is high enough to overcome the energy barrier. Lastly, the research notes that the availability of suitable experimental techniques to measure the interactions between the doping ion and neighboring ions, resulting in a magnetic effect, is necessary for confirming the theoretical prediction of the underlying mechanics of the observed magnetic properties in Te-doped CdTe. The research suggests the use of RES, where the doping ion and surrounding ions are excited simultaneously using a laser, to measure the interactions between the doping ion and neighboring ions, resulting in a magnetic effect.

To achieve practical applications of robot learning in real-world settings, the limitations of available data must be addressed. The constraints are further exacerbated by the complexities of sensory information and inherent confounding factors. We present a hierarchical Bayesian model that accounts for unobserved confounding elements in a context where some features can be hidden from view. The model utilizes a shrinkage strategy to estimate weights, thereby mitigating the negative effects of confounding on prediction performance. Through theoretical analysis and experimental evaluation, we demonstrate that our approach surpasses a standard Lasso regression method in terms of both theoretical and experimental results. The proposed solution has the added benefit of facilitating fast online learning in scenarios involving streaming data. Furthermore, the model is scalable and can be applied to a range of robot tasks, including noise reduction, category learning, and individual object recognition. The feasibility of our method is verified through online prediction experiments using a Wyrobis robot, where it is used to select the best visible view for object recognition. The success of these experiments validates the model as a suitable model for robot learning in real-world settings. We propose a novel framework for end-to-end control through motion planning.
We recognize that a key limitation of deep reinforcement learning is the rapid
decrease in performance after training of a policy model, often referred to as
retraining fatigue. To address this issue, we have developed a multi-stage
motion planning approach, beginning with a initial plan, followed by a sequence
of decision-making steps guided by the policy model. In contrast to traditional
motion planning methods, our approach is knowledge-free and incorporates the
policy model in a way that optimizes overall trajectory cost. We have applied
this new approach to solving complex driving tasks, such as lane-keeping and
intersection management, and the results show significant reductions in
trajectory variability and retraining frequencies by up to two-fold and
suspended retraining cases respectively, without compromising performance. Our
approach is efficient with only a training time of about 20 minutes compared to
other models. Moreover, we have observed that our method often produces better
results and a significant amount of variability reduction at test time by
incorporating an optimal control step. The framework's source code is available at
https://github.com/strivesmc/mmc. A video showcasing our approach is available
at https://youtu.be/6iz2lD_T5Yg. \textbf{What's paper title?} A novel motion

reinforcement learning achieves a significant improvement in driving scenarios such
as lane-keeping and intersection management with reduced trajectory

respectively without performance compromise. The training time is about two-fold
faster. Moreover, an optimal control step significantly improves outcome at

Deep neural networks have exhibited exceptional performance in various classification tasks, but a major limitation affects their reliability - they often produce false alarms from marginally certain predictions. Leveraging the concept of uncertainty quantification, we aim to enhance classification outcomes by effectively utilizing unsureness levels. Specifically, we integrate Bayesian uncertainty estimation and utility functions to develop a decision-making framework that dynamically adjusts confidence thresholds. By applying this approach to the ResNet model on the MNIST dataset, we observed a substantial reduction in base rate false positives, resulting in an impressive 93% improvement. Moreover, we achieved substantial gains in classification accuracy after implementing the uncertainty-based decision procedure, particularly in low-data scenarios. Notably, this method yielded state-of-the-art results on MNIST with a model trained on merely 10% of the standard dataset, hosting model code available at https://github.com/amanbasu/BayesDecisions. In essence, this uncertainty-based decision framework enables the wise distribution of our limited resources - time, money, and computing power - by strategically balancing deep learning model complexity and environmental interactions. The current implementation renders a contingent, uncertain decision that may be described as 'often right, sometimes wrong'. In the long run, our goal is to perfect this approach to 'always right, occasionally uncertain'. Ultimately, this methodology serves as an example of the potential applications of uncertainty estimation, especially in situations where the cost of misclassification differs drastically. It is also one of the several ways to leverage the power of uncertainty in decision-making within deep learning. The other instances include uncertainty-based data selection, reinforcement learning, and resource allocation based on uncertainty. For a comprehensive review of this subject, please refer to Section 2.3. Additionally, the code for the project can be found at https://github.com/amanbasu/BayesDecisions. In the near future, we intend to expand our research by exploring various other methods for utilizing uncertainty in decision-making, such as the variational inference approach. In the short term, we aim to extend the applicability of our approach to more intricate datasets, like those found in the field of medicine, by collaborating with relevant healthcare professionals. In the long term, we aspire to develop an end-to-end framework for decision-making that integrates the decision procedure with the learning process, much like the concept of meta-learning. For an in-depth understanding of the underlying theory and our approach, please refer to Section 2 and the accompanying figures and diagrams. Graph neural networks have significant implications in various tasks related to dimensionality reduction, including both traditional methods and deep learning approaches. These algorithms utilize graph structures to organize data points and facilitate efficient dimensionality reduction. Inspired by the success of graph neural networks in self-supervised learning tasks, researchers have adapted and applied them in multiple other domains. However, the application of graph neural networks in subspace learning algorithms has been limited until recently. This study aims to address this gap by introducing an unsupervised graph neural network for subspace learning algorithms called graph neural network-based orthogonal Procrustes algorithm (GNO-Proc). GNO-Proc leverages a graph neural network to create a compact, interpretable subspace that closely mimics the true subspace, resulting in superior performance compared to existing benchmarks. Furthermore, the study showcases the potential of graph neural networks in traditional algorithms, highlighting their vast application possibilities. The associated code can be found on the GitHub repository https://github.com/agrija9/GNO-Proc. The experimental results mentioned in this study were produced using the PyTorch framework (L Ardila et al., 2020) and the NetworkX library (M Newman and Aitziora, 2006). In this research, we address the completeness problem of Sidon sets in the finite affine plane of order n, and extend a result from $\mathbb{F}_p$ to the general case. A Sidon set is defined as a subset of vectors in the affine plane such that the sum of any two distinct vectors from this subset is a non-zero, uniquely determinable element of the field $\mathbb{F}_n$. The completeness problem concerns identifying necessary and sufficient conditions for a set to be a Sidon subset of the affine plane. Building on prior work by Pahlevan Shahriar and Shokri, we establish that for hyperbolas or ellipses, the condition of not containing parallel elements is both necessary and sufficient for a Sidon subset. We extend this result to include quadratics and sextics, and provide examples of Sidon subsets in these cases. Furthermore, we present a criterion for determining whether a complete set of sextics exists in the affine plane of order n. The research also yields insights into the maximum size of Sidon subsets consisting of polynomials of the same degree. The results generalize to the infinite affine plane of type (m,m+1), and specifically to the case of m=2, by providing a maximum size of 16 for Sidon subsets in elliptic curves over fields of prime order. The research also establishes a maximum size of 8 for Sidon subsets in conic sections over such fields, and provides examples to verify these findings. The results further generalize to the projective plane of order n, by considering sets of reduced degree. The theorems presented hold for an infinite range of n values, and are applicable to orders n of the form p^k, where p is a prime number and k is a positive integer. The results also hold for infinite ranges of p values. The research is made more transparent by the use of von Neumann's complementation theory, by expressing Sidon sets as complements of intersecting hyperplanes in the affine plane. The theory allows for a precise calculation of the maximum size of Sidon subsets, by determining the maximum number of hyperplanes through which a point in the affine plane can pass. Starting point analysis involves determining the smallest number of rows in a binary matrix that can ensure all columns have non-zero entries when sampled randomly. This problem has been well-studied for uniformly distributed samples, but less is known for non-uniform distributions. This research explores non-uniform sampling of binary matrices, presenting an algorithm thataccommodates a broader range of distributions and offering comparative findings. Moreover, the paper introduces a new parameter, the expected sample size, which serves as a criterion for measuring how effective a distribution is for solving this problem. It proposes an efficient method for determining the optimal row sampling order and shows that the expected sample size can be calculated efficiently using a dynamic programming approach. In addition, the study provides simulations to illustrate the performance of different distributions in binary compression. Ultimately, the paper demonstrates that a specific non-uniform distribution can yield significant improvements over uniform sampling in certain scenarios. For example, it requires, on average, at most $n/\log n$ fewer samples from the non-uniform distribution than the uniform distribution, with the ratio potentially as low as $1.04$ even when $n$ is very large. As a consequence, the non-uniform approach can be substantially faster than uniform sampling. Additionally, the paper offers another algorithm for solving an approximate version of the starting point analysis problem by providing specific row completions that can efficiently cover many columns. This approach yields efficient samples for these row completions and ensures that at least $1-\delta$ of the columns can be covered with an error rate of at most $\delta$. Furthermore, the paper provides a new method for determining the optimal sample size in a previous greedy algorithm called Sublinear-SP. This approach yields an almost linear time sample size reduction at the cost of a slightly higher $\delta$ value. Furthermore, the paper presents a new greedy algorithm called Non-Uniform-SP for the approximate problem, employing an adaptive row completion strategy that offers superior row completion rates and a reduced number of adaptive samples. We demonstrate that any instance of Baum's conjecture can be resolved by a specific type of group, namely those with a characteristic random subgroup exhibiting weak mixing and faithfulness properties. This speculative outcome arises from a probabilistic framework developed for measuring the rigidity of measure-preserving systems, specifically systems with almost periodic components. The framework involves a novel notion of subshift, which we refer to as APSP, characterized by almost periodicity, weak mixing, and faithfulness, used to identify a system that proves Baum's conjecture. Notably, the APSP system can be shown to have a continuous action that is both ergodic and faithful, providing additional context for Baum's original question. Furthermore, the specified system shares a key characteristic with the Dueren system, described by Host and Kra, in that both systems possess a strong van der Waerden property. Lastly, by shifting our focus to continuous systems, we obtain an alternative proof of the continuous version of Baum's conjecture. Additionally, we show that any system exhibiting the continuous strong van der Waerden property must contain a continuous system with a linear almost periodic component, which can then be used to establish an equivalence between two distinct almost periodicity notions. Ultimately, these findings lead us to conclude that the continuous strong van der Waerden property is, in fact, equivalent to the existence of a linear almost periodic component. The outcomes of this research not only resolve Baum's conjecture but also yield multiple other significant results. The principal ideas underlying this research are a generalized Furstenberg almost periodic theory, a probabilistic framework for rigidity, and a focus on continuous systems, which provide valuable insights into the interplay between almost periodicity, weak mixing, and faithfulness within these systems. The proof of Baum's conjecture is further simplified by removing a necessity condition previously identified by Host and Kra, thereby illustrating that the Furstenberg almost periodic framework offers a more flexible approach to achieving weak mixing and faithfulness. Utilizing this approach, a relationship is identified that connects local state probabilities to the branching rule in representation theory, thereby yielding explicit, combinatorial expressions for certain probabilities. Furthermore, a connection is established between the model's Hamiltonian and a quantum analog of the raising operator for a specific type of polynomial module, whose properties are studied in detail. In a particular instance, calculating the probability of finding a southward pointing arrow at every second lattice site reveals a connection to a type of representation theory known as the centralizer of a regular semisimple module. As a result, exact averages of arrow variables can be computed for a wide array of parameter values, including those associated with key quantum integrable systems such as the XXZ model with a specific value of XXZ parameter and the fermion model's 'finite temperature' system. Additionally, a computational strategy is presented that enables the determination of the critical threshold values of XXZ parameter for models with specific periodic boundary conditions and a specific highest weight module, along with analogous results for models with open boundary conditions. This study investigates the performance of a collective group of algorithms rooted in interior point methods, known as IPMs, in achieving optimal solutions. The specific methods examined are part of a broader methodology called Proximal Augmented Lagrangian Method (PALM), utilized for solving convex optimization problems defined by nonsmooth, nonconvex tasks. The implementation of stabilization techniques within PALM is examined in depth. The stabilization methods analyzed are part of a systematic approach called the Stabilized Proximal Augmented Lagrangian Method (SPALM) and involve sequential execution of contraction enforcers, contraction boosters, and contractive safe guardians. The latter is particularly significant as it ensures consistent behavior despite data perturbations. The investigation focuses on an in-depth, step-bystep analysis of one representative stabilization method, contractive safe guardians, in addition to other related aspects such as data perturbations and an analytical comparison with an ideal, unhindered PALM process. The study demonstrates that PALM is resilient to perturbations and guarantees convergence to a optimal solution. Furthermore, the incorporation of various stabilization methods contributes to enhanced algorithm robustness and performance. The research includes numerical tests on random datasets, which demonstrate the individual and collective efficacy of each stabilization method in achieving accelerated convergence and superior results. Interestingly, the experiments reveal that combining multiple stabilization methods results in accelerated convergence and superior performance, underscoring the significance of algorithmic analysis. Advanced observational facilities like WFIRST and Roman will utilize highly advanced imaging systems that produce significant anisoplanatic distortion due to the atmosphere, requiring a highly efficient nonlinear coaddition algorithm to preserve the point spread function for faint objects. Previously developed algorithms include median and clipped-mean, but they fail to maintain a consistent PSF profile due to dropping bright-star images from the coaddition. This paper presents a new adaptive nonlinear coaddition algorithm called $\text{ANCilla}$, which incorporates a hybrid approach using a clipped-mean for faint images and a custom $\ell_1$-minimization algorithm for inclusion of bright-star images with optimal attenuation. $\text{ANCilla}$ outperforms existing algorithms in the sense that it approximates the behavior of a ideal $\ell_0$-minimization algorithm, achieving the optimal balance between faint-image preservation and bright-star attenuation. This approach yields a more stable and efficient algorithm suitable for real-world applications. $\text{ANCilla}$ has been successfully tested on real-time image simulation data and actual WFIRST image data, demonstrating its capability to maintain a consistent and persistent PSF profile for multiple guide stars. This algorithm is currently being operationalized for the processing of actual spacecraft data as part of the mission's data analysis pipeline.

We establish a construction for chordal Schramm–Loewner evolution (CSLE) evolutions on the upper half-plane by connecting them to the concept of imaginary surfaces, thereby revealing a broader context for these evolutions within the framework of conformal field theories (CFTs) governed by a unique parameter $s$. Utilizing this construction, we derive an explicit formula for the derivative of a CSLE evolution, which enables the calculation of its associated scaling function. Consequently, we obtain the scaling limit of a CSLE evolution, which is equivalent to a SLE$_k$ evolution with $k$ corresponding to the given $s$ value. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the cross-ratio distribution for a CSLE triangle undergoes a non-trivial asymptotic transformation as the vertices become closely grouped. When $s$ equals 1/2, the cross-ratio distribution displays a log-normal character, thereby aligning with the hypotheses proposed by Galtsev and Kondoshvili. Our research further includes an exploration into the geometric harmonics framework introduced by Buczkowski et al., which leads to the derivation of unique integral equations for functions belonging to this framework. Notably, we prove the tightness of the geometric harmonics measure with respect to the Wiener measure, which provides critical insight into the domain marking process. Finally, we showcase the applicability of the geometric harmonics framework in calculating the asymptotic behavior of certain Doob $h$-martingale fields defined on a growing domain. When combined with the results obtained by Galtsev and Shkolnikov concerning the Doob $h$-martingale fields, this enables the calculation of the scaling limit of a Doob $h$-martingale field under the condition that its centered growing domain contains a closely grouped collection of points. This research focuses on obtaining a maximum norm estimate for the Navier-Stokes equations in a 2-D domain, demonstrating that the norm of the solution's derivatives remains bounded by the norm of the initial conditions and is further influenced by the Reynolds number and a constant derived from the solution's decay rate. This finding applies to any smooth initial condition within a specified ball and holds for all positive Reynolds numbers, providing a non-conservative estimate. This work builds upon similar non-conservative estimates for the heat equation and the heat equation with a forcing term. Unlike existing work on the Navier-Stokes equations, which often involves constructing a weak solution, this study uses a weak solution that satisfies the Navier-Stokes equations in a weak sense, allowing for the employment of classical techniques such as the Lagrange identity. This approach also allows for the extension of the findings to a related model of the Couette flow and raises questions about the lower bound of the Reynolds number for the Navier-Stokes equations. Although the maximum norm estimate is of limited usefulness for local well-posedness, it has practical applications in numerical computations, where the solution's spatial maximum norm is often employed as a criterion for stopping the iteration in various methods. Additionally, this research provides an innovative method for estimating the spatial maximum norm of the solution to the Navier-Stokes equations without relying on the construction of a weak solution. This approach can be extended to other equations and includes a new estimate for the spatial maximum norm of the solution to the linear heat equation with a forcing term. This research also provides an initial understanding of the spatial maximum norm of the solution to the Navier-Stokes equations that the construction of a weak solution does not offer. Furthermore, this approach can be extended to obtain a new estimate for the spatial maximum norm of the solution to the linear heat equation with a forcing term. This paper proposes and examines a novel approach to quantum control verification, known as CVQC. In this protocol, a verification server relies on classical data from multiple testing labs to confirm the correctness of a quantum control unit's instructions. The proposed CVQC improves efficiency by reducing the measurement frequency and data transfer volume, thereby significantly outperforming existing protocols in verification speed. Additionally, CVQC supports a hybrid measurement model that simultaneously measures both the quantum state and quantum gate applications, yielding the best performance among all quantum verification protocols. Experimental implementations of CVQC using coherent populational error and field programmable gate arrays highlight its practical potential for quantum network applications. The underlying source code is publicly accessible on GitHub at the address https://github.com/UseQT/CVQC-verifier.

In the realm of biomedical imaging, image analysis is frequently reliant on manual, labor-intensive processes that could be streamlined by advanced computer algorithms. Certain problems necessitate novel image constellations as inputs, prompting the examination of deep generative models in this context. We introduce a new neural generative model, called CGN, for producing realistic collections of cells that can adapt to varying densities, facilitating automatic cell tracking and segmentation across different scenarios. Through extensive testing with manually created training data and application to two real-life microbiology challenges, we verify the efficacy of our approach and outperform a competing model on cell tracking accuracy and purity. Furthermore, cells produced by CGN exhibit higher quality and synthetic capacity, enabling more efficient and automated analysis of microscopic videos and images. You can access the code for CGN at https://github.com/alexeydg/cellgan. 

Our work has important practical implications, as the generated images and sequences can serve as mock data to train other deep learning models, such as segmentation and tracking algorithms, thereby reducing the necessity for manual, time-consuming analysis. In addition, the ability to produce realistic, high-density cell collections could facilitate the simulation of flow cytometry experiments to assess the impact of experimental design on data distribution. You can find more information about the projected applications of your work in the supplementary materials.
