To enhance sound detection accuracy using automatic classification, researchers use data augmentation techniques by modifying existing data instead of collecting new information. We applied various augmentation methods to an established dataset and observed significant improvements in classification performance. One effective approach involved mixing sound events by combining short signals with lengths of 10, 50, and 100 milliseconds. Another effective technique was time stretching factorized by a common divisor. Notably, using pre-trained convolutional neural networks as feature extractors resulted in superior outcomes compared to custom-designed acoustic feeature extraction methods. Our findings indicate that data augmentation can be an effective solution for enhancing sound detection accuracy. Furthermore, our analysis aimed to understand the underlying data patterns, and the results show that the current dataset poses significant challenges for accurate recognition of distinct sound events. We propose future research directions, including expanding the sound duration range and incorporating more diverse sound patterns with variable repetition factors. A novel Python module, xactsim, has been created to simulate the motion of particles in a physical system using the Leapfrog Integrator. This integrated solution combines numerical integration with symbolic computation, enabling it to integrate arbitrary functions with high precision, a capability that is particularly useful for applications in computer algebra systems.

The process of quantum measurement is foundational to understanding how measurement affects an information engine's behavior. Conventional measurement methods, however, typically rely on projectors that distort the system state, differing from the continuous measurement used in experiments. We have developed a method for simulating projectors as a limit of continuous measurements based on Hermite polynomials. Applying this approach, we derive a simplified model for an information engine undergoing continuous measurement and show that its temperature, defined by the system's residual energy, can be adjusted by means of laser power. We have also introduced a new decay rate and found that the engine's performance can be maximized at a critical point between low and high temperatures. Notably, the temperature can be reduced without compromising the engine's efficiency. Furthermore, the novel decay rate has facilitated the introduction of a lower bound on the generator of time-scale asymmetry, $\Delta \tau$, which can be interpreted as a fundamental quantum property. Finally, the results of our research suggest the information engine's operating principles could be mimicked in macroscopic systems, offering potential new applications. High-precision measurements of wide binary star systems' velocity dispersion are achieved in three dimensions, taking into account the movement of the binary and its observer. Previous research has shown that using line velocities can enhance the measurement's accuracy by at least a factor of five, even without accounting for the three-dimensional motion. We have recalculated the line velocities for twenty systems using the most up-to-date information available in the Simbad database, and our results reveal that line velocities offer significantly improved high-precision measurements in the presence of all possible motions. Moreover, our findings agree exceptionally well with the previously calculated three-dimensional velocity dispersion values. Lastly, the study highlights the need for accurate parallax measurements and extensive line velocity data for further enhancing the precision of high-precision measurements. \\

In federated learning, a centralized server guides multiple clients in a distributed training process using a semi-supervised approach.  However, clients with limited labeled data may not benefit fully from this approach, depending on their specific data distributions and available labels.  We address this issue in a novel personalized semi-supervised learning paradigm called PSSL, in which the centralized server tailors its guidance to meet the unique needs of each client.  PSSL achieves this by using two distinct models: one that combines supervised and semi-supervised learning, trained on the client's data and labeled information, and another that is trained only on labeled client data with the goal of generating high-quality pseudo-labels to enhance the client's model performance.  We test PSSL's effectiveness in various federated learning scenarios involving different clients and data distributions and demonstrate its superiority over traditional approaches.  Additionally, the pseudo-labels produced by PSSL are of high quality and effective in improving client performance.  We highlight the benefits of PSSL's customizable guidance and its potential to benefit a diverse range of clients in future federated learning applications.  The source code for PSSL is publicly available at https://github.com/damiengj/PSSL.  Empirical results and model information are presented in the supplementary document.  Discussion of potential extensions and limitations of PSSL is presented in the concluding section. PSSL incorporates a pseudo-label generation module that produces high-quality labels and improves model performance when training with these pseudo-labels.  PSSL outperforms traditional approaches in various numerical evaluations and has the potential to benefit a diverse range of clients in future federated learning applications. Urgent care visits to the Emergency Department have been on the rise, pressuring resources and public healthcare systems. One potential solution is to identify emergency patients who can be treated elsewhere and reduce the length of stay in the ED. In this study, we explore the effects of length of stay in the ED on subsequent healthcare utilization and find that even small changes in length of stay have noticeable effects on readmission rates within thirty days. Specifically, increasing the length of stay by half an hour or one hour results in significantly higher 30-day readmission rates compared to shorter stays, although the relationship becomes less pronounced for longer stay durations. This raises questions about the optimal length of stay in the ED and whether some patients might benefit from earlier discharge to alternative healthcare settings. In order to optimize ED length of stay, clinicians should focus on patients with longer stays who can be transferred early, rather than those with shorter stays, and also identify patients who can safely be discharged early to other healthcare settings. In a multi-agent system, we study how agents with varying task difficulties distribute their effort across multiple tasks. The difficulty distribution among tasks is unknown and assumed to follow a specific pattern, while agents' effort allocation methods are assumed to be consistent, although their specific approach remains unknown. The system achieves optimal cooperation when agents evenly divide their effort, as shown through an analysis involving quadratic rewards and bounded effort constraints. When effort allocation strategies are complex, the system achieves near-optimal performance, at least to a high degree of accuracy, by simply having agents divide their effort equally. To accurately measure the relationships between charges and various properties in particle collisions, it's crucial to understand how events that don't follow local charge conservation rules affect our results. This study uses a synthetic model of particle collisions to examine how events with large charge conserved values impact the measurement of correlation between charges and transverse momentum. We found that these events that don't follow the rules significantly affect our measurement of correlation and often lead to incorrect conclusions about the existence of relationships. Additionally, we found that the rules of local charge conservation also influence the distribution of charges and the relationship between momentum and mass. We found that the rules of local charge conservation do not change the overall number of particles in the central region of collisions, but rather, they cause a transfer of momentum from high to low pseudorapidity values. This study highlights the need to carefully investigate events that don't follow local charge conservation rules to get accurate measurements of correlation between charges and other properties in particle collisions. We also found that events with large charge conserved values often have high pseudorapidity values and are usually found on the opposite sides of collisions. We found one particularly significant rule of local charge conservation that applies to all pseudorapidity values - the sum of the charges of particles in one side of the collision is usually zero. This finding is consistent with a previously proposed model of local charge conservation, known as the model of charge exchange, which was first proposed by a physicist Stepanov. This study produces predictive models that forecast four indicators of success for crowdfunded projects: completion, meeting funding goals, on schedule, and attracting recurring donations. Analyzing both project and user features, our investigation reveals that project characteristics offer more valuable insights than user credentials for project owners. By integrating machine learning algorithms with an external crowd behavior dataset, we evaluate the likelihood of project success, assess user credibility, estimate project duration, and predict pricing and future fundraising goals. Compared to using user credentials or static features alone, incorporating crowd behavior data leads to improved accuracy in predicting project outcomes and evaluating user credibility. Additionally, incorporating external crowd behavior data allows us to mitigate information bias found in project descriptions and titles, thus enhancing the predictive models. Lastly, this study highlights the potential for misunderstanding in predicting project durations, as identified in the dataset, emphasizing the need for more precise duration prediction methods. The findings suggest that using crowd behavior data yields better results than solely using project or user characteristics in predicting fundraising success. The models developed in this study outperform the traditional method that relies solely on project features, resulting in a 9-15% improvement in accuracy for binary success predictions. Similarly, using crowd behavior data results in a 26-42% boost in accuracy for predicting recurring donations compared to using project features alone. The performance of a semiconductor device is heavily influenced by the properties of its gate material.  Using the non-linear catechol interaction with silicon surfaces, our study reveals a new class of materials that can be used as gate materials, yielding significant improvements in mobility and threshold voltage.  These discoveries were made by scanning silicon surfaces with a library of 188 small organic molecules using near-edge absorption fine structure (NEafs) measurements.  By combining theoretical predictions with experimental results, we identify three specific molecules with promising properties for next-generation transistors:  4-hydroxy-3-mossylic acid, a-furan carboxylic acid and a-benzyl urethane carboxylic acid.  According to theoretical calculations, these molecules achieve a threshold voltage of 0.22, 0.29 and 0.25 volts, representing significant improvements over existing mid-gap gate materials.  Furthermore, they offer superior carrier mobility at 116, 118, and 125 cm^2/Vs, surpassing the best-in-class gate materials.  These findings demonstrate the potential of catechol interactions to accelerate the discovery of superior gate materials, thereby enabling the development of higher-performance semiconductor devices.  Our technique of organic-based gate material discovery could be applied to other materials as well, broadening the scope of existing material discovery methodologies.  These advancements could lead to a new generation of faster and more powerful semiconductor devices.  In addition to their use as gate materials, we identify potential applications of these organic materials as surface passivation layers to enhance device yield and as bio-compatible surface coatings.  Molecular structure design presents a unique blend of surface engineering challenges and opportunities, and our discovery of mid-gap gate materials highlights the significance of addressing chemical and structural imperfections at the surface of materials.  By combining advanced simulation methods with the statistical analysis of a comprehensive molecular library, we illustrate the effective use of targeted molecular discovery in the development of novel materials.  This methodology can be extended to other material classes as well, facilitating efficient material development through a systematic exploration of targeted molecular design.  A corresponding gate material database is presented, offering a comprehensive list of gate materials with associated properties, and presenting a potential solution to the long-standing issue of achieving precise reproducibility in materials development.  Our study showcases the benefits of an integrated approach to materials development, combining simulation, experimentation, and database management to accelerate the discovery of new materials.  These results present an initial step in a comprehensive strategy for a targeted, systematic development of new materials

Networks of oscillators have an inherent tendency to stabilize through group synchronization. This process is commonly seen in various biological and mechanical systems. Researchers have introduced the concept of group synchronization as a unified idea, drawing inspiration from the stability of fixed points and limit cycles. However, the robustness of this concept has been called into question. Certain systems can be analyzed using the group synchronization framework, yet their actual stability relies on other analytical methods, such as linearization or geometric methods. This raises questions about the small divisor problem - can the group synchronization theory provide accurate information about stability in systems where other analytical methods are applicable? We explored this question in this study, focusing on fully connected systems of two and three coupled oscillators. We found that slight inaccuracies in system parameter measurement can lead to significant effects on the theoretical predictions for stability. This raised concerns about the small divisor problem in the group synchronization theory. To confirm our theoretical findings, we conducted numerical simulations, demonstrating that even very small errors in accuracy can cause discrepancies in the predicted stability phases. This led us to investigate the stability of an equilibrium point in a simplified model, known as the Henry model, with varying levels of approximation accuracy. We established that slight inaccuracies in measurement can lead to inaccuracies in the predicted phase boundary, often resulting in incorrect predictions for the phase boundary. This incorrect prediction may lead to incorrect inferences about the dynamics of the system, particularly its susceptibility to bistability and the existence of heteroclinic connections. We observed a comparable effect in the three-coupled oscillators system, where small errors in measurement led to inaccuracies in the predicted phase diagram, often resulting in incorrect inferences about the existence of Hopf bifurcations, heteroclinic transitions, and bistability. This highlighted the potential drawbacks of the group synchronization framework, particularly its inability to accurately represent the stability of the equilibrium point in systems where other analytical methods apply. These findings suggested the need for further research, focusing on developing a new analytical method both for confirming the stability of the equilibrium point and for evaluating the robustness of the group synchronization framework. Semi-supervised node classification in Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) has received significant attention in recent years, with many studies employing pseudo-labeling techniques to leverage unlabeled node data. Nonetheless, these methods can introduce noise into the training process, causing the model to converge on suboptimal equilibria. In an attempt to address this limitation, this study proposes a novel pseudo-labeling approach called Iterative Pseudo-Labeling (IPL), which seeks to leverage unlabeled node data to enhance GNN performance through iterative model refinement. The proposed IPL method resembles a game theory concept called iterative learning, eliminating noise from the training process and allowing the model to achieve better performance. The experimental outcomes demonstrate the effectiveness of IPL in improving GNNs for semi-supervised node classification tasks. Furthermore, IPL's iterative model refinement has positive implications for open-world and few-shot learning applications. The study also examines the relationship between step size and iterative model learning rate, as well as the model's average node confidence, to gain insights into IPL's iterative model refinement process. By analyzing the performance of various path-length iterative modeling approaches, the study shows that IPL can be an open-world learning paradigm, enhancing the GNN's robustness and shelf life. This work investigates the multi-point distribution of a discrete time TASEP with initial conditions, building upon a prior study by Aiden et al. who examined this same model under uniform initial conditions. We develop a novel method of solving this problem, yielding an explicit, integrable equation for the multi-point distribution, along with specific analytical solutions for two- and three-point distributions. Unlike the prior approach, our solution accommodates arbitrary initial conditions without requiring time averaging. We also derive an explicit formula for the one-point distribution with arbitrary initial conditions, expanding upon existing results, including TASEP with uniform and weighted initial conditions. Notably, our derived multi-point distribution formula differs significantly from the prior time-averaged approach, exhibiting distinct time dependence that can result in non-intuitive behavior, such as oscillations, in certain scenarios. In the large time limit, the multi-point distribution converges to a product of exponential distributions, with our analytical solutions offering precise, time-dependent corrections to this asymptotic behavior. We present detailed, illustrative examples highlighting the form of our multi-point distribution for low starting conditions and comparing it to the time-averaged multi-point distribution. Furthermore, we define and compute the semi-variance for TASEP with arbitrary initial conditions, identifying positive and potentially oscillating behavior, along with its determination in the large time limit as proportional to the square of the time, multiplied by the semi-variance of the initial distribution. Additionally, we establish a precise relationship between the multi-point distribution of TASEP and a variant of the discrete time TASEP with 'frozen' particles, which enables the computation of certain TASEP moments, as well as proves the integrability of this variant. Lastly, we extend our results to the multi-point distribution of TASEP with 'frozen' particles, which enables the computation of certain TASEP moments, as well as tasep with step initial conditions, exhibiting distinct time and josting behavior. Our new method, the Generalized Chebyshev method, sets a baseline for average-case efficiency in a wide range of situations, surpassing traditional optimization techniques like gradient descent. Despite occasional exponential worst-case performance, it provides the best overall average outcome. The Generalized Chebyshev method builds on Chebyshev's solution to a quadratic equation and incorporates his signs rule, yielding a unified algorithm applicable to various settings such as convex and non-convex optimization, both with and without constraints. The method's efficiency is demonstrated through mathematical proof of its average-case properties in several scenarios, including harmonic regression, logistic regression, and matrix factorization. The results show the Generalized Chebyshev method reaches optimal solutions at a pace 5-30% better than gradient descent, with comparable or even better performance in non-optimal scenarios. The method's efficiency makes it a suitable alternative to gradient descent for similar optimization tasks. The accompanying source code can be found at https://github.com/alexrame/GeneralChebyshevMethod. The increase in the scale of formal verification demands innovative solutions for the review and validation of proof representations. Previous studies have examined the utilization of machine learning for proof verification, however our work focuses on leveraging generative models for the effective exploration and validation of proof representations. We introduce a novel deep generative model called DeepGP that employs antisymmetry to navigate the complex structure of formal proofs. Through extensive analysis on various verification tasks, our results indicate that DeepGP significantly surpasses existing machine learning approaches and human proof lengths by 3.31 and 2.03 times respectively. Furthermore, DeepGP-enabled tools have been integrated into the HOL Light proof assistant as part of the dpfp and metagp projects, providing users with access to proof generation and validation via interactive interfaces. These tools have been successfully applied in the verification of at least 10 complex properties, incorporating 2 from the Isabelle/HOL Math library and an independently verified version of the Akers model of VLSI circuit verification. Additionally, DeepGP-enabled tools have successfully validated 16 out of 17 manually constructed proof representations for a particular property. In contrast, traditional verification tools failed to validate any manually constructed proof representations. The efficiency gains provided by DeepGP also facilitate the generation and validation of multiple, alternative proof representations for complex properties such as the four-color theorem and Akers model of VLSI circuit verification. These developments have the potential to greatly accelerate and automate the process of formal verification in the future. The associated code is publicly available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/dylanjonesdpfp/dpfp. The metagp project can be accessed at https://github.com/dylanjonesdpfp/metagp. This research investigates the transition function $A_{gq}^{(3)}(N)$ within a variable flavor number (VFN) theory, where $N$ represents the number of active flavors in the strong interaction. By considering the ratio of parton distribution functions (PDFs) and their evolution at next-to-next-to-leading order (NNLO), the study analyzes the transition from four to five active flavors. The analysis utilizes the APPEGII differential distribution tables to derive $A_{gq}^{(3)}(N)$ and compares it with analogous results from other studies. The findings show the sensitivity of this transition at the level of momentum $Q=94$ GeV, corresponding to about 5\% in the case of gluon-to-quark transitions. This article introduces an embedded, higher-order embedded language called Proto-Quipper-M. In contrast to the original Proto-Quipper, Proto-Quipper-M is designed as a stand-alone language, built on top of a new, fundamental circuit semantics. This novel semantics serves as a universal model for quantum gate model circuit languages. A crucial property of Proto-Quipper-M is that it incorporates a quantum state cloning prohibition, analogous to quantum gate model circuit languages based on a finite number of universal gates. Additionally, the article presents a method for translating Proto-Quipper-M programs into a widely used universal gate model, revealing that the length of the translation is contingent on the maximum connectivity of the graph representing the program's underlying universal gate circuit. This translation method ensures that the non-cloning property of quantum states is maintained, provided that the graph has a finite maximum connectivity value. A demonstration of the system's effectiveness is shown through the translation of a Proto-Quipper-M program designed to solve a mixed-cluster state decomposition problem. Specifically, the authors successfully demonstrated a rapid, efficient solution to this problem using a randomly generated mixed-cluster state with 10 qubits, followed by an equally swift decomposition of the resulting quantum state into its constituent cluster states. Key aspects of the system include its scalable architecture, built on top of a distributed memory system, and a dynamic memory allocation method that allows for adaptability based on the size and structure of the input data. A key advantage of this system is its ability to process large datasets quickly, thanks to its ability to efficiently distribute data and free up memory space as needed. For instance, the authors were able to process a 10-qubit mixed-cluster state in less than 300 nanoseconds, an speed comparable to or better than specialized hardware solutions. Lastly, the authors discuss potential future research areas, including a potential integration of the system with existing quantum computing efforts and a possible expansion of the system to include classical simulation of quantum circuits. Specifically, the authors note the potential for a hybrid approach that combines Proto-Quipper-M's quantum state cloning prohibition with a classical simulation method, such as the quantum query model, to leverage the strengths of both approaches. As an example of this potential, the authors note the possibility of using Proto-Quipper-M to solve a complex quantum computing problem, such as a logarithmic-depth approximation of a quantum oracle, and then employing a classical simulation method to translate the Proto-Quipper-M circuit into a universal gate model circuit. A major constraint in quantum-enhanced sensing is the availability of precise, non-destructive measurements. The process of optical phase detection serves as a useful case study. Utilizing two-mode squeezing (TMS) as a key resource, a novel method for quantum-enhanced optical phase sensing is presented. By implementing TMS and a controlled unitary transformation, the problem of destructive measurement necessary for obtaining phase information is overcome. The developed approach offers an optimal advantage in phase measurement accuracy, limited only by the degree of TMS. The implementation of this method in a Michelson interferometer enables genuine quantum-enhanced sensing of optical phases. Additionally, the introduced technique holds potential for widespread application in a wide range of quantum sensing technologies. \textbf{Published in: arXiv:2206.07781 (2022)}.

Advancements in digital technologies generate vast amounts of unstructured event data. This research paper proposes an innovative method for transforming normalizing flows into gauge invariant models, with particular application to U(1) symmetry theories. The prior approach in [1] established a framework that converts any normalizing flow into a gauge invariant model, yet this model's generative potential was poorly utilized because it generated a space that was not directly relevant to the original variables. The paper demonstrates the efficacy of this method through three concrete examples, each illustrating the advantages of using gauge invariant flows in distinct contexts: symmetric density generation, conditional generative modeling, and learning from partially masked data. As artificial intelligence becomes increasingly integrated into various sectors, its environmental impact is beginning to be considered a crucial factor in service development and procurement. Conventional sustainability assessment methods are typically confined to a product's lifecycle, yet to provide a more comprehensive understanding, they must be extended to encompass the entire service lifecycle, including usage and disposal. To facilitate life cycle assessment (LCA) simulations, a framework called SIMA is introduced, comprising a modular simulation model that represents the interactions between AI systems and the energy market. A case study involving a visual recognition AI service was conducted using SIMA to estimate the environmental impacts of the service during various usage scenarios. The parameters influencing these impacts were also identified and structured according to a classification system known as Ecoinvent. The outcomes of this classification, along with the specified usage scenarios, demonstrate how usage phase factors contribute to the overall environmental effect and show that usage variables can significantly impact the environmental comparison of services. Ultimately, this research underscores the significance of understanding the interactions between services and the underlying infrastructure systems, as well as the necessity for clear service model definitions. Furthermore, this classification can serve as a reference for developing simulation-based LCA models in the future. A comparison between SIMA-based and traditional LCA-based environmental assessments of the visual recognition service revealed a 2 to 3 order of magnitude difference in computation time, underscoring the value of using simulation for illustrating complex service dynamics and effects on the energy market. Lastly, the outcomes of this research can guide developers in optimizing AI services from an environmental perspective and showcase the potential for artificial intelligence to contribute to sustainable development. A relatively unexplored area of numerical analysis in fluid dynamics is coupled problems, which is essential to understanding various physical phenomena. In this study, we develop an error indicator for coupled Arima and Navier-Stokes equations using a dual-weighted residual method. Although the method initially seems complicated due to the nonlinear interactions, it can be simplified and quantified through energy-type inequalities. The study provides an error estimate of the form of no greater than $\|u-\tilde{u}\|_{H^1(\Omega)} +\|p-\tilde{p}\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\leq C\delta$, where $\delta$ is the norm of the residual as approximated by the equations, resulting in a logarithmic convergence for smooth solutions. Additionally, we demonstrate that the method can be used to determine the existence of solutions to the coupled equations and verify the convergence of numerical schemes. The study includes experimental results that validate the theoretical findings. The process of gene expression involves transcription, splicing, and translation, yet many studies focus on DNA, RNA, and protein sequences without considering the underlying biological mechanisms in a cell-wide context. A fundamental question arises: how long does it take for a protein to be produced after transcription of a gene completes? To address this, we developed a model describing the production of mature mRNA from individual genes of various lengths, assuming a fixed delay between transcription completion and mature mRNA production. According to this model, the longer the gene, the greater the delay, and for very short genes, the time gap is negligible compared to the total duration of the mRNA production process. Since our model represents the average behavior of numerous genes, it is applicable at the chromosomal or whole-genome scale, and has potential applications in the analysis of high-throughput sequencing and protein production data. Additionally, we used our model to estimate the maximum rate at which the instructions contained within a genome can be translated into proteins, and demonstrate that this rate may be the key to explaining the rapid evolution of large genomes during extended periods of stability. Our model provides a fundamental understanding of the connection between DNA and protein production, and is a crucial component of the broader framework for gene expression analysis that we are developing. A whole-genome expression simulation algorithm is presented, and is shown to be compatible with the GEXP package for R, a comprehensive tool for analyzing gene expression data. As a testament to the effectiveness of our model, we successfully used it to reproduce the observed peak in the protein production rate as the length of a gene increases from zero to several thousand base pairs, a phenomenon that was previously documented in a study on the relationship between gene length and frequency. A detailed comparison of our model-based predictions with the experimental results reveals remarkable agreement, emphasizing the importance of accurate transcription and processing completion times for understanding the underlying mechanisms of gene expression. To facilitate further research and analysis, we provide a step-by-step instruction guide for developing the GEXP package, and highlight its capabilities in a comprehensive summary of its features. Ultimately, we conclude that our model-based approach to analyzing gene expression offers a more effective method for discovering new principles and phenomena in the field. The $^{64}$Ni nucleus serves as a testing ground to explore the connection between its large excitation energies and the new physics phenomena arising from the formation of the neutron N = 40 subshell. Using the large-scale $^{64}$Ni beta-gamma decay study, researchers have identified numerous key properties, including the 0$^{+}$ energy level, the B(E$^{(2)}$) values for transitions from the next-higher 2$^{+}$ state to the 0$^{+}$ state, and the P$_{2}$ body deformation parameter. These key properties allowed scientists to investigate the evolution of the excitation energies within the N = 40 subshell. Results show that the shape of the excitation spectrum in $^{64}$Ni can be accurately reproduced only by incorporating a strong monopole component in the shell-model calculation, which corresponds to a significant N = 40 subshell gap. We investigate various anomalies in SU(N) gauge theories that include Weyl fermions in the adjoint representation and an additional, regular fundamental representation. The anomalies with the largest order of the fermion determinant are examined, with the focus being their dependence on the complexified action. The results demonstrate that when there are N+1 Weyl fermions in the adjoint representation, the anomalies with the largest order of the fermion determinant in SU(N) gauge theory are equivalent to those of the SU(N+1) anti-symmetric fermion theory. This finding suggests that the large-N limit of the SU(N) theory can be reduced to an SU(N+1) theory with a fermion in the adjoint representation, an observation that can be applied to other theories that include fermions in the bi-fundamental or regular fundamental representations. The resulting reduction can be applied to the SU(N) theory with fundamental and anti-fundamental fermions, as well as the SU(N) theory with N=2 fermions in the symmetric and anti-symmetric representations. The resulting reduced models can be used to compute the large-N limit of various correlation functions. The results of the large-N limit of the two-loop anomalous dimensions, the large-N admixture rates, and the large-N correlation functions of various fields are in agreement with the results of the 1/N expansion. For group codes C and D, that encode messages from a group G, we establish a connection between their dual codes D^⊥ and C^⊥ in terms of group homomorphisms. This connection allows us to prove that under specific conditions, codes C and D are equivalent if their dual codes are equivalent. This result enables us to extend a previous finding by Schaub that directly links the equivalence of group codes C and D. Additionally, we explore situations in which the equivalence of codes C and D implies the equivalence of their dual codes D^⊥ and C^⊥. This analysis provides insight into the relationship between group codes and their dual codes, and it has implications for the study of secret sharing schemes. Our study is particularly relevant for prime order groups G, but it can be generalized to other types of groups G. We also illustrate our findings with several examples. Finally, we establish a lower bound on the size of codebook D required for achieving code equivalence with code C when the group G has prime order.

We introduce a generalized version of Bucket Elimination (BE) called Multi-Value Bucket Elimination (MVBE). The standard BE algorithm is specifically designed for modeling and solving inference and optimization problems on graphs with a single variable type. In contrast, MVBE is an extension that accommodates variables with multiple discrete value sets. We further present an efficient specialization of MVBE, known as Specialized Multi-Value Bucket Elimination (S MVBE), which offers a more optimized approach with reduced computational costs. The proposed MVBE and S MVBE algorithms can solve various problems, including Maximum a Posteriori Inference and Minimum Energy Approximate Message Passing, in multiple contexts. The techniques have been applied to solve two practical problems: learning parameters from labeled data, and making predictions based on unknown model parameters, both in graphical models and multi-type random field domains. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of MVBE and S MVBE in outperforming existing methods. The proposed algorithms have been implemented within an open-source C++ library called BE.h, freely accessible on GitHub under the BSD license. Evaluations of BE.h on benchmark datasets can be found at BE.h Evaluation. MVBE and S MVBE have been successfully integrated into two popular package repositories, DLib.h and FGES, also available on GitHub under the mentioned license. The integration of BE.h facilitated the implementation of two novel features: BE-based inference on multi-type random fields, previously unreported; and the application of BE to optimize parameter learning on multi-type random fields, a capability yet to be utilized. The computational evaluations demonstrated the superiority of the BE-based approaches over existing techniques. The proposed MVBE and S MVBE algorithms have significant advantages over the current state-of-the-art methods. The efficiency of these new methods is revealed through computational evaluations, specifically, an average of 2 to 100 times faster for the random field domain and 2 to 1000 times faster for the graphical model domain. The open-source BE.h library, freely accessible on GitHub under the BSD license, serves as a versatile, efficient, and adaptable toolkit for solving various inference and optimization tasks across multiple domains. New research focuses on dropping objects, a common occurrence in daily life, and how humans identify them. This problem requires integrating multiple factors, including physics-based information about the object's shape, motion, and gravity's impact. A key challenge is balancing the needs of object detection, which requires clear visual details, with the incorporation of physically plausible trajectories. Our proposed solution, Dropping Objects Recognition with Physics-Aided Object Detector (DROP-AOD), utilizes a dual model structure that separates object detection and trajectory analysis. This allows for efficient object detection, even in complex scenarios with multiple objects. By incorporating trajectory information, we enhance the accuracy of dropped object detection and reduce false positives. Experiments on a diverse set of dropping scenarios demonstrate that DROP-AOD exceeds state-of-the-art performance. As a result, we make our dataset publicly available, consisting of 11,960 images with accompanying trajectory information, obtained from merging various dropping object datasets. Moreover, we introduce the Dropping Objects Challenge (DROPCHALLENGE), a competition to foster new research techniques in this area of study. Our code is available for download at https://github.com/hywhoomin/DROP-AOD. A dataset can be obtained at https://droppings-object dataset hywhoomin.com. The concepts of isotropic jamming and shear jamming are foundational to understanding amorphous materials. Research has revealed that shear jamming possesses a more complex phase diagram, characterized by distinct types of critical behavior based on friction levels. A recent study by Olson and Govno uncovered varying exponents in different regimes of shear jamming. Our research aims to expand on this work by exploring the impact of particle size disparity on jamming transitions. By simulating both isotropic and shear jamming processes with equal volumes of spherical particles with varying sizes, our findings align with a phase diagram containing jamming and shear jamming transitions for both types of scenarios. However, when size variation is present, the shear jamming scenario requires lower confining pressures to occur, a phenomenon observed across all tested friction levels. Conversely, the jamming transition shows pressure independence. A key observation is that both types of jamming transitions display similar critical behavior in terms of exponent values. Our research also uncovers that the shear jamming transition for size-disparate systems occurs at a pressure higher than its isotropic counterpart, with the difference increasing as the difference in particle size increases. A theoretical explanation for this behavior involves the application of constraints in jammed configurations, leading to a proposed connection between the excess entropy of a disordered phase and the shear modulus. This connection is predicted to hold for both isotropic and shear jamming scenarios. Furthermore, our research suggests that the jamming point lies on a boundary that divides configuration space into ordered and disordered regions, a concept supported by a proposed entropy representation of jamming transitions. A critical observation is that jamming transitions exhibit a third-order phase transition characteristics, a notion previously proposed by Dauchier and Edge and further studied by a group of researchers, for both isotropic and shear jamming scenarios. A key advantage of our entropy representation is that it facilitates the exploration of jamming transitions within multi-component systems with varying compositions. As a test of this idea, our research applies this approach to a system where size and species variability coexist, a scenario in which the jamming transition occurs at a pressure independent of the number of components, a feature shared by both isotropic and shear jamming scenarios. A key outcome of this research is the identification of a jamming criterion grounded in entropy concepts, a ground-breaking idea in amorphous materials science. We introduce the MS(2)-AR(4) model, which combines the primary periodic components with an autoregressive component, to capture electricity demand dynamics. The performance of this new model is assessed against the autoregressive model and other established techniques using real-world data. Results indicate that the autoregressive approach lacks power in detecting periodic components, while the proposed MS(2)-AR(4) model exhibits superior power capabilities within a testing environment. Moreover, in a real-world application, the former fails to identify essential periodic patterns in demand data, which are crucial for demand forecasting. The research highlights the benefits and capabilities of the MS(2)-AR(4) model as a powerful tool for analyzing and forecasting complex time series data. The study also investigates the stochastic properties of the MS(2)-AR(4) model through theoretical and numerical analyses, confirming its asymptotic normality under certain covariance stationary conditions. The findings suggest that a sufficient condition for asymptotic normality is a sufficient condition for stationarity in the MS(2)-AR(4) model. The proof utilizes a novel approach, balancing on both the monthly and weekly cycles, and their interactions. The research also establishes almost sure convergence of the estimators and the asymptotic distribution of the estimators, providing insights into the complexity of the time series data. The results show that the estimators achieve asymptotic efficiency only under a specific scaling of the sample size. The study suggests a potential direction for further research in time series modeling, exploring the implications of the 'bandwidth problem' in achieving efficient estimators. A significant challenge that public sector professionals face today is determining how to utilize search engines effectively for tasks involving information retrieval. Despite their widespread use, algorithmic biases within search engines remain little understood by public sector professionals. This study seeks to address this knowledge gap by exploring how different search engines and query framing impact algorithmic biases in search outcomes related to crime and justice information. Through a mixed-method approach, this research provides essential insights that can inform the development of effective search strategies and highlights potential implications for public sector professionals to consider. The study's findings emphasize the necessity for public sector professionals to remain vigilant about potential biases within search engine results and suggests potential areas for search engine improvement. Ultimately, this research aims to enhance search engine utility for public sector professionals by shedding light on the underlying algorithmic biases that shape search outcomes. Based on the research's findings, a conceptual framework for evaluating Web search utility from a public sector perspective was developed and presented. Additionally, this study offers recommendations for further research and practice in this domain. Overall, this research aims to promote discussion and debate among information professionals and scholars, as well as to inform policy and educational initiatives focused on Web search education and training for public sector professionals. Deville and Rondinelli's program synthesis framework has been enhanced to handle a broader range of tasks, employing a panel of synthetic programs, along with a metric that assesses the efficiency of each algorithm by calculating the time it takes for the program synthesis engine to generate a program and compare the output of the program synthesis engine with actual results, with an average response time of less than one second. Through comparison with the algorithmic efficiency of established testing methods, it has been demonstrated that the program synthesis engine can test specifications more quickly, with the program synthesis engine also revealing novel testing techniques that can be incorporated into existing algorithms to expand their capability in detecting errors. Furthermore, a web-based program synthesis engine has been developed to provide easy access to this testing technique for the development of test cases. Current program synthesis libraries, such as Z3 and MathSat, have been upgraded to incorporate a new program synthesis technique that allows the program synthesis engine to synthesize programs more quickly while maintaining the accuracy of the results by eliminating unnecessary computations by combining program synthesis tasks more efficiently. As a result, programs can be synthesized up to fifty times more quickly, with a response time of less than one hundred milliseconds. With the program synthesis technique, it is now possible to automatically detect specification errors in the implementation of a model, a task that would otherwise require the effort of a team of three to four experts for just one of the concepts tested. In addition, the program synthesis technique has been successfully applied to detect specification errors in the implementation of eight key concepts in linear rational cell structures and has also been adapted for the detection of errors in the implementation of the Ramsey theorem. In each of these instances, the program synthesis technique was able to accurately identify existing implementation errors and, through modification and optimization, the program synthesis technique played a key role in developing better algorithms for the problems that were tested. Ultimately, the program synthesis technique presents a powerful tool for the detection of specification errors, with the potential for wide application in various fields of computer science. In the process of developing the program synthesis technique, a new web-based program, known as SynthDef, has been created for the automatic generation of correct programs from specifications and for the automatic detection of errors in the implementation of models, with features including the efficient use of computer memory and rapid response times. Furthermore, the program synthesis technique has been successfully integrated with existing computer algebra system to synthesize more complex programs more quickly, with up to fifty times faster synthesis times for difficult to synthesize problems. To comprehensively address climate change, it is necessary to analyze the Earth system's variability, ranging from the atmospheric and oceanic systems to biogeochemical processes and the carbon cycle. Reducing complex Earth systems to manageable representations is crucial for understanding, observing, and predicting climate dynamics. By incorporating relevant physical, biological, and chemical mechanisms into simplified models, we can facilitate further research into climate phenomena. These reduced models can be used in conjunction with optimal state estimation techniques to reconstruct the Earth's internal state from observational data, which is essential for validating model predictions and assessing climate parameter uncertainty. Furthermore, these reduced models can be instrumental in identifying and eliminating inconsistent trends in climate datasets. This research outlines various reduction techniques applicable to Earth climate studies and demonstrates their effectiveness through illustrative case studies. It also discusses the potential of these techniques to streamline climate modeling, data assimilation, and data analysis, enabling the optimization of observational networks and the identification of emerging climate phenomena. Additionally, we examine the utility of these techniques in detecting climate signals within datasets and constructing climate data assimilation algorithms. This research culminates in a proposed strategy for utilizing reduced order models to initiate proactive data collection efforts, which is exemplified through a ground-breaking application in ocean climate modeling. The research concludes by highlighting several areas of ongoing work and proposed future areas of investigation in the field of Earth climate studies. Ultimately, the integration of reduction techniques with other computational techniques enables the efficient solution of increasingly complex Earth climate problems, enabling researchers to derive valuable insights from datasets and inform climate data assimilation algorithms. This enables the efficient utilization of computational resources, allowing the practical application of proactive data collection strategies that can inform and guide ongoing and future field campaigns to monitor and understand climate dynamics. This research provides several areas of investigation for further exploration in the field of Earth climate studies, which may contribute to and enable the efficient derivation of climate information from datasets, which in turn can inform climate model predictions and assessments. Future infrared telescopes like the James Webb Space Telescope will be capable of observing kilonovae via specific infrared lines, and by doing so, it will be possible to connect the electromagnetic and gravitational waves observables emanating from these events. In order to make the most of this connection, researchers must develop an in-depth understanding of kilonova models, including complex macroscopic phase transitions that impact the observables. This paper delves into a novel approach to modeling these transitions, using a framework based on nonequilibrium thermodynamics and macroscopic kinetic theory. It particularly highlights the role of mesoscopic fluctuations and their effect on the matter's velocity distribution, and proposes a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution as a suitable closure model for the nonequilibrium hydrodynamic equations. The study also involves a first principle modeling of the transition in the context of nonequilibrium quark-gluon plasma, applicable to the early stages of kilonovae, and shows that the transition dynamics can be accurately represented through the resonance damping of collective excitations. Furthermore, the model is used to investigate the observable impacts of transition dynamics on kilonovae, including the potential light scattering effects and electron scattering opacity modulation. The study reveals that the observable impact of transition dynamics can vary greatly depending on the specific model used, underscoring the need for further research into the transition dynamics and its associated uncertainties. Finally, the study suggests potential future research paths, including the incorporation of dynamical quantity coherent zones in modeling the transition dynamics and the reduction of this phenomenon to an equivalent lattice structure model. The study also proposes an alternative model for the lattice structure, utilizing nonequilibrium lattice dynamics and affecting electron scattering and thermalization rate in the lattice. The nonequilibrium lattice model can be utilized for various astrophysical events including neutron stars mergers and proto-neutron star phases. The model can be used to investigate various phenomena including the equation of state, the formation of the proto-neutron star, the structure of the proto-neutron star, the stellar emission, the magnetic field generation, the hadronization process, the quark radiation, the neutrino emission, the hadron quark transition, and the equilibration processes. Radiation oncologists face considerable challenges when administering X-ray irradiation due to various inaccuracies in tumor targeting, radiation source calibration, and external noise influences. The accuracy of radiation field alignment is crucial to deliver prescribed radiation doses directly to tumors while minimizing exposure to surrounding healthy tissues. The precise positioning of X-ray beams can be achieved by verifying the alignment using imaging modalities, such as fluoroscopy or X-ray cone beam computed tomography (CBCT), before each treatment session. Although this approach requires an extensive decrease in radiation dose, it is sufficient to determine the position of radioactive sources and compensate for organ movements. The main limitation of this method is the lack of information on the displacement of tumors relative to the position of radioactive sources, which requires higher-resolution dose imaging. In this research, we present a novel technique for high-resolution dose imaging using Bayesian reconstruction methods, where we analyze pre-treatment CBCT scans, corresponding treatment fields, and real-time dose measurements to accurately determine tumor and source positions, as well as the radiation dose distribution. The effectiveness of this method was evaluated using simulated and actual clinical data, where we successfully determined the average dose error for artificially introduced source displacements of 5 mm, as well as analyzed real-time dose variations under varying treatment parameters. The results show that this method can accurately determine tumor and source positions, as well as radiation dose distribution, in both simulated and actual clinical environments. The overall average dose error for this method was found to be less than 0.3%, with corresponding treatment fields showing a maximum dose error of less than 0.7%. The precision achieved through this method supports its use as an accurate supplementary tool in radiation treatment, where we have found that clinical decisions based on this method result in an average dose reduction of up to 13% compared to the standard treatment protocol. The implications of this method's performance on treatment outcomes are yet to be determined in ongoing clinical trials and studies and will be reported in subsequent reports. High-dimensional data analyzed using techniques from multivariate statistics can be characterized by the constraint that the sum of component values remains constant. This constraint significantly affects statistical calculations, resulting in biased estimations and complications in modeling processes. The field of compositional data analysis specializes in addressing these challenges, with one common approach involving the partial least squares method. This method includes a crucial transformation step using the simple components, often based on standardized log-ratios. We have developed an alternative transformation method incorporating a weighted component calculation, with the weights influenced by variance estimates. This new transformation, along with a modified version of the partial least squares method, has been mathematically validated and demonstrated to be effective in high-dimensional systems, specifically through integration with the matrix factorization method of Neighborhood Component Analysis. Applications have been illustrated using synthetic data and datasets related to the fields of biochemistry and environmental science. The proposed approach shows promise in facilitating meaningful data interpretation and improving model representations for these domains. This research contributes novel mathematical concepts to the field of compositional data analysis, with potential extensions to partial description regression and canonical correlation analysis. The associated code can be accessed on the GitHub repository https://github.com/lcrs-UdeM/Generative_CCA_NCA. Specifically, the implementation of the alternative transformation method can be found in the file assets/alternatives.py, along with a quick comparison of its efficiency and effectiveness in comparison to standard techniques. Additionally, the code for the partial description regression variants is available in the repository https://github.com/lcrs-UdeM/PDR_FastFD. The core accretion theory suggests that once a planet's mass reaches a certain threshold, it undergoes rapid growth through gas capture, potentially resulting in observable patterns in the exoplanet population. By using simulations that mimic this process, we examined the exoplanets detected by the Kepler mission and the TESS survey, focusing on the mass distribution of close-in planets. However, the observed distribution shows a significant decrease in the number of planets with masses greater than approximately 10 Earth masses and close proximity to their host stars. The models predicting gas capture at high masses due to binary star interactions or unstable disk patterns do not align with the observed exoplanet population. The models predicting gas capture at high masses due to binary star interactions or binary star influences on the disk's density and thermal gradients also do not align with the observed exoplanet population. The observed exoplanet population is inconsistent with the scenarios predicting gas capture at high masses due to binary star interactions or binary star influences on the disk's density and thermal gradients. In the Episodic Memory module of our latest paper, we've developed a specialized component of a cognitive agent's memory system, designed to follow changes in unobserved environmental conditions and provide the ability to make predictions from incomplete observations. Our method, based on attention mechanisms and graph neural networks, enables efficient updating of memory representations both when new observations arrive and when they don't, and we've tested its effectiveness in scenarios involving periodic hidden patterns. Notably, our approach balances computational simplicity with a robust capacity for learning and representation. A fully fledged model of dark matter is proposed, incorporating a complex scalar field representing dark matter and its interaction with the standard model via a particular mediator, also a complex scalar. Given that dark matter has a smaller abundance than Standard Model particles when the two are produced simultaneously at high energies, the model can naturally attribute the correct abundance to dark matter through freeze-in production, either directly from the scalar potential or through the Standard Model particles. The model also features the possibility of the dark matter having an appreciable number of nuclear recoil detection events within existing direct detection experiments, depending on the mass relationship between the dark matter and the mediator, as well as the coupling strength between them. The model is therefore distinguishable from conventional WIMPs and can potentially be identified through experimental tests. Moreover, the model offers the possibility that the dark matter candidate may hold its own symmetry, resulting in the candidate having a smaller mass than the mediator. This study proposes an improved image registration algorithm, SIFT-CPD, designed to align two medical images, despite variations in shape and features. Building on the Keypoint-Detector framework, SIFT-CPD utilizes a complex probability distribution model to describe image registration, considering the uniqueness of landmarks, applications of partial and sparse point correspondences, and reductions in dimensionality. To overcome the challenges of finding complex minimal solutions, a iterative optimization process based on the EM algorithm has been implemented. Specifically, we utilize the Gaussian-Newton method to efficiently optimize parameters in each iteration. The effectiveness of SIFT-CPD has been tested on 3D medical images, comparing its performance with other registration algorithms in terms of accuracy and computational time. The results show that SIFT-CPD consistently achieves high correlation coefficients and precise spatial overlap between images, while its computational time is comparable to other successful registration algorithms. Moreover, SIFT-CPD successfully handles image pairs with significant intensity variations and local irregularities. Overall, the results confirm that SIFT-CPD is an efficient and accurate registration algorithm for medical imaging applications. The proposed algorithm has been successfully applied to register DECT images, showing potential clinical benefits, such as improved segmentation and registration accuracy in the treatment planning of NSCLC patients. Specifically, we utilized SIFT-CPD to align DECT images taken at different iodine concentrations, demonstrating improved registration results compared to conventional image modulation transmission algorithms. The improvement in registration results using SIFT-CPD facilitated the automatic transfer of enhancement and dilation parameters between the two image sets. As a consequence, the treatment planning could be optimized by applying the parameters of one image, which had been previously undergoing external beam radiation therapy, to the other image, which showed greater iodine concentration and organ boundaries more distinctively. This allowed us to apply the parameters of the two images to generate a single, uniform phase, which increased the accuracy of external beam radiation therapy and reduced the dose to adjacent critical organs by minimizing exposure to multiple doses of varying intensity. The application of SIFT-CPD to register DECT images contributed to improved treatment outcomes, including a reduction in the exposure of organs and tissues to radiation, which may ultimately lead to a reduction in the required dose of radiation for NSCLC patients. A binary star system SDSS J082239.54+304857.19 consists of two compact stars orbiting around a common center in space, in a highly eccentric orbit. Observations of this system have revealed significant variations in brightness as the stars periodically pass in front of each other. Analysis of these variations suggests that both stars are white dwarfs with roughly equal sizes and overlapping outer layers. This system provides a unique opportunity to study the physical processes involved in the long-term evolution of compact stars.

This study utilizes spectrograms taken over 37 nights to examine the 2018 and 2020 photometric eclipses of this system in detail. Spectroscopic analysis during the 2020 eclipse revealed an unexpected spectral feature around 6640 Angstroms. However, this feature failed to appear in subsequent eclipses and is believed to be an artifact resulting from an unusual geological phenomenon affecting the telescope's equipment.

Further investigation of the 2020 eclipse shows that the star on the right side of the system exhibits a broad absorption feature with a wavelength of around 6670 Angstroms, which is strongest near the point of behind the white dwarf. This feature is likely caused by the presence of a hydrogen-like iron compound, which is behind the white dwarf and excited by the star's intense gravitational field. This is not an unusual phenomenon and is similar to a feature detected in the binary star system NY Vir.

In contrast, the other star in the system does not show the same level of excited iron compounds when it is behind the white dwarf, which suggests its hydrogen layer is thinner than its counterpart. This could mean the star with the thinner hydrogen layer will eventually merge into a single white dwarf with a unique chemical composition further in the future.

Recently, transformer-based models have gained significant attention for their applications in natural language processing and more recently, time-series analysis. Despite their success, they do pose a challenge in the context of limited annotated training data, a common issue in time-series data. To address this limitation, we have designed a novel data generation framework called Time-cube (TCube), which incorporates a data sampling method utilizing a time-cube data structure. This approach adapts the principle of adjacent sampling to gather statistically independent segments of time-series data, thereby substantially decreasing the required annotated samples by around 50%. Furthermore, experiments conducted on four diverse signal types using the generated data have demonstrated comparable results to a fully labelled dataset, thereby validating the effectiveness of our method. Based on these findings, we have openly released the TCube framework at https://github.com/Alibaba-TA TCube. Our analysis suggests that TCube can significantly mitigate the need for extensive annotated training data, making it a desirable solution for practitioners working on time-series tasks. Additionally, including explicit temporal structure in models, such as via TCube, may enhance their performance. Furthermore, studying the trends within time-cubes might aid in the automatic creation of labelled training datasets, a promising area of research for further exploration in the future. Such an approach could potentially accelerate development of scalable dataset annotation methods for time-series data. Lastly, TCube has the potential to support the development of more sophisticated temporal models, such as Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, in favour of a Hamiltonian Monte Carlo method, with results showing a 10% improvement in sample efficiency in the later model favouring TCube. We intend to maintain TCube as an ongoing project, aiming to expand its applications to additional use cases in the future. Additionally, we aim to gather more empirical insights into the characteristics of time-series data by studying the trends within time-cubes, such as the observed prevalence of PARSE features in the generated samples. These trends may hold significant scientific value and could potentially guide researchers in their pursuit of developing more efficient algorithms for sampling time-series data. Ultimately, we hope that TCube may serve as a viable solution to address the challenge of limited annotated training data in time-series analysis, such as for deep learning-based seismic interpretation, a critical application in the oil and gas industry. As an example, we found that TCube's generated samples for seismic data exhibit similar properties to actual images obtained from seismic surveys, thereby substantially reducing the required annotated samples by around 50% for training a classifier on PARSE features. The primary contribution of this research is to demonstrate that an equation's loss of regularity is related to its associated Hamiltonian flow on the equation's phase space, when the equation represents the propagation of a physical field. Specifically, when an equation's solutions experience a loss of regularity, the generating symbols of the equation become irregular. This principle can be applied generally to equations with symmetries and their associated bicharacteristic curves, as well as to equations that involve first-order differential operators, such as the linearization of the Einstein equations. This research also reveals that an essential criterion for an equation to be well-posed is the accessibility of its phase space by the bicharacteristic curves. This criterion can be applied to various types of equations, including those with characteristics that enter singular regions, such as black and white holes and conical singularities. This research further provides insight into the types of equations that are well-defined in a neighborhood of a conical singularity and those that are not. Additionally, this research explores the phase space properties of the Einstein equations and the equations of the hyperbolic system of the Dirac equation. A crucial finding is that the Einstein equations preserve regularity, as do the equations of the Dirac equation when the underlying manifold is flat. However, when a curved manifold's curvature is non-zero, the Dirac equations' regularity may decrease, and this loss of regularity can be predicted based on the manifold's curvature tensor's properties. This research examines the application of LSTM in Japanese word segmentation and assesses its effectiveness using data from KAKENBOS's Japanese corpora, consisting of texts from 1960-1980 and 1981-2000. Our analysis reveals that LSTM outperforms traditional methods featuring massive modeling, including Bi-LSTM and Bidirectional LSTM with attention mechanisms. Additionally, our results demonstrate that pre-training on undivided texts can enhance LSTM's performance when applied to various training and testing data combinations. Specifically, this pre-training approach yields a significant improvement of 5.6 points in F-score when using LSTM models. When combining LSTM with a massive modeling model, we observe an improved accuracy of 93.0, representing a 0.7 point gain. Our study indicates that pre-training can be a valuable technique for enhancing Japanese word segmentation models. Furthermore, our analysis suggests that massive modeling may be unnecessary if a more efficient LSTM model is utilized. Ultimately, our research aims to provide valuable insights into the various methods employed in Japanese word segmentation. Based on our findings, suggestions for future modifications and optimizations are offered. Our proposed solution, ReShare, aims to address the issue of external resource reuse on Stack Overflow by tracking and providing accessible links to shared resources. In this paper, a method based on text similarity is presented for ReShare, which identifies relevant resources based on question-text similarity. The solution's effectiveness is evaluated through a comparison with the Stack Overflow's established resource sharing feature, and the results demonstrate that ReShare has the potential to be an acceptable alternative. Furthermore, user study findings indicate that developers prefer a more balanced approach to resource sharing, incorporating a minimum threshold for resource reuse as an essential parameter to enhance the existing feature. Consequently, a proposal for an improved Stack Overflow resource sharing mechanism, incorporating the concepts of resource ownership and limited resource reuse, is presented. A pilot implementation of this mechanism has shown promising outcomes. The paper's validation was accomplished during an online conference held by ACM. The normal rotation curves of galaxies provide substantial evidence for the existence of dark matter. However, the diversity of galaxy rotation curves is more than can be accounted for by dark matter alone. This research proposes a new explanation by suggesting that some dark matter halos contain an isothermal core that affects the outer parts of galaxies with low surface brightness. Using numerical simulations, we modeled galaxies with an isothermal core surrounded by dark matter halos and calculated their rotation curves. These simulated rotation curves were compared to those of 62 dwarf and low-surface-brightness galaxies. Our findings indicate that a galaxy's morphological type and surface brightness significantly influence its core radius. These simulated rotation curves match observed data for 65 percent of galaxies and can account for 40 percent of galaxies with flat rotation curves and those that exhibit rising rotation curves. Therefore, a galaxy's rotation curve may be flat or rise due to the presence of an isothermal core surrounded by a dark matter halo. This explanation can account for some galaxies and is consistent with others having dark matter halos. Ultimately, a combination of these explanations may be necessary to fully explain the diversity of galaxy rotation curves. This research also predicts the presence of an isothermal core in the center of dark matter halos and can inform further studies on the properties of these halos. This theory may be tested through observations of galaxies with the MAVERIC instrument on board the space mission Euclid and through data analysis of galaxies with narrow bands of optical depth. This research provides a new perspective on the properties of dark matter halos and its relationship with galaxies and can inform further studies on the properties of these halos. Individual actions against climate change are significant, yet they often compete with other daily priorities, causing many to question their own effectiveness. To boost motivation and encourage personal climate change efforts, it is suggested that people's personal values be taken into account. In this study, a values-based, interactive climate change action recommendation system was developed to motivate daily actions, especially for those with limited environmental knowledge. By aligning recommended tasks with users' core values, the system aims to promote consistent behavior, enhance task commitment, and eventually foster a commitment to daily climate action tasks. The system's interactive structure includes three components: a values assessment, a task database indexed by personal values, and a task recommendation algorithm generated randomly to initiate task variety. An experimental evaluation demonstrated the system's systematic approach to be effective in increasing daily climate action reports, even among users lacking environmental knowledge. Notably, users exhibited notable progress in maintaining their daily climate action routines. Additionally, feedback indicated the system's values-based recommendation feature to be a crucial factor in its overall success. This research made available on YouTube/Lecture videos, shows promising results and serves as a groundwork for further research on using technology to support both environmental and human values.  A video of the final presentation is available at https://doi.org/10.13140/R.978.10212.64732. All relevant project files are accessible at https://github.com/NikhilGudipati/Values-Based-Climate-Action-Recommendation. Additionally, the system can be tested at https://nikilg.com/climate-action/. Lastly, survey results can be found at https://umich.edu.

In this research, we explore the impact of a powerful magnetic field on the state equation of spin-polarized strange quark matter, taking into consideration the presence of mass terms derived from QCD. We specifically investigate how the magnetic field influences the density of quark matter and its critical values for various flavors of quark matter. Furthermore, we assess how the magnetic field affects the stability of quark stars in terms of their mass and radius. Our analysis also involves identifying the maximum mass and radius of quark stars subjected to a strong magnetic field, as well as the effects of the magnetic field on their masses and sizes in terms of different critical values of quark matter density. Lastly, we estimate the effects of the magnetic field on the gravitational redshift and the energy emitted due to the emission of photons at the surface of quark stars. Our results indicate that a strong magnetic field significantly alters the state equation of spin-polarized strange quark matter, resulting in increased maximum mass and radius values for quark stars. Moreover, the research reveals that quark stars of 1.4 solar mass under the influence of a strong magnetic field emit 1.5 times more energy due to photon emission compared to their non-magnetic counterparts, and that such a strong magnetic field results in increased light suppression of the emission process.
