We have developed a model to simulate visibility in interferograms produced by entangled two-photon interactions with certain nonlinear materials. Our model uses a probabilistic approach based on the initial state of the photons and the spatial profiles of their interaction, which corresponds to scanning electron microscopy images of these materials. By applying this model to silicon, we have made adjustments to visibility to match experimental results and used it to calculate the quantum correlation coefficient $\gamma$ for different wavelengths. Additionally, we have used our model to estimate the entanglement period and efficiency loss in various silicon regions. These calculations show that practical problems such as detection inefficiency and differences in photon interference phase can be overcome, resulting in considerable increases in visibility and the potential for periodic distributions of $\gamma$ to exceed 0.90. These findings indicate that carefully fabricated materials with controlled imperfections can enhance quantum visibility and may be useful in applications like quantum key distribution. Furthermore, we have observed that materials with distinct absorption properties at various wavelengths can exhibit distinct visibility patterns, which may lead to the development of novel quantum devices. Lastly, we propose that research on entangled photon interactions could provide insight into the development of advanced silicon photodetectors, potentially enabling the creation of silicon-based devices that leverage quantum phenomena to enhance detection efficiency and speed. This research opens up new avenues for exploring quantum technologies in conventional semiconductor manufacturing processes. Moreover, we highlight the advantages of integrating our model with commercial software designs to assess the quantum properties of semiconductor materials and devices. As a case study, we calculate the quantum correlation coefficient for a silicon photodetector designed to operate at specific wavelengths. By integrating our model with commercial software designs, we can efficiently analyze the quantum characteristics of complex devices and identify opportunities for quantum-enhanced innovations within existing manufacturing processes. This brief overview illustrates the connection between $T$-equivariant elliptic cohomology and the properties of an elliptic curve. More specifically, it explains how elliptic curves can be represented as torus-fixed points in a specific moduli space, which arises in the context of derived algebraic geometry. Drawing on this geometric framework, the talk presented in Paris in March 2021 focused on the development of a little string theory Eilenberg-Mac Lane space, constructed as a derived stack. This little string theory Eilenberg-Mac Lane space shares formal properties with the Eilenberg-Mac Lane space of integral chains on the compactified board, which represents the cohomology of the board as a graded $T$-equivariant ring. Similarly, the first cohomology of the little string theory Eilenberg-Mac Lane space corresponds to a subring within the cohomology of the board, which is generated by the square of the point representing $[pt]$ in the board's cohomology. Furthermore, the presentation of the little string theory Eilenberg-Mac Lane space is analogous to that of the elliptic curve, which is a component of the fixed point locus in the singularization of the derived stack ${\bf El}_{T}$, as constructed by Pannier and Zavaleta. This paper tackles the challenge of temporal knowledge graph completion using a novel approach that encodes cycle patterns in time. Current methods relying on time encoding often lose the original cycle relationships due to the non-markov property of sequential time models or the linear nature of vector-based encoding schemes. To address this, we propose a new cycle-aware time-encoding method that considers the circular nature of time and leverages bidirectional recurrent neural networks to capture time dependencies. Our approach starts by fluently encoding discrete time steps into continuous vectors, preserving the original cycle pattern. These encoded time representations are then combined with node embeddings to predict missing links in temporal knowledge graphs. To enhance model performance and reduce the influence of noisy time constraints, we introduce a time-aware graph attention network that prioritizes crucial time-dependent relations. Our approach exhibits superior results on four benchmark datasets, outperforming state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, we achieve success in the related time-to-prediction (T2P) task, demonstrating the capacity of our model to generate practical time-dependent knowledge graph predictions. Our source code is available at https://github.com/jinho9403/CTRE.

The sound of objects hitting various surfaces is called ground sound or impact sound. It becomes noticeable in quiet environments and under specific conditions, notably smaller objects landing on soft surfaces or larger objects landing on hard surfaces with minimal sliding velocity. Current computer-generated ground sounds are typically produced using instrumental samples or synthesized sounds without considering the physical aspects of impacts. However, in fields like virtual filmmaking and gaming, realistically created ground sounds can enhance the immersive experience. A new simulation method is proposed in this study, which involves linking the impact of objects into a soft surface through a continuous flow of material elements. We utilize this method to create a finite element model that allows for the separation of sound-producing phenomena from the impact process itself. Using a framework called adaptive simulation sampling, noise is added to the model to accurately reproduce the statistical properties of real ground sounds. Experimental results confirm that the generated ground sounds closely resemble the sounds produced in real-world environments. The proposed method demonstrates its practical application in a gaming scenario, producing high-quality, realistic ground sounds that contribute to an immersive audio-visual experience. The effectiveness of the method is quantified through listener evaluations and objective sound quality assessments. The developed ground sound simulation model is made available online for public use. The Bell nonlocality metric, which gauges how nonlocality is evident in quantum distributions, has been explored using scenarios with N parties sharing N qubits. It was previously proven that perfect correlations occur only in the case of two parties and estimated the maximum non-perfect correlations metrics for three or more parties to be at least $\frac{3}{4}$. In contrast, our findings with the metrics for non-perfect correlations, derived from the non-identity CPTP maps, reveal that it can be at most $\frac{1}{2}$. We also demonstrated that the difference between the maximum values of the Bell nonlocality metric and the non-perfect correlations metric for multiple parties can be significant. Given that non-perfect correlations are typically the norm in practical applications and research, our results may alter the outlook for Bell nonlocality in quantum information technologies. In particular, the non-perfect correlations metric may be more suitable for designing quantum systems, as the incremental gains in non-perfect correlations can be crucial in achieving efficient quantum networking. Our findings could further pave the way for the use of non-perfect correlations in random number generators to maximise unpredictability. In addition, our investigation of non-perfect correlations may offer novel avenues for controlling quantum transitions based on Bell nonlocality metrics. Ultimately, the Bell nonlocality metric, derived from the non-identity CPTP maps, provides a more versatile tool for achieving higher non-perfect correlations, making it more useful in these applications. We establish a distinction between actions occurring within the character space of a group's character variety and those that resemble toroidal behavior. Specifically, it is demonstrated that for a character variety of a group that is virtually nilpotent but not toroidal, there exists a character space action which satisfies two criteria: it is partially hybrid, yet lacks two key properties characteristic of partially hyperbolic actions, particularly those of Bowen and Nekora. Additionally, it is shown that partially hybrid actions exhibiting certain mixing behavior are essentially equivalent to partially hyperbolic actions. Furthermore, it is observed that the set of actions displaying partially hybrid behavior is dense within the set of weakly mixing actions, characterized by those preserving a ergodic measure that distributes evenly across the character space. Lastly, we outline a potential framework for constructing partially hybrid actions on character spaces of groups that are solvable but not toroidal. Lastly, we elaborate on an open-ended conjecture related to partially hybrid actions, positing that for character spaces of solvable groups that are not toroidal, there exists an action exhibiting partially hybrid behavior.}

A significant challenge in studying complex nonlinear systems is that they often default to simplistic linear behavior under standard conditions. As a result, conventional solution methods that assume linearity may fall short, making it necessary to explore alternative approaches within the dynamic systems literature. In this context, the Koopman operator theory offers a useful tool for exploring nonlinear systems' behavior while exposing their underlying linear structure. By applying the state-only model, which utilizes the Koopman operator, it's possible to map the system's state space into a linear environment while retaining the capability to model the system's behavior over time. Despite the advantages of this method, it fails to account for time-varying systems, which are prevalent in various applications. This paper proposes a new algorithm, known as the extended Koopman operator bank (EKOB), that addresses this limitation. EKOB detects the instantaneous linear structure within time-varying systems by using an observer-based approach and exposes the dynamic nature of these systems through a matrix decomposition method. This novel work facilitates the design of an adaptive data-driven observer that enables the estimation of the system's state while accounting for unknown parameters and the system's dynamics. In addition, the EKOB reveals the system's instantaneous linear structure, offering a new pathway for applications such as system identification, control, and health monitoring. The theoretical validity of the proposed algorithm has been confirmed through numerical case studies in aircraft and magnetic bearing applications. These experiments highlight the practical applications of the algorithm in discovering the system's linear structure and enabling adaptive state estimation, data recovery, and fault detection and identification. The development of the EKOB algorithm opens up the possibility of utilizing this method in dynamic systems that are difficult to model analytically. Consequently, the approaches presented in this work may find applications in a wide array of systems, including those with significant parameter variability and discontinuous transitions. The research is self-contained, with all necessary information provided in the supplementary materials. The method proposed in this paper offers a new approach to discovering the system's linear structure in time-varying systems and has potential applications in health monitoring, data recovery, fault detection, and the adaptation of system models. The research is significant because it addresses a significant drawback of the Koopman operator theory and enables various applications that were previously impossible. The approaches presented in this work may find applications in a wide array of systems, including those with significant parameter variability and discontinuous transitions. In addition, the proposed algorithm has theoretical validity and was validated through both numerical case studies and practical applications in magnetic bearing and aircraft systems.

Although Leibniz's views on infinity are widely recognized as central to his metaphysics, the varying meanings of infinity in his writing have led to disparate interpretations of its significance. As a result, some scholars see infinity as a fundamental principle of his metaphysics, while others consider it a secondary concept. A key area of disagreement among these interpretations lies in the bounded and unbounded infinity, as described in the Calculus, and its relation to infinite series. Some interpreters see the bounded infinity as the primary concept, while others believe the unbounded infinity has priority. Additionally, the notion of contingency has been overlooked in analyses of infinity, which some scholars see as inherent in the infinitesimal rather than extrinsic. By examining Leibniz's text in the context of his broader metaphysical system, this research proposes a unified interpretation of bounded and unbounded infinity, highlighting their mutual implication and relationship to his concept of negation. This research also explores the connection between the infinite series and negation in Leibniz's metaphysics, which is reflected in the alternating sign rule, thereby revealing the metaphysical system's integration with the Calculus. Furthermore, this research identifies the concept of negation as a key to understanding infinity in Leibniz's metaphysics and argues that infinity should be recognized as both fundamental and diverse in his metaphysics, encompassing both the metaphysical system and the Calculus. By emphasizing the various meanings of infinity in Leibniz's writing, this research aims to promote integration and unity among the different aspects of his metaphysics and scientific work. Lastly, this research examines the potential links between Leibniz's concept of negation and modern mathematical concepts of negation, such as in category theory, although this theme requires further investigation. A crucial step in cosmological research using galaxy clusters is typically the foreground removal process, although its impact on accuracy and results is yet to be certain. We conducted a comprehensive study which included finding the best method for removing foregrounds using CMB data and galaxies with a lensing profile typical of galaxy clusters. The methods used for the comparison were maximum likelihood estimation, genetic algorithms, artificial neural networks, artificial selection, and a novel artificial beam telescope. After evaluating the effectiveness of these methods, ten distinct foreground removal techniques were applied, resulting in the conclusion that none significantly impacted the accuracy of parameter estimation. To further minimize biases in cosmological research using galaxy clusters, we suggest incorporating an additional step in the analysis, namely numerically simulating noise in maps before the removal process, and thus making the method more reliable. This step can be implemented before a general optimization of the model and is compatible with any other method. We also observed that utilizing a beam profile instead of a simple Gaussian for galaxy distribution can significantly improve the accuracy of parameter estimation, specifically a deviation of ~1.5σ for some of the best methods considered in this study. Given the varying impact of foreground removal on analysis, we suggest making use of this simple modification to ensure unbiased results in cosmological research using galaxy clusters. To facilitate the replication of our results by the community, we made available the code used for this study in https://github.com/ivanvarughese97/Beam_Validation. Additionally, we establish a criterion for unique encoding based on a dimension called the generalized frequency spread, demonstrating that any sequence with a spread greater than the localized spectrum's dimension is linearly independent. Since the smallest possible spread is 1 plus the spectrum's dimension, this criterion is quite conservative. We also explore the relationship between codes with a spread and those that are secure against an opponent who controls multiple frequencies, discovering a surprising connection and near-optimal security for certain classes of secure codes with a spread. Furthermore, we propose a new construction, called the difference-diagonal (DD) code, which offers significant security advantages against an opponent who controls the frequency, and can be adapted for other dimensions, providing an extensive code family with considerable security benefits. We examine key aspects of the DD code, such as its linear independence, uniqueness, and capacity for multiple opponents, as well as its behavior under frequency hopping with a generalized frequency spread. We complement these findings with a detailed comparison between the DD code and frequency hopping sequences with a generalized frequency spread, revealing various similarities and distinctions between these two areas of study. Lastly, we outline potential future applications for the DD code. Document modeling-based methods have proven effective in enhancing recommender system accuracy, especially in scenarios with limited data. This is because they account for the underlying structure of user preferences and item similarities. However, a significant drawback to these methods is the potential for a large model size, which can be problematic due to memory constraints. In this research, we address this issue by proposing a compressed document modeling approach that leverages expanded contextual vectors. The key innovation is a novel contextual expansion module capable of learning representations from user and item context. This allows the model to learn a reduced document representation while still accurately capturing key contextual information. The effectiveness of our method was validated through experiments on two real-world benchmark datasets, which consistently outperform the baseline models in terms of recommendation accuracy. Notably, our approach achieves this improvement while requiring significantly fewer parameters than the baseline models. The total number of parameters in our method is approximately 18.5% that of Sofuoglu et al.'s model and 13.5% that of Hadsell et al.'s model. Building upon existing knowledge, we establish that the eigenvalue distributions of these models are characterized by a unique symmetry, resulting in the convergence of their eigenvalues to a specific point, known as the spectral anchor, with a frequency and magnitude that can be calculated precisely. To prove this, we introduce a new method of analyzing the spectral properties of these models, which involves deriving explicit bounds on the eigenvalue density that account for all order statistics of the matrix entries. This approach enables us to derive a generalized version of the Erdős-Kornai theorem for our models, which reveals a new level of detail in the behavior of the eigenvalues. The Capacitated k-Supplier with Outliers problem is a modification of the Capacitated k-Center problem, where we are given a set of potential supplier nodes and a set of customer nodes. The goal is to select at most k supplier nodes and assign each customer to one of these suppliers, with the distance to its assigned supplier being within a given tolerance ε. To achieve this, we aim to minimize the maximum assigned distance to customers, effectively finding the barycenter of customers to its assigned supplier.

In contrast, the Capacitated k-Center problem requires customers to be assigned to the closest available supplier, with no potential suppliers resulting in a customer's assigned distance being further than (1+ε) times its closest available supplier.

We present a simple approximation algorithm with a guarantee of (1+1/β + ε) times the optimal value for the Capacitated k-Supplier with Outliers problem, where β is a parameter that allows us to adjust the approximation quality. This also yields an approximation algorithm with a guarantee of (1+1/H + ε) times the optimal value for the Capacitated k-Center problem, where H is the highway dimension, a well-known metric dimension that affects the problem's approximability.

We also prove that the Capacitated k-Supplier with Outliers problem can be solved exactly in polynomial time for a reduced version of the problem, where we know in advance the barycenter of customers to its assigned supplier.

Building on prior research of Franken sources, we propose an innovative approach to generate controlled pairs of photons, as well as larger groups of photons with specific, alternating energy increments. To achieve this, we model a cavity QED system consisting of two-level atoms and a qubit reservoir to outline a method for nonlinear radiation processes. These processes activate a photonic mode that is not affected by the atoms, resulting in the emission of correlated photons. By adjusting the system's parameters to mimic Franken-laser behavior, we demonstrate the creation of single-photon and dual-photon states with controllable energy increments. Furthermore, we show the emergence of a multiphoton Franken-laser-like regime characterized by the correlated emission of odd and even numbered photons. This finding enables the controlled creation of all-photonic Schrödinger cat states. Lastly, we present a method for converting a weak classical signal into a strong quantum one, thereby enhancing sensitivity in metrological tasks. Our research offers an alternative pathway for quantum state engineering and potential applications in quantum technology. Additionally, this approach may be adapted for nonlinear cavity QED systems based on graphene for applications in optoelectronics. Both theoretical models and experimental setups are discussed. A refined Informer model is proposed, addressing two limitations of current time series forecasting models. Firstly, the original Informer model fails to exploit interdependencies between different dimensions in multi-dimensional time series, only considering linear correlations when constructing ensembles. To overcome this, an enhanced Informer model incorporates self-attention mechanisms, enabling the model to capture intricate relationships between dimensions. Secondly, the model's predictive power is hindered by its reliance on inaccurate future information, limiting its potential. To mitigate this, a new model introduces an innovative framework comprising adaptive fusion and dynamic ensemble distillation methods, allowing the model to make more informed predictions by fusing past and future information adaptably and distilling key insights from an ensemble of models. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed model consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art time series forecasting models, including LSTM, ARIMA, Prophet, GRU, GRU-D, and StGM, on diverse real-world datasets. Furthermore, the proposed model offers superior scalability and efficiency, enabling fast inference even on resource-constrained devices. Specifically, it achieves faster inference than the leading DeepAR+ model in an actual world 5-minute forecasting task, showcasing its practical utility. We introduce Pairwise Iterative Logits Ensemble (PILE), an innovative ensemble method that iteratively generates predictive models, each informed by the labels of the previous models. By starting with an initial model, PILE selects pairs of samples, adjusts its loss function to match model predictions, and trains a new model. This process continues until a predefined stopping criterion is met. The novel deep pseudo-labeling technique employed by PILE ensures that each model trains on data labeled by its predecessors. Our experiments show that PILE outperforms current state-of-the-art ensemble methods in image classification, model selection, and self-training methods, and has the added benefit of providing interpretable results. Additionally, we successfully applied PILE to solving label propagation for graph classification and reducing the impact of biased labels in image classification. Furthermore, our method surpasses the performance of current ensemble methods when combined with data augmentation and attention techniques, and we expect PILE to become a valuable resource for researchers. We investigated the numerical stability of the basis pursuit problem when using randomized singular value decomposition, and our analysis revealed how the spectrum of a specific matrix influences the representation of sparse solutions in a particular linear system. This insight led us to develop a new algorithm termed sparse basis pursuit, which reliably yields sparse solutions even in the presence of small but significant eigenvalues. The proposed method outperformed existing sparse recovery algorithms in various numerical tests. Furthermore, we demonstrated that a modified version of sparse basis pursuit can accurately solve the group basis pursuit problem, a task particularly crucial in magnetic resonance imaging signal recovery. The significant advantage of our method over other group sparse recovery algorithms was also observed in numerical studies. A key aspect of our work was the development of a protocol to rigorously establish the stability of the basis pursuit problem, a problem of considerable importance in high-resolution magnetic resonance imaging and the analysis of gravitational wave signals. A mixed finite element approach is presented for solving the vector transport equation. This method involves combining the conservative vector transport equation with the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations to simulate a variety of natural flow phenomena and solve precision navigation problems. A novel mixed finite element method is proposed that seeks the conservative velocity vector and the pressure as part of a mixed solution. This method achieves high-order numerical solutions with minimal constraints on the velocity and pressure fields. Unlike traditional finite element approaches, this mixed formulation eliminates the need for a Schur complement system, making it more efficient and easier to implement. This new method is compared to standard finite element approaches in several 2D and 3D test cases, resulting in substantial time savings without compromising accuracy. A key advantage of this method is that it facilitates conservative remapping and preserves mass in the numerical solution, reducing common issues associated with standard finite element methods. This approach is particularly beneficial for multi-physics simulations and solving navigation problems in complex systems, as demonstrated by approximately 15% time savings in 2D and 15% time savings in 3D compared to established finite element methods. This new method is expected to contribute to more efficient simulation tools for a range of application domains. Human Action Recognition, a key problem in computer vision, involves identifying human actions within video footage. The effective recognition of actions relies on detailed analysis of both spatial and temporal aspects of a video frame, enabling the identification of key regions and movements. In this research, we introduce a new multi-step spatial-temporal attention network (MS-SCAN) that focuses on detecting key actions across various human body parts. The proposed network incorporates a multi-step spatial attention mechanism with a temporal attention filter, enabling better detection of key actions by allocating more importance to certain body parts. The growth gap issue for various groups has garnered interest, with significant progress being made recently on nilpotent and solvable groups. Building on prior work by the second author, we investigate the growth gap for metabelian groups. Notably, we establish that metabelian groups with a finite presentation have a growth gap of at least linear growth. Furthermore, for free metabelian groups, we demonstrate a growth gap of at least exponential growth, with a specific growth rate constant of $\exp(1)$, thereby resolving a question posed by the first author. Additionally, we show that metabelian groups with a torsion component have an infinite growth gap, with a specific growth gap ratio constant of $1+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$, and metabelian groups with a torsion-free component have a growth gap of at least quadratic growth, with a specific growth gap ratio constant of $\frac{3}{2}$, with all obtained constants being expressed as irrational numbers to avoid a being called a spillkill property as per Diophantine theory principles. Lastly, we model the growth gap for metabelian groups with specific symplectic and unipotent properties, drawing connections from geometric invariant theory, arithmetic geometry, and the theory of formal group laws, thereby providing an innovative link between these diverse fields of mathematics. It is worth noting that the concepts applied here could also be extended for nilpotent groups with a Krull dimension of at least two. Also, this research provides an explanation of Novikov's conformally natural classification for metabelian groups with a finite presentation. We discuss a novel method to analyze a complex wave propagation problem by characterizing waves through eigenchannels, which are determined by solving a non-Hermitian eigenvalue problem. These eigenchannels correspond to distinct wave propagation modes, and analyzing them helps in identifying areas with high energy transmission and low energy scattering. This approach is applied to a two-dimensional, piecewise-constant negative refractive index slab and its associated time reversal property is explored, revealing that certain eigenchannels exhibit unusual properties, such as propagating on the other side of the slab and re-emerging in the initial location, and demonstrating that time-reversed eigenchannels can be recursively re-built from time-reversed scattering responses. Additionally, we derive a formula that calculates the number of eigenchannels in a given frequency regime and establishes that this count increases with the thickness of the index slab, and not its overall size, by determining the effective index for specific frequency ranges. Furthermore, since every wave mode can be decomposed into eigenchannels with real and imaginary amplitudes, and considering that eigenchannels with purely imaginary amplitudes are blocked at the edges of the index slab, the associated Q-factor is shown to solely depend on wave propagation parameters within the slab. Finally, by utilizing eigenchannel characterizations, we clarify the overlap relationship between wave modes and eigenchannels, demonstrating that certain wave modes can be perfectly reconstructed from eigenchannels, and identifying other wave modes that cannot be expressed through eigenchannels, particularly those involving asymmetric intensity distributions and multiple field and spatial harmonic components. This research provides a thorough mathematical understanding of waves, their characterization, and the overlap relationship with eigenchannels, thereby promoting the development of new strategies for wave manipulation and scattering through index slabs. New findings from the study of the Milky Way's center are emerging, suggesting the presence of a central bar structure that shares similarities with the center of the Andromeda galaxy. In order to investigate this claim, we carried out a computational study of the way light moves through the center of the Galaxy, using data from the Gaia Data Release 2. We modeled the center of the Galaxy as both a rotating, disk-shaped system and a separate, stationary mass pattern. By comparing computed images with real ones, we found evidence supporting the presence of both a rotating bar and a separate, flat plate of stars. We found that images of stars in the near-infrared light band fit well with the model that includes both a bar and a plate. Conversely, images of stars in the visible light band $K_{\mathrm{obs}}$ fit better with a model that includes only a plate. We outline a strategy for measuring the system's state after a specified time, incorporating a controlled outcome channel to analyze various properties. We also demonstrate that our model can emulate complex systems of interacting particles exhibiting challenging behaviors, such as instability and disorder-induced phenomena. We anticipate that a middle-ground approach, balancing simplicity and realism, can facilitate the development of practical quantum simulation systems. Furthermore, the possibility of using existing quantum simulators increases the likelihood that digital-analog quantum computing will contribute substantially to the advancement of quantum technology. \\

A graph-level feature matrix is necessary for applying plain supervised machine learning on graph-structured data.  However, graph feature extraction is often an iterative process, involving specified iterations of local node feature extraction and aggregation.  This traditional approach can be tedious and challenging, particularly when the underlying data graphs are complex and non-homogeneous.  To streamline this process, an efficient algorithm called Bonsai has been developed, accelerating the training of graph neural networks by eliminating redundant computations in feature extraction.  Bonsai achieves this by introducing a test-driven strategy that dynamically controls the depth of feature extraction, extracting features faster and reducing training time by up to 2.5 times in practical applications.  Bonsai's capabilities extend to multiple model types, including graph convolutional networks, spatial temporal graphs, and self-supervised learning tasks like graph classification and graph generation.  Bonsai is an open-source model available on the GitHub platform for public use. The discovery of neutrino oscillations has significantly altered our understanding of neutrino characteristics and the possibilities for new physics in the leptonic sector. In the long-baseline neutrino-oscillation program spearheaded by DUNE, consisting of a large isotope decoder and its near detector, a comprehensive investigation of multiple aspects of neutrino interactions within low-energy ranges is undertaken. By examining various features of the Near Detector's design and functionality, this study determines the suitability of the DUNE Near Detector for a wide range of innovative designs and functions, with a particular emphasis on enhancing the detection of new physics in the leptonic sector, specifically in searches for sterile neutrinos. It is concluded that the DUNE Near Detector, designed primarily to study neutrino and antineutrino events, can be perfectly adapted to detect differences between various neutrino appearance signatures without significant alterations to its current layout. However, substantial upgrades to the detector's functionality and capabilities can be achieved by implementing more substantial changes to its design. Consequently, this study offers valuable insights and perspectives that will benefit the enhancement of the DUNE Near Detector, thereby facilitating progress in the search for sterile neutrinos and a broad range of innovative physics in the leptonic sector. Our innovative approach refines existing estimators using complex small sample techniques, such as bias correction methods and the Fisher information matrix, to build upon existing models. We have adapted the multiple-time-step integration algorithm (MTSA) originally used in computational fluid dynamics to simulate flows involving solid particles to solve the variable density Navier-Stokes equations in an arbitrary mesh composed of non-overlapping hexahedra. This approach, modified to account for particles, can handle a wide range of time steps without compromising accuracy, even for flows with buoyancy effects that lead to chaotic and turbulent patterns. By optimizing the solution procedure, we have successfully reduced computational time, achieving a significant speed-up of around five times in a simulation of particles suspended in a fluid flowing through a 3D cube cavity. This enhanced method demonstrates an average relative error of less than 10^-5 in velocity and <10^-5 in pressure, when compared to solutions obtained using very small time steps. This efficient algorithm has potential to extensively simulate diverse flows involving solid particles and fluids with differing densities. Furthermore, we have introduced a technique to account for the solid particles in the pressure solving process, which ensures accurate pressure prediction. This approach expands the possibilities of utilizing MTSA in solving a broader range of computational fluid dynamics problems. Code implementation revealed that the main limitation of this method lies in solving a large linear system resulting from pressure solving, as other steps have a minimal impact on computational time. This barrier could be overcome by splitting the 3D hexahedral mesh into smaller cells or using alternative mesh types. This research presents a crucial step towards efficiently simulating complex buoyancy-driven particle-laden flows in a comprehensive and accurate manner. We examine the resolution to the information paradox in black holes through a theoretical framework known as the quantum gravity, particle number definition, and entanglement principle. Initially, our investigation focuses on the general principles behind the information paradox. Next, we establish the link between particle number definition and the information paradox. Following this, we discuss the entanglement principle as a fundamental quantum gravity concept that explains the behavior of entangled states throughout the black hole evaporation process. Finally, we examine the future state of the entangled system, where the thermofield decomposition plays a key role in determining the degree of entanglement between the helmet and the shell regions. The outcomes of our analysis support the idea that the information paradox can be resolved through the entanglement principle without resorting to measure problem-based solutions. Moreover, our findings indicate that the information in the black hole is indeed dispersed throughout the surrounding environment, but this occurs according to a predefined pattern that is not apparent from the HDFD perspective. As an added advantage, our approach provides a clear relationship between quantum gravity concepts and those from quantum information theory, making it essential for developing future quantum gravity resources that rely on principles from quantum information gravity. The interpretation of experimental results on nuclear broadening in proton-proton and proton-deuteron collisions depends heavily on the model used for dipole cross sections. We investigate how different models affect predictions of nuclear broadening in proton-deuteron collisions, considering that the proton-deuteron case is more sensitive to dipole models than proton-proton collisions. Our analysis reveals that utilizing a model with a dipole mass parameter varying with energy, as suggested by the GLVP model, yields significantly greater nuclear broadening compared to a model with a fixed mass parameter. Moreover, by applying the Satogata parameterization, which mimics the GLVP model's behavior at low energy, we observe that increasing the energy scale in the parameterization leads to agreement with the GLVP model's predictions. As a result, we propose combining the saturation momentum from the color dipole framework with the energy-dependent saturation momentum from the color glass condensate, as proposed by the GLVP model. This approach allows us to eliminate two free parameters in the saturation momentum, as proposed by the BDMPS Shuryak model, which provides a good approximation at low energy but fails to reproduce the correct low-$Q^2$ behavior of the dipole cross section at high energy. Finally, we demonstrate that utilizing a saturation momentum with an energy-dependent mass parameter in the Drell-Yan process is essential to reproduce the correct rapidity distribution and to explain the onset of quark-gluon plasma modification in proton-deuteron collisions at the LHC. Therefore, this variable mass parameter in the dipole cross section is a crucial factor for identifying the onset of quark-gluon plasma modification in nuclear collisions. Moreover, we emphasize the importance of utilizing an energy-dependent mass parameter for dipole models to provide consistent descriptions of nuclear broadening, of electromagnetic proton form factor at high momentum transfer, and of the onset of quark-gluon plasma modification in proton-deuteron collisions at the LHC. Additionally, we emphasize that our analysis of nuclear broadening in proton-deuteron collisions provides crucial information for determining the energy dependence of the dipole mass parameter and hence of the saturation momentum, which can be utilized to estimate the size of the proton at high energy. Consequently, we propose that the detailed study of nuclear broadening in proton-deuteron collisions at the LHC could be an excellent opportunity to explore the distinct features of dipole models and to identify the onset of quark-gluon plasma modification in high-energy collisions. This research examines the dynamics of a liquid jet confined to a channel with empty spaces at its base. As the liquid flows out of the narrow passage, it creates a region of low pressure that draws air into the space between the walls and the top of the channel. The air that enters is not simply stagnant, but rather becomes "attached" to the rising liquid and acquires a velocity that's coupled to the liquid's speed. The resulting flow pattern forms an entrained air layer with properties similar to those of a viscoelastic fluid, particularly in the sense that it resists deformation and can transfer stress across the channel width. Despite this resemblance, however, the air's behavior is ultimately determined by self-sustaining oscillations that arise from hydrodynamic mechanisms, rather than any inherent elastic properties. By comparing the experimental findings with numerical simulations using the Double-Airnumerator Method, the researchers are able to provide a detailed explanation of how the liquid and air interact and affect each other's behavior. The study is relevant to a range of applications, including fluidic actuators and active flow control systems. The research is further supplemented by an accompanying video showing the experiment in question. This experiment was conducted as part of a Ph.D. research project supported by the University of Bath. The resulting thesis has been made available online through the University's e-theses platform. The research presented here has expanded into a new area of study focusing on unsteady channel flows, which is ongoing and continuously evolving. A key outcome of this research is the development of an analytical approach, drawing on the Double-Airnumerator Method, that can be used to describe and interpret a broad range of phenomena in unsteady channel flows. This new approach shows great promise for applying statistical stability theory to analyze and understand various types of instabilities in both open-channel flows and closed channels. The statistical stability analysis suggests the presence of a sub-stable branch in the stability spectrum, which arises due to the nonlinear interaction between the primary instability and a secondary instability. The presence of this sub-stable branch could be responsible for the observed delay in the onset of shear-driven Rayleigh-Bénard type instabilities in confined geometries and might also account for the observed blocking effect, where the liquid jet tends to avoid areas where it encounters variations in the channel walls. The research also highlights the importance of considering the interactions between different length and time scales in multi-scale flows, where the utilization of an entrained air model offers a promising new direction for further research in this area. This research introduces the Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), a novel Bayesian statistical method for analyzing complex networks composed of interconnected documents. The HDTM builds upon traditional latent variable models by incorporating a graphical representation of the network, thereby enabling the identification of shared themes within documents and their associations with specific network structures. A key advantage of the HDTM is its ability to provide coherent and actionable insights into the dynamics of information dissemination within the network. In this study, the HDTM is applied to analyzing Twitter conversations surrounding emerging trends on campus at Stanford University, with the results showing the model's capability to detect sensitive information sharing among student groups. Furthermore, comparative analyses with alternative methods, such as non-negative matrix factorization, demonstrate that the HDTM offers a more comprehensive framework for examination of the network. The research provides technical proofs of the model's performance, as well as showcases real-world applications of the HDTM in two distinct scenarios. The findings emphasize that the model is an effective tool for conducting in-depth and structured analyses of social media information networks. The HDTM is made available online through the RStudio repository as part of the hdtm package. Additional technical information can be found in the accompanying user manual and technical report listed in the resources. The project is supervised by Professor Jure Leskovec at Stanford University and involves collaboration with Professor Sharad Jaiswal at Rutgers University. The current implementation of the model is based on the latent variable models described in the paper, but the authors intend to expand it to utilize the network structure more efficiently in future updates. This paper proposes an analytical technique that tracks modifications in the usage patterns of software components over time. By applying the singular value decomposition algorithm to the matrix of client-component interactions, we can identify clusters of software components that share similar usage traits. The resulting cluster analysis enables the detection of both expected and unexpected changes in software systems, as well as the identification of software components that are no longer being used. A case study employing the OpenStack software platform demonstrates the efficacy of our proposed method in detecting system modifications. Furthermore, the study reveals insights into the evolutionary trends of software components within OpenStack. We hypothesize that our proposed method can serve as a reliable tool for managing software evolution, particularly in large collaborative software development projects akin to OpenSource development. We hypothesize that our method can facilitate various applications grounded in the notion that software components that are no longer used signify past achievements, whereas those currently popularized represent the current standards of software development. Grounded on these assumptions, we endeavor to explore how software developers perceive the evolutionary trends of software components as revealed by our method. A qualitative investigation involving ten software engineers who maintain the OpenStack platform was conducted to verify our hypotheses and explore their perceived impact. We found that our method reveals useful insights into the evolutionary trends of software components, thereby aiding developers in understanding the system evolution, pinpointing past failures, discovering unused code, and identifying successful components. However, their effectiveness can be compromised when they're applied to data with varying interval lengths, as irrelevant information from longer sequences can harm the prediction. To address this, attention mechanisms are employed to mitigate the impact of irrelevant data points, regardless of the sequence length. A new attention model is proposed, combining lateral and temporal attention mechanisms to balance the trade-off between compression and information retention. The proposed model outperforms existing deep learning-based methods in forecasting the activity levels of preclinical models of neurodegeneration, using a novel benchmark dataset to evaluate model performance. To develop diverse views of the sequence, the model uses a strategy known as sampling variable-length segments, which inspires novel applications in the analysis of long time series data. A comprehensive study of Cassiopeia A was conducted through multi-wavelength observations, incorporating data from eROSSTA (radio), NuSTAR (X-ray), and Fermi LAT (gamma-ray). The analysis revealed distinct polarization characteristics in X-ray emissions from different regions of Cassiopeia A. Notably, the polarization angle of X-rays showed a notable angle of approximately 45 degrees with respect to the magnetic field orientation inferred from radio observations, as evidenced by Fermi LAT data. The absence of X-ray filaments corresponding to radio brightness indicates that the jet component has ceased to exist. The energy distribution of X-rays from Cassiopeia A follows a power law with a index of approximately 2, consistent with observations from other systems. The presence of a break in the energy distribution at an energy of approximately 100 MeV is speculated to be caused by the momentum loss of relativistic electrons due to curvature radiation. The gamma-ray emission from Cassiopeia A is contemplated to be a consequence of the interaction between accelerated electrons and nearby ions, emitting synchrotron radiation in the process. The model also offers an explanation for the distinctive, shell-like structure observed in X-ray images of Cassiopeia A. The model's sensitivity to varying parameters such as particle energy, magnetic field strength, and the size of the acceleration region was explored, resulting in certain constraints on these parameters that are expected to be further refined in the future. A crucial aspect is that the precision of the compass state can be enhanced by adjusting the number of states, thus enabling accurate calculation of a gyroscope's damping parameters even with moderate compression levels. Specifically, the variance of the compass state grows linearly with the square root of the total number of states, and is influenced by the product of the damping rates and an angular measure representing the range of the damping parameters. This finding suggests that the selection of a suitable number of states necessitates a careful balance between achieving high precision and minimizing storage requirements. This paper presents a novel technique utilizing transparent surfaces to reflect light onto a jet, enabling effective illumination in various environments. A mathematical model has been developed to analyze the light patterns produced by this method, which can be utilized in jet classification through image recognition. Experimental results demonstrate that this technique produces distinct light patterns for different jet geometries, thereby facilitating their identification through vision. Moreover, the model shows potential in applying pressure and vibration effects on jet geometries to analyze their dynamics. Overall, this approach offers an accessible and universal method for determining a jet's cross-sectional geometry with minimal setup requirements. This methodology can be applied to various research areas such as acoustics, medicine, and manufacturing processes. A specific class of spiral galaxies, known as S-type warped galaxies, exhibits a distinctive appearance of their outer rings, differing from another type, U-type warped galaxies. To investigate the origin of this difference, we conducted a study using extremely high-resolution simulations of galaxy interactions, resolving down to 10 parsec levels. Our findings suggest that S-type warped galaxies are largely influenced by the environmental factors, including tidal forces and interactions with nearby galaxies, whereas U-type warped galaxies are primarily the result of internal galactic dynamics. Furthermore, we discovered a correlation between an S-type warped galaxy's orientation and its major companion galaxy's mass and distance. This relationship suggests that a galaxy's shape is affected by a neighbor's mass when the distance between them is comparable to or larger than the galaxy's radius. This finding provides insight into the environmental factors that shape spiral galaxy appearances. To better comprehend these phenomena, four realistic galaxy models were created and added to a controlled simulation, varying factors such as a galaxy's mass distribution, spin orientation, and spin axis alignment. This allowed us to replicate both S and U type warped galaxies through their entire extent, and examine how their respective orbits, associated mass distributions, and structural characteristics varied. This research implies that for an S-type warped galaxy, the star formation outside the outermost spiral arm is typically extinguished due to the galactic companion's gravitational force, resulting in a disk with reduced mass and width in this region. Conversely, for a U-type warped galaxy, the star formation outside the outermost spiral arm is less affected, resulting in a broader area with reduced mass in this region. Additionally, we simulated six realistic encounters between an S-type warped galaxy and its major companion, modeling their orbits in detail. This led to the discovery that in most cases, an S-type warped galaxy's outer ring collapses, transforming it into a U-type warped galaxy. Conversely, in most cases, an U-type warped galaxy's star formation decreases in the affected area, turning it into an S-type warped galaxy. However, in both scenarios, a significant change in galaxy appearance requires an impact that is both strong and has a proper orientation, a phenomenon that occurs at a pericenter distance similar to or smaller than the galaxy's radius. This note presents a denotational and operational probabilistic semantics for higher-order programs that incorporate continuous random variables, with key equivalences identified between the two frameworks. Unlike existing operational probabilistic semantics, our denotational formulation employs a contextual equivalence that equates randomly generated programs, regardless of their generation order. However, this approach struggles to capture higher-order properties effectively. In response, we introduce a novel denotational property for measuring randomness, allowing us to characterize random properties within a higher-order program context. Conversely, the operational formulation adopts a big-step operational probabilistic semantics, distinct from existing steeple-chasing and small-step operational semantics approaches. Interestingly, both denotational and operational approaches converge on a key property: equivalence of random program denotations yields equivalence of their generated distributions. Furthermore, this relationship holds for any random program context. In contrast, the standard operational formulation does not validate random context randomization properties. To resolve this discrepancy, we adapt the random context framework, incorporating random contexts into a higher-order probabilistic program structure. Ultimately, the adapted random context formulation surpasses the operational formulation in their corresponding probabilistic properties. Additionally, the denotational formulation exhibits advantages in generating random variables, particularly in higher-order settings, as well as in its increased robustness to domain domain changes. In contrast, the standard operational formulation is less adaptable in these situations. In response to these observations, we propose an alternative random context formulation that directly incorporates random contexts into a higher-order probabilistic program, thus providing a more direct representation of randomness. This approach offers a more natural and intuitive framework for characterizing randomness in higher-order programs. In particular, random context randomization provides a more general property, encompassing random program equivalence, as well as random context-free properties. Furthermore, both random context randomization and random context random analysis provide more accurate measurements of randomness in higher-order programs. In addition, both frameworks can effectively capture random properties of random program context composed with other random properties. In contrast, the standard operational formulation falls short of providing random context randomization properties. To verify the feasibility of random context formulation, we examine a specific instance of random context randomization, as well as random context random analysis, in a context of probabilistic API calls. A particular type of optimization algorithm known as disjoint gradient descent was first proposed in a 2018 study, with the idea being to improve the efficiency of certain optimization problems by splitting them into multiple, simpler tasks. This paper explores an even more innovative approach, which involves not only splitting the problem but also transforming the optimization space itself. This transformed space is called a differentiability manifold and is associated with a Lie algebra structure, which allows for the simultaneous conversion of the original problem into a combined, simplified version. This new approach not only speeds up the optimization process but also guarantees a more stable and reliable solution. This paper introduces a novel method called MetroGrad, which exploits the manifold structure to accelerate the convergence of the optimization process. This new method surpasses the performance of disjoint gradient descent and achieves comparable results to established algorithms, while also being significantly more stable and efficient. This study validates the effectiveness of MetroGrad through exhaustive experiments on a variety of applications, which demonstrate its ability to produce highly accurate results both quickly and reliably. This new approach has significant practical implications, as it enables the optimization process to reach a more stable solution without excessive adjustments. This makes it possible to produce a more precise solution with fewer iterations, which in turn reduces the risk of over-fitting and achieves better performance in general. This research is significant, as it opens up new avenues for improving optimization algorithms through the transformation of optimization spaces. This study is extensive, as it investigates the various structures of differentiability manifolds and introduces a new concept of Riemannian vector fields, which are essential for developing efficient and stable optimization algorithms. A statistical method employing multiple experiments is utilized to measure the branching fractions of $\Xi^{-}$ meson decays into various states. Utilizing lattice QCD results for the Xi to baryon transition form factors, a likelihood ratio is used to calculate the branching fractions for $\Xi^- \to K^- p \pi^-$ and $\Xi^- \to \bar K^0 p$. The likelihood ratios are determined by integrating the product of two factors over phase space over multiple experimental results. The first factor represents the observability of a given signal in an experiment, while the second reflects the consistency of multiple experiments' findings. By leveraging Monte Carlo simulations, the characteristics of experimental datasets are evaluated. The analysis indicates that current experiments are incapable of detecting the $\Xi^- \to \bar K^0 p$ decay due to substantial background from $\Sigma^- p \pi^-$ decays. Simulations also suggest that future experiments with larger datasets may be able to detect this decay, while a likely systematic error in the branching fraction measurement for $\Xi^- \to K^- p \pi^-$ decay is associated with the uncertainty in the $\Sigma^- p \pi^-$ decay amplitude. The study indicates that a precise measurement of the $\Xi^- \to K^- p \pi^-$ branching fraction is attainable in experiments with XENON1T, using electron and muon tracks, and that similar research can be conducted with PANDA at FAIR utilising $e^+ e^-$ collisions as well as $\bar B$-factories. Conversely, detecting $\Xi^- \to \bar K^0 p$ decay is more challenging than determining the $\Xi^- \to K^- p \pi^-$ branching fraction. The technique can be applied in various scenarios, such as observing binary systems that produce gravitational waves and electric pulses. We demonstrate the technique's effectiveness in a simulated binary system simulation. The time delay measurement precision can be achieved with existing experimental equipment and is dependent on the quality of the signal, with the potential for significant improvement in high signal-to-noise ratio conditions. The widespread adoption of smartphones offers access to cutting-edge image processing technology, yet many developing countries lack the necessary infrastructure to benefit from automatic road condition monitoring systems. To address this gap, we propose a novel smartphone-based solution that employs existing camera capabilities to detect and classify road conditions, leveraging machine learning algorithms. By collecting and combining features from raw images, we effectively classify roads with high accuracy, outperforming existing methods. Furthermore, our system dynamically adjusts image resolution and processing complexity based on the available device processing power, ensuring optimal performance across diverse smartphone platforms. In field tests conducted in Israel and South Africa, we demonstrated the efficacy of our solution, which has significant potential to improve road condition monitoring in various countries. In particular, this method could enhance public safety and awareness in developing countries by automatically identifying and reporting hazardous road conditions. In addition, our study sheds light on the trade-offs between accuracy and processing complexity in smartphone-based road condition monitoring, which may inform the design of automatic driving systems in the future. In terms of future work, there is an opportunity to expand the system's functionality by integrating other existing smartphone sensors, such as GPS or acoustic features, to expand its applications and improve its overall performance. Additionally, it would be interesting to explore potential applications of the system in other domains, such as assessing the condition of aircraft runways or building damage following natural disasters or military operations. Finally, our study offers a novel smartphone-based solution that may reduce the risk of accidents by automatically reporting road conditions, which could lead to increased public awareness and improved local governance. In essence, this method could serve as a social tool for creating positive change. As such, we suggest that future research focus on designing and implementing successful strategies to promote the widespread adoption of the system among the general public, which would ultimately contribute to improved road safety and efficiency. To facilitate this effort, we propose that a dedicated task force be established to develop and implement an actionable plan for promoting public awareness and driving the large-scale adoption of the system. In conclusion, our study presents a groundbreaking smartphone-based solution for automatic road condition monitoring, which offers a pioneering approach that integrates image classification, processing complexity adaptation, and public awareness promotion. In the future, we aim to continue developing this system, which we envision as a key component of a fully autonomous driving system, which could revolutionize the field and make driving safer, more efficient, and enjoyable for all. Imitation learning seeks to mimic an expert's behavior by translating their actions into comparable agent environments. However, discrepancies between these two spaces can hinder the process. We develop a new approach, "Adversarial Environment Alignment" (AEA), combining techniques from importance weighting, adversarial training, and bilevel optimization to align expert and agent actions efficiently. AEA introduces an adversarial loss that enables direct alignment of sequential variables, like actions, through a variable elimination strategy. We prove the effectiveness of our method under a general condition and demonstrate its performance on complex tasks, outpacing current best methods in a continuous control experiment. A related technical proof is provided in the supplementary material. Project resources can be found at https://imitation-learning.github.io/aea/. Code is available at https://github.com/ghsghs/AEA. Research on star formation within molecular clouds has resulted in several theories, some suggesting fragments of clouds collapse into multiple stars, while others propose single stars form through core accretion. A key assumption in many of these theories is that disks formed around protostars eventually give birth to planets. However, it is debated whether these disks are stable and capable of fragmenting into new stars. Computer simulations model this process, focusing on how angular momentum influences the formation of stable disks. Contrary to previous expectations, it has been observed that protostars develop high rates of accretion without necessarily forming new stars in the surrounding cloud. This discovery challenges various cosmological theories and suggests that stable disks may be less likely than previously thought. Furthermore, it has been observed that the dust emission in some clouds correlates with the rate of protostar formation, indicating that the mass of these systems could be 10 times that of the protostars within them. This raises implications for understanding multiple star systems and the formation of planets. Most notably, it has been observed that the time it takes for a protostar to form a disk is on the order of 0.1-0.5 million years, which is a key piece of information for understanding the development of the planetary system and the potential for future star formation in the remaining cloud material. Overall, it has been observed that the time protostars take to develop a disk varies depending on their mass, indicating a level of randomness in the star formation process that could impact theories of planetary formation. This research ultimately aims to understand the relationship between the mass of a cloud and the number of stars it gives birth to, which could impact broader cosmological theories. Covering on demand, a method that was initially proposed to create the smallest possible set of association rules based on a given dataset, has been modified to work with user-specified support and confidence levels. This updated method, which characterizes redundancy among association rules by viewing it as logical entailment, has been incorporated into a new theory. This updated method, along with other associated concepts, such as the duality between covering and covering absorption, has been mathematically reinvented and its properties reestablished. This work is significant because it provides a solid mathematical foundation for the modified covering algorithm and its associated duality, which in turn has numerous practical applications in data mining. These applications include using association rules to identify key components of a customer's shopping basket contents based on transaction data and market surveys. Furthermore, this updated method has been demonstrated on a small dataset of customers' shopping habits. Additionally, computational tests using 462 datasets from the public UCI repository revealed that the modified covering algorithm is typically faster than the original covering algorithm and other existing methods. While the speedup rates varied depending on the different datasets, the tests showed a general improvement in performance, with an average speedup of'sup 1' times. More importantly, the modified covering algorithm often yielded exact results, meaning it didn't compromise on its output quality by introducing association rules that weren't already present in the original dataset. On the other hand, existing methods, such as the a priori algorithm, often produced extra, unnecessary rules that didn't reflect the underlying market dynamics. In contrast, the modified covering algorithm, much like the original covering algorithm, didn't suffer from this issue and was found to be more accurate and versatile when applied to transactional data, binary data, and gravitational potential data. Lastly, the theoretical framework of this work provides a solid foundation for future research, which could involve incorporating user-specified constraints on association rules, extending duality to utility-based association rules, or exploring new applications of covering and covering absorption in data mining. Individuals with mental health conditions are more likely to experience crime and
subsequent incarceration than those without such conditions, highlighting a need for
early mental health intervention to reduce crime rates. To identify crime types most
responsive to mental health treatment, we analyzed data from North Carolina's Disposition
Index, a comprehensive database containing information about mental health services and
criminal offenses. The data revealed that incidents of violence, property crimes, and
driving under the influence offenses decreased significantly following mental health
treatment. Furthermore, individuals with anxiety or depression were found to have lower
recidivism rates compared to those with other mental health conditions. The benefits of
mental health treatment varied greatly across different Crime Types, prompting a need
for personalized mental health advice tailored to an individual's specific criminal history. 
Our research also highlighted a significant discrepancy in mental health access among
high-risk, low-income populations and explained how incorporating AI-powered mental
health dispersion can minimize health disparities. Ultimately, our study emphasized the
importance of integrating AI systems in the criminal-justice ecosystem to facilitate
effective collaboration between law enforcement agencies and mental health service
providers, achieving optimal outcomes for both purposes.

We analyze the symmetry, reciprocity, and other characteristics of degree n polynomials with coefficients determined by sums of binomial coefficients mod n, and investigate how these properties correspond to values of the n-degree polynomial for various integers and primes. Additionally, we show that generating functions can be utilized to identify these special polynomials, as well as their general form, which enables a new method for calculating the sums of binomial coefficients mod n. This approach leverages the fundamental theorem of arithmetic, allowing us to decompose n into its prime factors and polynomialize the summation process. Furthermore, we establish a connection between the degree n polynomial and the finite Fourier transform, as well as the Laplacian operator on a cyclic graph, which demonstrates an interesting geometric intuition behind our findings. We also derive explicit formulas for degree n polynomials that are solvable mod p for any p, which showcases their applications in number theory, including the computation of p-modular polynomials. We name a particular type of these special polynomials Q-polynomials, which have the property of being solvable mod p for every p. We then investigate the properties of Q-polynomials, which have applications in studying polynomials solvable in integers. We also find connections between Q-polynomials and other known polynomials such as Euler, Fermat, Lucas types. We name a specific class of Q-polynomials as Euler-Q polynomials and study their properties. We prove that Euler-Q polynomials have the desired properties and are solvable mod p for every p. We also investigate other special polynomials such as Fermat type and Lucas type, which have similar properties to Q-polynomials. We also find connections between Q-polynomials and Chebishev scattered polynomials. We show that Chebishev scattered polynomials have the desired properties and can be obtained from Q-polynomials. We also find new results for scattering polynomials. We prove that one specific class of scattering polynomials has the desired properties and can be obtained from Q-polynomials. We also find connections between Q-polynomials and other known polynomials such as Frobenius, Jacobsthal, Faro, Koschitzki types. In order to establish a comprehensive and reliable indoor radio map, a targeted measurement collection process must be employed. This measurement process involves a data-driven optimization strategy that identifies specific locations to collect radio signal measurements from. A designated metric, called map uncertainty, is used as the basis for this optimization strategy. This metric assesses the accuracy of initially created radio maps and can be minimized through repeated measurements at specific locations. We propose an efficient method for the map uncertainty metric that facilitates optimal coverage and radio frequency accessibility. This method involves a two-stage approach consisting of an initial stage that divides the map into evenly sized blocks and calculates the map uncertainty for each, and a secondary stage that utilizes a Markov decision process to determine the optimal collection location of signal measurements. Simulation results demonstrate that this method achieves optimal results compared to alternative methods. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the map uncertainty metric exhibits a geometric relationship, thereby simplifying the computation required for each measurement collection location. This approach reduces computational complexity from an exponential factor to a linear one, thereby enhancing the efficiency of the measurement collection process. Finally, we present the results of the proposed method and compare them to the established Gecko algorithm, showcasing that this new method offers a considerable computational advantage with minimal additional computational requirements. This new method is characterized by a rapid runtime of seconds, as opposed to minutes required by the Gecko algorithm. This work presents a groundbreaking solution to a critical problem in radio map estimation and data-driven indoor localization. To this day, this problem has been the subject of numerous studies and remains an essential area of research in the field of location-based technologies. With the proposed method, we achieve a considerable reduction in average path length, averaging 35% to 45% across various scenarios, and demonstrate optimal coverage with minimal irregularities at 98.5% and 99.5% for map uncertainties of 0.1 and 0.01, respectively. This accomplishment marks a notable advancement in the field, as previous methods could only attain 92% of this coverage with irregularities at 98.5%. This work establishes a foundational template for tackling similar optimization problems, facilitating their solution with minimal computational requirements. This new method serves as a pivotal example of this approach, thereby contributing to the advancement of data-driven optimization in location-based technologies. This work is appended by an online supplementary material, accessible at <https://cybermcresearch.github.io/MDP-MapUncertainty/index.html>. This supplementary material includes an expanded explanation of the method, supplementary simulation results, and additional information on the map uncertainty metric

Unsupervised learning methods are efficient in detecting anomalies within datasets, especially when normal behavior is well-defined, by identifying deviations from typical patterns. Anomaly detection is crucial in various applications such as identifying network intrusions, detecting unusual medical conditions, and flagging fake online advertisements. Deep neural network architectures, well-suited for anomaly detection due to their ability to learn complex features, have shown impressive performance in this area. This research survey provides an in-depth analysis of using one-class classification and unsupervised anomaly detection methods that do not require labeled data, discussing their applications in real-world scenarios and standard datasets. Furthermore, the review explores techniques to improve the effectiveness of anomaly detection by utilizing side information and incorporating semantic considerations. Finally, the survey examines the challenges associated with implementing anomaly detection using deep neural networks, particularly in diagnosing mental disorders and detecting network intrusions. Some potential solutions to these challenges are suggested. This research is essential in providing a comprehensive framework for future works in this domain. Keywords: Anomaly Detection, Network Intrusions, Digital Forensics, Microservices, Data Sequences, Information Security.

Several recent advances in vision tasks have been attributed to data augmentation policies, which can often match the gains seen from increasing the size of your training data. However, the question remains whether this holds true in general, particularly since different models process information differently. A closer examination suggests that certain self-supervised and supervised models exhibit an evident correlation between data size and the effectiveness of augmentation techniques. Nonetheless, this relationship is not consistently seen in all models and is likely influenced by their design. A potential explanation is that certain models may be able to efficiently process augmented information, reducing any potential error increase and thus yielding comparable outcomes from both data size expansions and augmentation techniques. Furthermore, we propose an information-theoretic framework that can quantify how much a model can learn from augmented data and connect this concept to the curvature of the model's information intake. This theoretical foundation enables us to develop more efficient augmentation policies that enhance both self-supervised and supervised models, achieving notable improvements in practice. For instance, applying our framework to ResNet, we achieved a 12% improvement in image classification accuracy and a 15% improvement in object detection accuracy on standard benchmarks, all while requiring less computational resources than previously used methods. Moreover, we observed and verified the proposed theoretical connections between data size and augmentation techniques, registering a 4% improvement in object detection accuracy when increasing the dataset from COPOD to COCO2017. Our proposed approach and accompanying code are publicly available at https://github.com/alexrame/efficient_augmentation.
