The article explores weak convergence in statistical models, focusing on functions of parameters. It establishes rate conditions and specific cases where weak convergence holds for functions of parameters. These results are crucial and universally applicable to models with independent and identically distributed data. These principles have numerous applications, such as understanding behavior of estimators and constructing asymptotic distributions of estimators. These concepts are invaluable tools for conducting statistical analysis. To illustrate their utility, this article includes various examples of how these results can be applied to specific models. These case studies cover models with mixed parameter types, nonparametric models, models at the boundary of parameter spaces, and functions of estimators with inconsistent limits. These case studies showcase the wide range of situations in which these principles can be employed. Additionally, this article provides references to prior research and introduces new theorems that record specific findings along with their proofs. These theorems cover singular distributions, functions that change behavior at the boundary of a parameter space, functions that behave differently at various points within the parameter space, and mixed functions that combine elements with distinct limiting behaviors. A comprehensive proof is presented for one of these theorems, and alternative approaches to this theorem are proposed. These theorems represent essential tools for conducting statistical analysis, and understanding their applications requires a grasp of limit theorems for functions of parameters. To facilitate comprehension, this article includes a detailed explanation of the concepts and methods used in the presented theorems. A secondary outcome from these evaluations is the identification of specific conditions required for the consistency of certain estimators. Protecting sensitive information in data sets is crucial for maintaining confidentiality. The application of data anonymization techniques aims to achieve this by concealing identity of individual records without compromising the overall data utility. Prior research often focuses on data utility metrics such as accuracy, loss, and recovery cost to gauge the effectiveness of anonymization methods. However, these approaches have been deemed insufficient as they fail to account for intelligence that adversaries may garner from parallel data sets and advanced machine learning algorithms.

The ExpandingEta software package introduces an advanced analysis method, Extensible Time-tag Analyzer (Eta), designed to efficiently handle increasing datasets from JAXA's X-ray Imaging Spectrometer (XIS). This technique accelerates data processing by leveraging multi-threading capabilities, providing a noticeable speed boost of up to five times the standard reduction methods. Our paper outlines the implementation details of Eta and showcases its effectiveness in analyzing time-segmented data from unsmoothed two-dimensional XIS images. We demonstrate the versatility of Eta by applying it to various data sets, including astrophysical events and laboratory data, all of which are publicly available on the XIS Calibration Database. The Eta method further enables the identification of signal patterns within multi-channel data sets and has future applications in analyzing data from various scientific instruments. Furthermore, our work focuses on an innovative approach to identify signal pattern within multi-channel data sets. To facilitate usability, our software package includes an intuitive graphical user interface (GUI) facilitating analysis operations. All the software tools used in this research are available for download on the XIS Calibration Database website. The current version of the software can be obtained via github, at the following address: https://github.com/XIS-CD/Eta. Our team welcomes user feedback and looks forward to collaborating with the scientific community to further develop Eta. The website provides information on the software's latest updates,eta version 1.3, released on March 31, 2021. Additionally, our section on known issues highlights ongoing challenges with Eta. Lastly, our paper outlines future plans for further enhancing the software. To this end, our work aims to promote transparency in software development by detailing the design structure of Eta in the accompanying figure. Although the specified approach has proven effective, we acknowledge that the separate implementation modules of Eta do present drawbacks in terms of modularity. Therefore, in future versions of the software, we intend to revisit this architecture and strive for a more streamlined, modular structure. In conclusion, our work showcases the versatility of Eta in analyzing various data sets, and we look forward to continuing to support the scientific community in their research endeavors. In this process, we plan to maintain close communication with the community via the etawaremail list. Interested researchers can join this list by sending an email to etamailinglist+subscribers@googlegroups.com with the subject "subscribe." Furthermore, our work highlights several outstanding issues with Eta, as listed in the section on known issues. We strive to address these challenges

We examine a multi-agent game model involving a large number of agents and their corresponding dynamics. Each agent adheres to specific system dynamics defined by ordinary differential equations, with interactions occurring through a mean field effect, where the outcome depends on the entire system. The objective of this study is to identify scenarios in which multiple equilibrium points can exist and to analyze how restricting these solutions to ones that meet certain regularity conditions affects the equilibrium dynamics. The work builds on previous research by Ganguli et al. and extends it by incorporating such constraints. The analysis reveals that imposing regularity conditions may complicate or eliminate situations in which multiple equilibrium points can exist. The study also explores the effect of limiting the number of equilibrium points on the corresponding small-time approximation. The findings indicate that restricting nonidentical equilibrium points comes with a cost, as it may introduce discrepancies during small-time periods. The support of our argument is provided by a time-three small-time approximation result. The research also offers a counterexample illustrating the importance of limiting nonidentical equilibrium points, as well as a result demonstrating the relationship between equilibrium dynamics and the distribution of solutions. The analysis reveals that identifying identical equilibrium points relies on solving a Liouville-type equation. The work concludes by proposing a candidate for a minimax problem involving growth constraints and mean-field interactions. The research offers a range of open questions and potential applications across the fields of partial differential equations, control theory, and macroeconomic modeling. The objective of this research is to assess stellar motions within strings of stars linked by shared ancestry. We concentrated on deciding if these cosmic structures are composed of chemically uniform stars also found in their surrounding fields. As a first attempt, we examined the open cluster NGC 2509, checking the chemical compatibility of its member stars and comparing these to nearby field stars sharing similar properties. To achieve this, we gathered data from multiple sources, specifically parallax measurements from the Gaia EDR3 and optical spectroscopic data collected from the 2.5m telescope at the Magellan Observatories. Our analysis involved determining stellar velocities, metal abundance, and radial velocities for 21 members of the cluster, discovering 11 new members and incorporating four previously studied stars. We established an internal metallicity dispersion of less than 0.10 dex and calculated the radial velocity dispersion as 0.63 km/s. Comparing the metal content of these cluster stars to nearby field stars showed them to be chemically similar, but with limited data available for the field stars. We concluded that the cluster stars have the same chemical composition as the nearby field stars. Nonetheless, a larger and more extensive study is needed to draw a comprehensive conclusion about the chemical homogeneity of these stellar strings. Our research also highlighted the usefulness of precise parallax measurements, coupled with accurate spectroscopic data, in determining the current and past movements of these stars, as well as their expected motion over time. For example, the spectroscopic data revealed that none of the cluster stars are moving rapidly enough to escape the cluster's gravitational pull, suggesting they have sufficient kinetic energy to remain within it. Additionally, we identified NGC 2509 as a rotating cluster, specifically establishing its net angular momentum and estimating its rate of change. Using the Gaia EDR3 data, we calculated the mean stellar velocity along the line of sight for the cluster as 15.1 km/s. Finally, our study found the cluster to be situated at a distance of 794+78 pc and showed the cluster's luminosity class II stars to be younger than the cluster's population. Specifically, we determined their ages as 200-250 million years for the II stars and 300-350 million years for the Ia and Ib mixtures. Additionally, we calculated the cluster's mass as approximately 1030 M⊙ and its radius as approximately 16 minutes of arc at a distance of 794 pc. Current methods heavily depend on trained models, which can fall short in handling unique, user-created outfits. Our proposed approach incorporates a novel network that identifies outfit pieces with high precision, also acting as a preliminary classifier for outfit items. We introduce an alternative loss function that enhances item detection on mismatched items, leading to improved performance. As a user creates an outfit, our system detects each piece and immediately removes matched items from the outfit description, preventing inflation of the description and thereby improving detection of additional pieces. We conducted experiments using a fashion dataset with user-created outfits and a related dataset with accurate labeling for training, revealing that our method surpasses existing techniques by at least 3% in accuracy. Notably, our method achieved a 9% improvement in detecting multiple outfit pieces at once. Our proposed approach and accompanying code are available at \url{https://github.com/Princeton-VL/DressCode}. Advances in quantum information science are propelling resource theories of quantum mechanics forward, where the objectives of such theories are to specify observable properties and usable resources to achieve those objectives. Nonclassical resource theories in particular have generated significant interest due to their potential to outperform classical theories in various applications. However, the existing framework for nonclassical resource theories is largely based on isolated quantum systems, which may not adequately account for scenarios where these resources interact with their surroundings in various ways. To address this limitation, we introduce a unified approach that encompasses diverse nonclassical resource theories based on how they handle environmental influences, thereby expanding the scope of such theories to cover a broader range of applications. To illustrate the utility of this new approach, we develop a nonclassical resource theory based on quantum jump conditions that incorporates tools like conditional free operations, and demonstrate its applicability to optical squeezing and directional squeezing applications. Importantly, we show that traditional optical squeezing resources can be expressed as a special case within our proposed framework, thereby establishing a connection between resource theories based on quantum jump conditions and traditional resource theories. Furthermore, we predict the ability to generate directional squeezing without sacrificing optical squeezing, thereby opening up new avenues for research and furthering our understanding of nonclassical resource theories. Additionally, we outline key comparison points with traditional resource theories, which enables systematic assessments of related achievements in different contexts and contributes to a deeper understanding of the resource theory landscape. Hence, our proposed approach offers a valuable framework for navigating and integrating diverse nonclassical resource theories, which will ultimately guide the development of achievable applications. Finally, we offer an outlook on the challenges and opportunities presented by the diverse nonclassical resource theories, and highlight potential research directions where quantum information theories outperform classical information theories. Importantly, we emphasize the significance of integrating advanced quantum technologies with their surroundings rather than isolating them. Furthermore, we showcase the immense potential for creating meaningful contributions to science and technology through the study of nonclassical resource theories, which will ultimately benefit the global community through innovative technological advancements. To achieve this, we encourage the integration of cutting-edge quantum technologies with environmental responses rather than their isolation. To promote this integration, we provide a general framework for nonclassical resource theories and illustrate its utility with a specific directional squeezing example, which creates new opportunities for research and development in nonclassical resource theories. Ultimately, we anticipate this research to inspire a new generation of researchers to develop innovative applications of quantum information theories, which will ultimately benefit the global community through innovative technological advancements. Federated learning is a decentralized AI paradigm that enables a shared neural network to be constructed across multiple devices while respecting their privacy. However, the existing efficient algorithms for federated learning typically sacrifice scalability by confining the parameter updates to individual clients. To address this limitation, we have developed FedBuff, an innovative scalable federated learning algorithm that maintains privacy while allowing collective parameter updates among clients. The FedBuff algorithm leverages a specialized neural network structure with buffering mechanisms that accommodate on-device training for multiple tasks simultaneously, thereby enhancing scalability without compromising accuracy. The key implementation details include the integration of a buffering mechanism for efficient computation of stochastic gradient and the creation of an adaptive learning rate framework that accelerates convergence. The comprehensive experimental results reveal that FedBuff surpasses existing scalable and private federated learning algorithms in terms of both generalization and communication efficiency, with notable performance superiority in distributed training of deep neural networks for classification tasks using real-world data sets, as well as in simultaneous on-device training of multiple neural networks for computer vision tasks at a constant communication cost. The associated code for FedBuff can be found at https://github.com/tieongong/FedBuff. The C++ implementation of FedBuff can be accessed at https://github.com/tieongong/FedBuff_C. The main technical contributions of this study are summarized as follows: (1) The introduction of the FedBuff algorithm for scalable and private federated learning, which enables collective parameter updates among clients at a reduced communication cost; (2) The proposal of a buuffering mechanism for efficient computation of stochastic gradient; (3) The development of an adaptive learning rate framework that accelerates convergence; (4) The experimental validation of the FedBuff algorithm on distributed training of deep neural networks for classification tasks and simultaneous on-device training of multiple neural networks for computer vision tasks. The study is motivated by the burgeoning needs of scalable and private federated learning algorithms due to the rising importance of privacy in modern AI applications. To address these requirements, the FedBuff algorithm directly contributes to the rapid advancement of AI technologies by facilitating the efficient and secure construction of a shared neural network across multiple devices. The existence of primordial black holes (PBHs) that comprise all dark matter is an intriguing hypothesis. To understand its plausibility, researchers must evaluate how the mass of PBHs affects the dark matter density. A 2021 study predicted that PBHs in the mass range of $10^{-16}$ to $10^{-18}$ solar masses could satisfy the dark matter requirement. More recently, scientists have used machine learning to model the outcome of an all-dark-matter scenario and found that PBHs with masses between $1.2 \times 10^{-17}$ and $1.4 \times 10^{-17}$ solar masses are most effective. Furthermore, they found that PBHs with intermediate masses have an advantage over those with lighter or heavier masses. To confirm these findings, researchers must look to future gravitational-wave detectors like LISA, which is expected to provide critical insight into the possibility of an all-dark-matter scenario. To improve their predictions, scientists must utilize more sophisticated models that account for the complex interactions of matter and dark matter, and how they impact the evolution of structures within the universe. Ultimately, finding answers to the mysteries of dark matter and primordial black holes requires collaboration across fields, including astrophysics, cosmology, and space exploration, as exemplified by the upcoming Nancy Grace Roman Telescope. By working together, researchers can ensure that future missions like the Roman telescope are designed to provide the necessary perspective for understanding the nature of dark matter and the universe. To this end, a panel discussion was held, featuring experts from NASA and other organizations, who shared their perspectives on the future of PBH research and the potential role of the Roman telescope in making groundbreaking discoveries. As the discussion highlighted, the path to understanding the nature of dark matter and the universe involves many options, and the decision of which approach to use is driven by the scientific questions being asked and the technological capabilities available. To this end, a decision-support tool has been created that evaluates various scientific objectives, such as observing the galaxy and the universe, searching for the signs of dark matter, and studying the potential of PBHs in making the dark matter requirement. Using this tool, researchers can compare the effectiveness of different approaches, such as using the Roman telescope for understanding the nature of dark matter and the universe, searching for the signs of dark matter, and studying the potential of PBHs in making the dark matter requirement. Simulations show that the distance between two adjacent islands in the raft increases exponentially, with a rate dependent on the viscosity of the surrounding fluid. This rate approaches that predicted by earlier theory when the fluid's viscosity is high enough to prevent particles from re-adhering to each other. Gallium nitride's practical limitations at room temperature stem from its low hole mobility. Introducing an aluminum GaN layer with a 2D electron gas proves effective in enhancing mobility, but this comes with a cost of elevated electron concentrations. A more efficient approach involves growing a template with a mobility-enhancing interface, allowing the electron concentration to be minimized. This is exactly what researchers in Japan have achieved, developing a room-temperature hole mobility of 102.9 cm^2/Vs in gallium nitride with a layer of ZnGeN2, and a remarkable 104.3 cm^2/Vs with a layer of MgSiN2, both surpassing the existing record by a significant margin. By chemically removing the template after mobility measurement, the researchers confirmed that the advanced mobility properties were a direct result of the underlying lattice structure. This breakthrough promises a major advancement in gallium nitride technology, opening up new possibilities in optoelectronic devices. A layer of MgSiN2 is particularly beneficial, as it also reduces the template's built-in electric field, enabling a more efficient transport of holes. This unique property makes gallium nitride with a MgSiN2 template an ideal material for high electron mobility transistors and Gallium Nitride Photonic Integrated Platforms.

Large-scale large-scale underwater glider navigation tasks pose challenges for optimal control due to large action and state spaces and delayed feedback signals. Current applications of reinforcement learning largely rely on experience replay but suffer from inefficiencies in policy evaluation, causing high computational requirements for large-scale problems. A new variant of the SRGP-SARSA algorithm called SPGP-SARSA is proposed, addressing this issue through a more efficient approximation of the Gibbs measure sampling process. A prior theoretical analysis proved the SPGP-SARSA algorithm's convergence under certain conditions and demonstrated a notable reduction in computational complexity by a factor of O(K^2) compared to previous methods. Empirical results show significant performance improvements over state-of-the-art algorithms in underwater glider navigation tasks, achieving a 5.45 times faster convergence on average. A 80% reduction in computational complexity also verified the theoretical convergence of the proposed algorithm. This successful application of SPGP-SARSA opens up new possibilities for solving large-scale optimal control problems and enables its application in various real-world problems. Furthermore, a range of new variants of SPGP-SARSA are introduced, including a distributional version known as SPGP-DM, offering enhanced calibration through a more efficient approximation of the empirical measure. A practical evaluation of SPGP-DM in navigating a virtual underwater glider via video footage yields superior navigation outcomes with only a marginal increase in computational complexity. This innovative approach paves the way for the potential application of SPGP-DM in real-world problem-solving. A comparative analysis of SPGP-SARSA and other leading experience replay algorithms reveals a notable reduction in computational complexity and efficient data utilization by a factor of O(K^2), yielding substantial practical benefits. A source code implementation of the proposed algorithm is available for public use at the specified URL. To promote further research into optimal control through reinforcement learning, a new variant of SPGP-SARSA known as SPGP-NSARSA is introduced, addressing a previously recognized shortcoming in prior algorithms. This new variant efficiently combines the benefits of natural policy gradients and experience sampling without incurring high computational costs. A key empirical finding is the achievement of near state-of-the-art outcomes in navigating a virtual underwater glider via a new variant of the SPGP-SARSA algorithm known as SPGP-NSARSA. Building upon the breakthrough by Pinkall and Schwarz in 1994, we explored a comprehensive framework for creating new isothermic surfaces by combining the minimal surface flow with specific transformations. This kind of framework was initially applied to elliptic surfaces, leading to the generation of novel minimal surfaces, such as a surface that we found to be a previously unknown scroll in spacetime. Additionally, we discovered that certain combinations of these transformations yield surfaces with unique geometric properties, including compatibility with a conformal parameter and the existence of a nonzero tangent vector, thus expanding the possible applications of such frameworks to isothermic surfaces, where the known solutions account for only a minority of all possible solutions. Furthermore, a direct relationship was established between the solutions to the Goursat problem and the isothermic surface flow, including a demonstration of the dependence on a specific singular solution, as well as a description of the general form of the solutions to the Goursat problem. Finally, as a direct result of the comprehensive framework, a new family of solutions to the minimal surface equation was found, including a demonstration of a surface that we found to be a previously known scroll in spacetime, as well as a collection of other extremal surfaces, including four newly discovered D-type solutions, a known scroll in spacetime, a known minimal surface, a known maximal surface, a known co-associative minimal surface, a known minimal surface, a known maximal surface, a known co-associative minimal surface. This report concludes with a discussion of potential future applications and research directions, including extending the framework to 1-forms and 2-forms, and using the framework to generate new D-type solutions, as well as a new minimal surface in spacetime.

This study proposes a novel kernel-based method for projection operators that outperforms traditional projection techniques like the Galerkin method in terms of convergence and approximation. Our approach generates a sequence of successive projections onto specific subspaces without explicitly constructing the subspaces or their associated operators, instead using a kernel function to determine the projection of interest. We analyze the method's convergence properties and demonstrate its superiority over standard projection methods in various numerical tests. Additionally, the method is adaptable to different kernel types and can be applied to diverse problem domains including nonlinear partial differential equations, random partial differential equations, and dimensionality reduction tasks. Our code is openly accessible on the GitHub repository https://github.com/amir-ataei/Kernel-Based-Projections. Furthermore, this study offers a comprehensive review of the mathematical underpinnings of kernel methods. We examine key concepts such as the reproducing kernel Hilbert space, kernel ridge regression, and kernel PCA, illustrating their relevance to partial differential equations and dimensional reduction applications. Lastly, we explore the recent advancements in machine learning kernel methods, including their use in solving nonlinear partial differential equations and random partial differential equations before arriving at the core of our research - a novel kernel-based projection method. This paper delves into the $\omega$-analogues of Dowling polynomials, a family of combinatorial structures that can also be represented as linear combinations of poset statistics. This study investigates the notion of strong shift equivalence among weighted graphs of finite height. We demonstrate that for graphs of finite height, insplits and outsplits are equivalent concepts, thus a graph is strongly shift equivalent to another if it can be transformed into the other through an insplit or outsplit operation. As a result, this relationship provides a unified explanation for previously obtained results involving flow graphs, motivational orientation, and biviosoidal graphs. In addition, this relationship leads to the development of a new criterion for determining if two flow graphs are strongly shift equivalent. Next, we show that the set of insplits or outsplits in a weighted graph of finite height can be reduced to a finite generation, meaning that a finite number of insplits or outsplits can express all other insplits or outsplits in the graph through a series of product operations. Finally, we explore potential applications of these findings to natural language models and the representation of semantic relationships among words. For an additional challenge, it is proposed that future researchers examine the potential connection between the semantic relationship among words and the topological structure of words within a sentence. This investigation could provide valuable insights not only into graph theory but also into the complex nature of language itself. Additionally, it is suggested that future researchers examine the potential connection between the geometric distribution over graphs and the distribution of words within a sentence in a corpus. This potential link could not only offer new perspectives on graph geometry but also reveal previously unseen relationships among linguistic elements. Lastly, it is proposed as a future area of research that the topological structure of a semantic relationship among words could provide more comprehensive and detailed information compared to the distribution of words in a corpus. This might be accomplished by constructing a new type of graph that encodes not only local interconnections among words, but also their complex organizational patterns at a deeper level of analysis. We utilized the fast moving probe technique to investigate the heavy quark potential at Intermediate energies (around the quark confinement scale). By incorporating spectral information and analyzing both string breaking and ground state properties, we examined the anisotropy of the potential in both spatial and temporal dimensions. Additionally, we enhanced the potential model to account for the string flux tube's spiral and quasi-chromoelectric field variations. Our analysis revealed the presence of an anisotropic string breaking energy difference and a temporal anisotropy, while spatial anisotropy was found to be negligible. Furthermore, we identified the quasi-chromoelectric field as the primary driver of string breaking in the flux tube. Our findings suggest that temporal glueball masses are more sensitive to the nature of the vacuum than their spatial counterparts. We also demonstrate that the string flux tube exhibits behavior akin to a quasi-one-dimensional system. Overall, our study provides crucial insights into the anisotropic properties of the heavy quark potential and the complex dynamics of the QCD ground state. The work is an essential extension of previous studies, offering a more comprehensive understanding of the heavy quark potential at Intermediate energies. The research is relevant to current efforts in lattice QCD, potential models, and string theory, making it a valuable contribution to the field. The calculations were performed using an $SU(3)$ gauge theory with three valence quark flavors, implemented on a $32^3\times64$ lattice with pion mass approximately $130$ MeV and a renormalization group fixed mass around $30$ MeV, utilizing an anisotropic coupling $\xi=s\rho=\frac{a_t}{a_s}=4$. The measurements included spectral data from moving probes with a speed of $v_\perp=v_\parallel=0.45c$ and an extensive range of distances $r$ (from $0.3$ to $6.2$ $F_{\sigma}$). The spectral projections onto the ground and string breaking states were sufficient to determine the anisotropic heavy quark potential. The potential analysis revealed the presence of an anisotropic string breaking energy difference and temporal anisotropy, while spatial anisotropy was found to be negligible. Furthermore, we identified the quasi-chromoelectric field as the primary driver of string breaking in the flux tube. Our findings suggest that temporal glueball masses are more sensitive to the nature of the vacuum than their spatial counterparts. The string flux tube exhibits behavior akin to a quasi-one-dimensional system.

In contrast to earlier studies using external knowledge, our method seamlessly incorporates this interaction into the existing model architecture, eliminating the need for additional processing or fancy designing. Experimental results clearly demonstrate that OREO-Longformer outperforms other models by a considerable margin, as substantiated in our findings. Furthermore, we create a comprehensive knowledge graph from Wikipedia's hidden sections, comprising approximately 202 million nodes and 417 million edges, to facilitate the interaction process. Lastly, we explore the underlying mechanisms of our enhanced model to determine how it harnesses the power of external knowledge to deliver superior performance. Our findings indicate that the longer model's capacity to interact with external knowledge correlates with improved performance in question-answering tasks. With these breakthroughs, we believe a paradigm shift in the development of language models using external knowledge has become inevitable. Alongside routing and computation, high dimensional expanders have numerous applications in theoretical computer science. Their combinatorial structure, particularly relevant to simulated routing and computation, has received significant attention in recent years. As simultaneous resource problems for high dimensional expanders can be mapped to a hypergraph, researchers investigate the threshold property in high dimensional expanders, understanding when a high dimensional expander transitions from a non-expander to an expander state. Inspired by Kahn and Szemerédi's work on a threshold theorem for tilings, researchers aimed to prove a threshold theorem for simultaneous resource problems, influenced by a conjecture by Tregenfeld. Our results reveal that the conjecture does not hold, and we present an alternative model where the threshold theorem's principles can be applied. We also demonstrate a novel application of the threshold theorem, and in conjunction with Tregenfeld's conjecture, reveal a sharp threshold for the hypothesis of efficient computation on expander graphs. Furthermore, our research yields a proof of a disjoint parallel partition property, a notion first introduced in a paper by Tregenfeld and an alternative model we proposed. In the course of our research, we introduced the concept of efficient computation on expander graphs and a hypothesis known as the efficient computation hypothesis, which suggests that the transition from non-expanders to expanders can be efficiently computed. We also analyze the thermodynamic limit of high dimensional expanders and observe a phase transition and a sharp threshold at a critical temperature. We present an alternative model for simultaneous resource problems and demonstrate a threshold theorem for this model. We further show that the efficient computation hypothesis is equivalent to a threshold theorem for simultaneous resource problems and speculate that high dimensional expanders transition from non-expanders to expanders at a critical temperature. We conclude by exploring potential applications (such as the phase transition in simultaneous routing and computation) and speculate that high dimensional expanders may transition from non-expanders to expanders at a critical temperature based on the behavior of the efficient computation hypothesis. Recent advances in large language models have highlighted their capacity to handle tasks via prompts. Typically, researchers and developers draft customized prompts that were either created before or analyzed during pre-training. Nonetheless, there remains a critical question of of how these models will respond to unseen, novel prompts. In this research, we explore how well LLMs generalize to unseen prompts while examining their performance when the task prompts themselves become part of the data to be predicted. We utilize the OMPD dataset and find that, while significant progress has been made, there remains a substantial performance gap when the models are asked to handle unseen prompts. Importantly, we identify that adapting task prompts can yield substantial gains in performance, underscoring the necessity to develop methods that can effectively craft prompt datasets. We also set out new goals for prompt construction methods, proposing that such methods should maintain their effectiveness even when the models are asked to handle unseen prompts, whereas others only show improvements when the prompts are from the pre-training phase. Lastly, we introduce a new metric called prompt diversity, suggesting that high diversity in prompt construction is correlated with improved performance when adapting task prompts. This research provides significant insights into the capabilities and limitations of LLMs and suggests fresh avenues for investigation in prompt construction. A thorough examination has been conducted for UGC 8839, a spiral galaxy with an extremely dense HII region population, exceeding that of the Milky Way by nearly 10 times. This study employed data from DSS, SDSS, and HyperLEDA to accurately identify and classify 203 HII regions within the galaxy. These HII regions were further categorized based on their angular sizes and peak surface brightness values, both of which were found to correlate strongly with the galaxy's luminosity. Notably, the distribution of these HII regions appears uneven, with a substantial absence of activity in the galaxy's central region. In contrast, the outer regions of UGC 8839 exhibit a dense concentration of HII regions. This unique pattern suggests the presence of a bar-like structure spanning from the galaxy's center to approximately 30 seconds of an arc, within which star-forming activity remains severely suppressed. Multiple theories, including the theory of a gas bar pinching gas out of the galaxy's center, may help to elucidate the underlying mechanisms governing UGC 8839's star-forming behavior. Overall, the complex and unusual population dynamics of UGC 8839's HII regions render this galaxy an especially intriguing subject of study in the field of research. This research work was done under the supervision of Dr. Rajiv Chaubal and was presented in front of the UC Berkeley Astronomy Department graduate students committee in May 2019. Generating high-quality audio data without direct supervision is extremely challenging. In our investigation, we create a supervised method for producing realistic, unconditional audio data by utilizing a spectrogram-based approach. This method combines a conventional generator network with a unique, adaptive loss function that analyzes a short-term spectrogram and a long-term average spectrogram. The adaptive loss function not only promotes spectrogam accuracy but also preserves the overall data structure. Additionally, our method incorporates a voice activation control mechanism, allowing the model to produce silent segments. By using this method, we produced high-fidelity audio clips without manual labeling. The produced audio data exhibits superior quality and structural integrity, outperforming previously published label-efficient methods. Notably, our method achieves comparable audio quality to supervised methods while reducing the need for expensive annotation processes. The proposed technique represents an efficient strategy for generating realistic, unconditional audio data in short videos. Due to ongoing uncertainty surrounding pandemic predictions, reliable data is often limited to state-level infection reports, with associated uncertainty. We develop a novel end-to-end framework, capable of estimating both infection rates and adherence to mitigation policies in contiguous states, with the aim of informing regional lockdown decisions. The framework involves a two-component neural network, designed to solve a constrained optimization problem, making explicit use of uncertainty quantification, especially concerning infection reporting numbers, thereby facilitating variable constraint enforcement. The framework is then applied to a model of disease spread and an economic model of pandemic costs to inform state-level lockdown decisions, guided by a decision theory that prioritizes both lives saved and economic losses. Numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of this integrated approach, highlighting its potential to inform policy decisions, particularly in scenarios involving limited data availability. The framework is further explored through various numerical analyses, addressing a range of decision-makers' priorities, such as a case study focused on New York and Connecticut during the initial COVID-19 wave. The associated code is publicly accessible on the Git repository https://github.com/atcold/COVID-Lockdowns. Additionally, a standalone web application has been developed for visualizing and interacting with pandemic data, accessible at https://covid19.cds.wisc.edu/. The authors declare no conflicts of interest. Funding information is available online. Both projects are open-source, maintained by the Cold Team at the University of Wisconsin-Madison. https://cold.team.

Recent advancements in Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) have significantly impacted Relation Extraction (RE), a crucial subtask of Information Extraction. Due to the cost and effort involved in manually labeling data, there is a significant shortage of high-quality annotated datasets, particularly for less common entity types. To address this issue, we introduce EFelidae, a innovative framework that leverages Embodied Cognitive Agents to automatically generate labeled datasets. This method's embryo has demonstrated impressive results in simulating human labelers' performance on the SemEval-2010 task. Building upon this foundation, we have established a comprehensive knowledge base containing over 100,000 annotated RE instances and corresponding arguments, which will serve as a resource for further research in RE. Moreover, we propose a novel and efficient agent that uses RE outcomes to refine its data-driven approach, demonstrating improved performance in the RE task. In a thorough evaluation, our system outperformed existing methods, achieving state-of-the-art results on six benchmark datasets. Notably, it achieved top-tier results on two newly introduced datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness in diverse domains. All associated model weights, pre-trained embeddings, and gold datasets are freely available for public use at https://github.com/argman/EFelidae. This research was supported by the Israel Strategic Academic Partnership (ISAP) funding.

Our analysis considers multiple scenarios, including cases where the boundary of the inner ball affects the overall eigenvalue. Conversely, when the inner ball's boundary does not impact the eigenvalue, variations in the inner radius lead to continuous changes in the eigenvalue. Lastly, when an external factor influences the eigenvalue, changes in the inner radius result in piecewise-defined eigenvalue functions. In addition to these findings, we also identify specific conditions under which certain nonlinear equations have no solutions. By applying a variety of mathematical approaches, such as approximate arguments and comparison theorems, along with further analysis and examples, we validate the efficacy of these methods in determining the properties and behavior of the resulting eigenvalue functions. Supervised learning approaches for graph data analysis can be effective, but they struggle with complex structures like hypergraphs. One solution is to apply graph neural networks (GNNs) to the subgraphs obtained from the projection of a hypergraph onto its edges. However, such an approach has its limitations, as it does not utilize the full information available in the structure. Another issue arises when multiple hypergraphs are involved, as their projections can be ambiguous, leading to possible wrong identifications. To address these challenges, we develop a novel method for learning hypergraphs from their projections, which incorporates the overall structure and provides correct identifications in cases of multiple hypergraphs. Our approach introduces a new technique for encoding hypergraphs and conducts extensive experiments on existing benchmarks, as well as new creations, to demonstrate its performance and validity. Notably, our method outperforms the best existing approach by 11.5% in correct classification and provides correct identifications for all hypergraphs in difficult scenarios of multiple hypergraphs. The source code can be found on GitHub at https://github.com/jase-clay/HyperGraphProjections. In addition, our study on new benchmarks highlights the need for increased scrutiny in the evaluation of GNN-based solutions for the projection task. To reproduce our results, more information can be found at https://hypergraph-projections.readthedocs.io/en/latest. A paper is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.05874. The project has also been presented at AISTATS 2022 under the title 'Learning Hypergraphs from Their Projections', as part of the best poster award nomination. Comprising 99,562 image-ray pairs, PAXRay is built upon the CXR8-Inst dataset and incorporates an augmented dataset with access to 40,000 cases from the NUHC dataset, it receives funding from FLI. We utilize two algorithms as baseline references for the evaluation process. One algorithm specifically designed to address the PAXRay dataset's complexity is the Multi-Mask Model, it excels in its performance with an $F_1$ score of $0.8139$ on the PAXRay dataset. Despite its effectiveness, the Multi-Mask Model is impractical for deployment in real-world applications due to its computational requirements. An alternative model, the Simple-U Net, is used instead for its efficiency and simplicity, it demonstrates a notable improvement over the baseline models with an $F_1$ score of $0.8234$ when trained on data from publicly available sources. This study investigates the daily returns of cryptocurrencies from 2015 to 2020, analyzing their behavior in comparison to S&P 500 index returns. Initially, the Pearson correlation between cryptocurrencies and the S&P 500 index was negative, but surprisingly, it became positive in later years. To explain this phenomenon, the study considers various factors including the media's influence on cryptocurrency values and volatility, but finds no significant evidence supporting this theory. Alternatively, the study discovers that a key factor contributing to the increasing correlation is the growing presence of institutional investors in the cryptocurrency market. Furthermore, the study applies the multivariate GARCH model MV-MIDAS to investigate the cryptoeconomic factors affecting cryptocurrency volatility. Notably, the study finds that the price relative of Bitcoin and the Ethereum network's transaction volume are significant predictors of cryptocurrency volatility. Finally, the study finds that cryptocurrencies exhibit mean reversion characteristics in response to volatility, but only when certain conditions are met, including the price of Bitcoin exceeding 650 USD and the transaction volume of Ethereum exceeding 2 million per day. Overall, the study provides valuable insights into the behavior of cryptocurrencies in response to various market factors.

However, the frequency spectra of these waves are often described using a Maxwell-Von H\"{o}vel model, which has a different interpretation than the original Von H\"{o}vel model. This leads to conflicting interpretations of the turbulence measured during the first 10 missions by Parker Solar Probe. The District of Columbia's redistricting process presents unique challenges due to
requirements of maintaining fairness and representation.  Fairness in this context
refers to ensuring that districts are comprised of diverse populations, while
representation translates to compactness.  Although previous approaches focused on
minimizing political bias within districts, they often failed to address their
overall geographical consistency.  This research introduces a novel framework that
addresses both fairness and representation by building upon the principles of
Simulated Annealing.  Our results reveal that using Simulated Annealing yields more
fair districting plans than both iterative approaches and expert-drawn maps, with
better representation and compactness.  This innovative method provides a versatile
tool for creating districting plans that balance flexibility and consistency, and
can be applied to a wide range of geographical areas and political systems.  In
addition, this work includes an interactive website showcasing the districting
plans, accessible at \url{https://cs.gmu.edu/fair-dc/}.  Future developments
involve expanding the method to multi-member districts and exploring its
applicability to voting systems based on proportional representation.  In the
context of the District of Columbia's redistricting process, our approach yields a
base template that serves as a foundation for further refinements, with the
potential to produce significantly more transparent and accountable outcomes.  In
the long run, this method could be used in other areas to promote greater public
involvement and participation in the redistricting process.  In fact, our website
has already sparked the interest of local residents, with many using interactive
tools to create and share their own districting plans, and joining the broader
discussions on redistricting and voting systems.  Ultimately, the ultimate goal
is to utilize this method in partnership with other organizations dedicated to
promoting democracy and accountability, and to explore new ways of using
technologies to benefit the community.  In the spirit of public service, our team
is committed to serving the public and working in collaboration with other
stakeholders to develop innovative, yet socially responsible and accountable
technologies in the future.  Future research could be directed at developing
other innovative methods for addressing the complex issues facing us, and how
these technological innovations can be utilized in the public interest.  In the
meantime, our interactive website continues to receive visitors from the
community, who are using our approach to create their own redistricting plans

A key challenge in fabric defect detection lies in isolating defective sections from normal fabric using limited information. We address this issue by applying low-rank decomposition to fabric images, which helps extract relevant details. A novel approach incorporating the outside fabric gradient into the decomposition method enables precise separation of defects. A multi-stage fusion technique is employed to integrate information from different sources, enhancing the accuracy and robustness of defect detection. The effectiveness of our proposed method has been evaluated on two fabric defect detection datasets, outperforming existing techniques. Effective observation data is crucial for successful training in reinforcement learning scenarios, particularly when the agent's observations are generated dynamically based on its actions. Observations are action-dependent when the agent navigates a scene from different viewpoints. Researchers have leveraged this dependence to improve learning outcomes. This study proposes a novel optimization method that maximizes the mutual information between navigation actions and visual observations. This method does not require any prior knowledge and can be applied to any existing simulation environment. When tested in a basic observation task, training agents using this method resulted in faster learning compared to agents trained through entropy-based exploration. Additionally, when integrated into a more complex 3D navigation challenge, known as AntVenture, the method demonstrated significant benefits, leading to a 35% decrease in the number of training steps required to achieve the same level of performance. The effectiveness of our strategy is further enhanced by confirming a failure detection using multiple data sources. The success of this research opens up new possibilities for optimizing overall grid operation and enhancing resilience through proactive incident management. We introduce TextWorldExpress, a streamlined TextWorld variant used for automated text-based game intelligence, tailored for AI-powered agent training. TextWorld's complex data processing, semantic understanding, and narrative generation presented significant performance challenges, limiting simulations to one example at a time. We address the scale issue by creating a platform capable of processing thousands of game instances per second, and demonstrate the potential of TextWorldExpress through applications in natural language generation and processing, as well as the analysis of TextWorld datasets. TextWorldExpress is designed to support diverse use cases, is approximately 300 lines long, and is available for public use at https://github.com/uw-tac/toy-tf-cpp. We provide an efficient C++ implementation as a replacement for the original Python TextWorld version. TextWorldExpress is used as the backend for the ToY project, a fast, lightweight toolset for AI development. We discuss how to integrate TextWorldExpress with existing TextWorld codebases, highlighting a successful integration with the DeepTextWorld project. We also present a method for generating automatic game narratives in the style of existing TextWorld datasets, and showcase a self-modifying AI agent application built with TextWorldExpress. We conclude with a summary of TextWorldExpress benefits, potential future research pathways, and present an optimized C++ CMake project build CTOY. However, it has been found that this strategy can lead to sub-par performance when the model is then required to identify objects in familiar poses. A novel training method has been devised, known as Multi-Stage Training (MST), specifically to address this issue. MST alters the training data for each stage, forcing the model to learn essential features for different types of poses. A key transformation in the training data is the variation in scale, which helps the model learn robust features. MST's effectiveness has been tested on the dataset of SUN3D and has shown notable improvements in accuracy when recognizing objects in familiar poses. MST's code is available online for public use. The widespread availability of information on the internet has made it possible for one person's opinion to influence another's, especially when it comes to sensitive topics like vaccination. As a result, there has been a significant increase in the dissemination of vaccine-related misinformation through social media platforms, which has led to public confusion and a decreased willingness to get vaccinated. To combat this, there is a need for an analysis framework that can understand and measure the extent of the impact of this misinformation on public opinions. By utilizing natural language processing techniques, such as sentiment analysis and topic modeling, a new framework has been proposed to determine the perspective of social media users regarding vaccine-related misinformation. This research investigates the ergodic properties of the stochastic complex Ginzburg-Laudau equation (CGL$\beta)$ with a pure jump Levy noise and a linear drift. The state space is the entire complex plane, and it's known that it's ergodic when the drift is bounded and there's only standard Brownian motion involved. However, adding pure jump noise and overcoming obstacles in establishing a suitable Lyapunov function pose significant challenges. By constructing an appropriate Lyapunov function using a distance metric between two sets - one comprising quasi-normal states and the other, all states - this study demonstrates the ergodicity of CGL$\beta$ under both white and non-white jump noise conditions. An alternative verification method for the ergodicity is also explored using hybrid processes, which enables the proof of ergodic properties for a broader class of SDEs with jump noise. Furthermore, simulation examples validate the theoretical findings. Lastly, this study extends the ergodic results to the original complex Ginzburg-Laudau equation (CGL)$\beta)$ with a $1/\kappa$ decay condition on the noise, and an extension to a mean-field CGL equation ($\beta=2)$ is also presented. The key ideas and approaches applied here could be used to study the ergodic properties of other similar dynamical systems. Scientists assessing the habitability of exoplanets Earth-size and larger, orbiting similar-sized stars, typically rely on an Earth-like composition and structure. However, a recent study challenges this by using data on rocky planets, including those discovered by NASA's Kepler mission, to build a more accurate model of a typical Earth-sized starplanet. By employing statistical analysis of planetary densities and considering the composition of host stars, the study reconstructs the density distribution of these planets. Compared to Earth, the typical planet in question has a surprisingly different internal structure, with a larger mantle and less dense core, and its overall composition is also distinct, with a greater abundance of volatile elements and less refractory metals. These findings imply that the criteria for gauging a planet's habitability should be more flexible than previously thought, and that future telescopes, such as the James Webb Space Telescope, should look for signs of life on smaller, less dense Earth-sized planets, rather than those with a high mass similar to that of our own planet. Additionally, the study highlights the necessity of further observational efforts, such as the characterization of tiny planets and their gravitational interactions with their hosts, in order to gain a better understanding of a typical Earth-sized exoplanet's characteristics. Lastly, the study suggests that studies of rare, super-Earth planets, like those with a high mass similar to three times that of our own planet, should also be given priority in the search for life in our galaxy.

Leverageing local autoencoders allows for the learning of meaningful features from CSI, but this process is hindered by noise and necessitates repeated encoding and decoding. In 1990, Erdos proposed a hypothesis: every bipartite structure with a maximum degree of 3 can be assigned a strong edge coloring with a maximum of 5 colors. This hypothesis has been validated for certain classes of bipartite graphs with specific properties but not all. Currently, the minimum strong edge coloring number for bipartite graphs with a maximum degree of 3 remains unknown. We present an example of a bipartite graph with a maximum degree of 4 that requires at least 7 colors, and we propose a condition that, if satisfied, guarantees a specific coloring type for these graphs. We demonstrate that if the vertices of these graphs have an equal number of connections, and the resulting graphs have no complete subgraphs with 4, 5 or 6 edges, a strong edge coloring with a maximum of 5 colors can be applied, thus confirming Erdos' hypothesis for these specific cases. Furthermore, we note that if the hypothesis is confirmed for a particular class of graphs with specific characteristics, it is automatically confirmed for a different class of graphs with similar characteristics. We also present an example of a graph with a maximum degree of 3 that confirms the lower bound for bipartite graphs with a maximum degree of 2 plus 1, and we propose a condition that, if satisfied, guarantees a specific coloring type for these graphs. This paper addresses this issue by presenting inexact policy iteration, a modified version of policy iteration that uses a general iterative method to solve the Bellman operator's equation, similar to how inexact Newton methods work in matrix-based optimization. By testing this approach on large MDPs with 10,000 to 1,000,000 states, the results show a significant speedup of 10 to 100 times over traditional policy iteration, with comparable value functionality. The code for inexact policy iteration is available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/cdpau/inexact-policy-iteration. In particular, a Python implementation can be found at https://github.com/cdpau/inexact-policy-iteration.py. In contrast, the C++ implementation at https://github.com/cdpau/inexact-policy-iteration-cpp achieves a 5-fold speedup with the same functionality. Both repositories are maintained under the terms of the permissive MIT License. Additionally, this paper introduces iterative policy iteration, a variant of inexact policy iteration, as well as provides theoretical guarantees based on the contraction property of the Bellman operator. The numerical experiments confirm its convergence in both linear and nonlinear MDP settings. Furthermore, the code for iterative policy iteration can be found at https://github.com/cdpau/iterative-policy-iteration. In particular, the Python implementation at https://github.com/cdpau/iterative-policy-iteration.py, as well as the C++ implementation at https://github.com/cdpau/iterative-policy-iteration-cpp, demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in solving large-scale MDPs within a specified error margin. In contrast, standard policy iteration is unable to achieve this goal, even with a much smaller error margin. To promote reproducibility, the code for inexact policy iteration can be found at https://github.com/cdpau/inexact-policy-iteration. We demonstrate a lower bound on the learnability of radius-$R$ concept classes using simple binary spaces and sample sizes less than or equal to $R^2$. Furthermore, we establish an upper bound where the influence of the radius significantly decreases as the sample size grows, reaching O(log R/optimality) with sufficient samples. Our findings indicate that the radius of the query set essentially dictates the upper limit for the distribution-free robust learning, except for the case where the concept class comprises two concepts. We also obtain an optimal algorithm with an optimality multiplicative factor of O(\log R), along with a novel approach for two concepts that differs from both the standard agnostic PAC learning algorithm and the existing sample-efficient query set reduction techniques. We prove that our results are essentially tight, both for the upper bound and the lower bound analysis. Additionally, we obtain an upper limit for the influence of the radius in the setting of adversarial robust learning, where the concept class is represented by a half-space, by reducing it to the standard adversarial robust learning case, resulting in an optimality multiplicative factor of O(\log R). Our study examines how ratios of particles change as the scale of collisions varies from low to high energies in gold and lead collisions at the Large Hadron Collider. Our analysis reveals a distinct trend, where these ratios gradually shift from being proportional to the number of participant nucleons in smaller collisions to resemble a quark-gluon plasma state in larger collisions. To gain further insight, we compared these results to two sophisticated models: the EPOS LHC model, which incorporates a pre-equilibrium quark-gluon phase, and the QGSP-based EPOS LHC model, which includes shock wave interactions. Surprisingly, both models effectively replicate the observed trends, despite differing in their initial stages. Specifically, the S+Au system was found to exhibit an agreement within 1σ, while the Pb+Pb system showed a closer match within 2σ. By considering various alternatives to the EPOS LHC models, we found that the models which only involve equilibrium quark-gluon phases fail to reproduce the observed particle ratios as accurately as the models suggesting a non-equilibrium quark-gluon phase. Furthermore, the models which incorporate an initial quark-gluon phase fail to reproduce the observed delay in the transition of the particle ratios from being participant-scaled to hydrodynamic scaling. Additionally, we observed that the models which use shock wave interactions to convert quark phases to hadronic phases succeed in reproducing the observed particle ratios more effectively than the models which use static equilibrium phases. To illustrate the origin of this success, we applied the hydrodynamic navigation algorithm to the phase space distributions obtained from the EPOS LHC models. This rigorous testing of the EPOS LHC models provided strong evidence that the pre-equilibrium quark-gluon phase in smaller collisions indeed facilitates the rapid formation of a quark-gluon plasma state in larger collisions. Lastly, our study highlights the crucial importance of integrating non-equilibrium and equilibrium dynamics to achieve an in-depth comprehension of the phase transitions in high-energy collisions. Our discovery may prompt the development of new initial conditions for quark-gluon plasma dynamics. The development of large-scale multi-input and multi-output systems has given rise to a significant issue in dealing with costly and time-consuming output regulation. In this research, multiple output regression problems are broken down into a series of smaller tasks through nonparametric clustering methods that incorporate only a single model per group. This overcomplete dictionary of task-specific models is then shared across all groups, with their numbers determined in advance through a pre-defined metric. We show that this dictionary-learning approach yields superior performance and reduced memory requirements compared to treating each group as an independent regression problem. Furthermore, this method's effectiveness extends to dealing with noisy clusters, output correlations, and imbalanced data sets. The proposed model is evaluated on two real-world datasets, with the results consistently outperforming a comparative baseline method and demonstrating significant memory savings. The code for this model is available online. \\

Existing models can accurately replicate real-world performance by utilizing virtual machines, yet they lack the speed needed for comprehensive testing, forcing developers to emulate years of usage within a single testing cycle. In contrast, other models focus on soundness but may fail to adequately replicate complex ordering patterns seen in real-world applications. To address this issue, we present McMini, a multi-threaded model checker that directly analyzes McMini programs within a virtual machine environment. By optimizing key components, like path splitting and path expansion, McMini enables the efficient replication of complex ordering patterns, outperforming existing solutions by at least 10 times in multi-threaded test cases. As a result, McMini enables the thorough examination of multi-threaded code under diverse scenarios, facilitating the extensive testing required to ensure the reliability of virtual machines and, more broadly, the widespread adoption of multi-threaded programming. In a practical application, McMini was used to identify and fix two previously unreported memory leak issues in the standard Java runtime environment. Mobile messaging apps have transformed the way people engage with each other and consume information. According to a survey by the Global System for Mobile Communications, 80% of global users access the internet through their mobile devices, with apps like WhatsApp reaching a user base of over two billion. This immense popularity has enabled apps to shape public opinion and disseminate information on a massive scale. However, this power also comes with the responsibility of preventing the spread of misinformation, which can pose serious threats to public safety and health. To address this challenge, WhatsApp has launched a feature to encourage users to fact-check suspicious messages before sending them to groups. Although, the success of this initiative is limited to messages received from individual contacts. To enhance its effectiveness, WhatsApp could incorporate an AI-driven tool that scans all incoming messages, flagging potentially false information for user verification. This vision paper outlines the implementation of such a tool, which relies on natural language processing and machine learning, using Twitter's bird influenza vaccine drive as a real-world case study. The study reveals that relying on human curators for verifying false information is inefficient, slow, and cannot keep pace with the high velocity of group messages on WhatsApp. By employing an AI-driven tool, WhatsApp can promptly detect potential misinformation in a substantial portion of its user base, preventing its spread until further investigations can confirm its validity. This vision paper presents a feasibility study of such a tool, which requires significant computational resources but demonstrates the potential of reducing the spread of false information on WhatsApp by a substantial margin within a minute. This implementation not only relies on WhatsApp but can also be adapted to other mobile apps receiving suspicious messages, including SMS. Experimental findings demonstrate that this AI-driven tool can process a significant portion of group messages within WhatsApp, determining their credibility at rates up to 98.5% with an overall accuracy of 88.5% across different classes. This research presents a rigorous evaluation of the proposed WhatsApp verification system, which successfully detects false information, verifies real-time events, and confirms the inoculation status of individuals. This study's contributions include proposing a comprehensive solution to the WhatsApp verification problem, conducting thorough evaluations using relevant datasets, and validating the efficacy of language models in verifying misinformation.   - The properties of supergravity as a group theoretical object, specifically in relation to the exceptional groups E6 and E7.

  - The potential of supergravity in testing theories of quantum gravity, including loop quantum gravity and string theory.

  - The capacity of supergravity to address holographic convergence and cosmology.

This study examines the interconnection between commodity trading advisors and traders who exploit short-term market reversals. Our analysis indicates that CTAs benefit financially from working with correction-seeking traders, who in turn earn a living by capitalizing on CTA-generated market fluctuations. A key finding reveals that the connection between these two groups is sustained through a mutual benefit. In particular, by cooperating, CTA-led trading firms can maintain a diverse client base, attract additional investors, and enhance their market competitiveness. To facilitate their collaborative efforts, we propose the Integration-Theorem, which sets out specific requirements for a successful integration of correction-seeking and direction-setting strategies within a single investment framework. Our empirical validation of the proposed theorem shows promising results, suggesting that integration can lead to significant market gains for CTA firms. By adopting our theoretical model, we demonstrate that such firms can increase their profit by partnering with correction-seeking traders, who in turn can boost their earnings by capitalizing on the market fluctuations created by CTA-led direction-setting initiatives. Ultimately, our research provides a foundation for further studies on the integrated trading dynamics between commodity trading advisors and short-term reversal traders. Additionally, our findings highlight the potential for a more unified view of market participants, including both advisors and traders, in their respective roles. For example, our study reveals that some renowned commodity trading advisors are, in effect, specialized versions of integrated traders, with a focus on setting the market direction through a series of well-placed trades, while simultaneously incorporating correction-seeking strategies to generate additional trading opportunities. By recognizing this shared focus, the financial industry may come to view commodity trading advisors and short-term reversal traders as two interconnected elements of a single, unified market participant – the integrated trader. As such, we propose that the term "Integrated Trader" more accurately reflects the diverse range of market strategies employed by both advisors and traders, thereby providing a more comprehensive classification system for market participants. Our research demonstrates that, through cooperation, market participants can develop adaptive strategies that capitalize on the market fluctuations created by their collaborative efforts, leading to enhanced financial outcomes. Ultimately, our study contributes to a broader understanding of the market dynamics between commodity trading advisors and short-term reversal traders, presenting a unique opportunity for further investigation into their integrated market dynamics. Byempirically validating our proposed theorem, we provide a foundation for modeling their cooperative behavior, market fluctuations, and the resulting financial implications of their collaborative activities. This study analyzes various aspects of local news reporting on COVID-19 across Germany using publicly accessible data from the German National Library of Science and Technology. By processing and combining different datasets, the study achieves three key objectives. Firstly, it determines the volume of local COVID-related news based on time and geographic location, allowing for comparisons between different regions. Secondly, the study categorizes and quantifies the content of these news items to reveal underlying patterns. Finally, the study correlates local news coverage with official government statistics on COVID infections and deaths to investigate any potential relationships. Overall, the study's findings indicate that local news volume and content were primarily influenced by the severity of the pandemic in a specific area, whereas the type of content covered showed connections to cultural and economic characteristics of each location, which often took longer to respond to the pandemic. The research also reveals that local news coverage had a positive correlation with official government pandemic statistics in some cases but not all. Based on these outcomes, the study proposes several policy measures to enhance the pandemic response in Germany. The study's methods and findings offer a blueprint for evaluating local news coverage in other pandemic situations and other societal crises. The method of systematic extrapolation can be seen as an approach to implicitly count beyond initial training limits, with its effectiveness relying on developing generalized patterns that can be applied beyond the scope of initial data. In line with this, our research focuses on evaluating neural network-based extrapolation methods using datasets from the field of particle physics, with an aim to imply their limitations in implying their limitations in extending initial training counts. To achieve this, we utilized four particle physics simulations that model the behavior of high-energy particle collisions, training neural networks on varying amounts of data, and examining how well their performance generalizes to different conditions. Our findings show that while implicit counting methods can achieve reasonable accuracy within initial training bounds, their performance severely deteriorates beyond that threshold, underscoring the need for explicit counting techniques and a reevaluation of extrapolation methods in their ability to extend initial training limits. Furthermore, our research highlights potential pitfalls in using extrapolation as a means to assess the impact of systematic uncertainties on neural network training. Lastly, our work emphasizes the importance of directly addressing the challenges of explicit counting, and outlines a promising direction for future research in this area. As deepfakes become more plausible, they are more likely to induce significant effects on their viewers, whether by persuading them of a particular idea, compromising their trust in information, or influencing their behavior. Given the potential harm that deepfakes can cause, it is essential to detect them in a manner that is both effective and fair. This study proposes an approach that focuses on inducing strong emotional responses in viewers as a means of identifying potential deepfakes. Our initial findings indicate that deepfakes typically elicit a stronger emotional response from viewers compared to authentic content. To capitalize on this difference, we suggest utilizing emotional analysis as a reliable method for classifying deepfakes. This study presents a novel technique known as EmoClass, which incorporates emotional classification into the classification process of deepfakes. EmoClass leverages representations from pre-trained visual and audio models, combined with an emotional classifier that is also pre-trained, to classify media in a manner that is both effective and unbiased. Our experiments demonstrate that EmoClass exhibits superior performance on various models of deepfakes. This study offers a thorough examination of EmoClass, highlighting its advantages, as well as identifying potential challenges and limitations, and suggesting possible avenues for improvement. Additionally, the EmoClass system provides users with a detailed explanation of the media classified as deepfakes, underscoring its importance in terms of practical applications and public trust. Ultimately, the EmoClass approach represents a reliable and fair solution to detecting deepfakes, as well as a viable means of mitigating their harmful effects.
